England captaincy could be what Root needs - Vaughan

BBC News Thu, 30 Jul 2026 16:20:36 GMT

Joe Root returns to the England captaincy having previously led them to 27 Test wins in 65 matches

Former skipper Michael Vaughan has said the England Test captaincy could be "exactly what Joe Root needs".

Speaking on the Test Match Special podcast, Vaughan said the 35-year-old's return to the role, having led the team from 2017 to 2022, might prove to be motivation in the later stages of his career.

"I just wonder from Joe's perspective if he needed this to get that real enthusiasm to get up every morning to play Test match cricket," said Vaughan.

"The amount of cricket that he's played, I just wonder whether he needed this little trigger, this little motivational tool.

"He hasn't got that many of his close friends in the team any more, a lot of his team-mates have retired or moved on, so maybe this is exactly what Joe Root needs as well."

Root returns to the captaincy under the charge of interim head coach Marcus Trescothick after Brendon McCullum was sacked, before New Zealander Stephen Fleming takes over the Test leadership for this winter's tour of South Africa.

He stepped down as captain in 2022 after a 10-wicket loss to West Indies, their ninth match without a win, citing the "toll" and "impact" the role had on him.

However, Vaughan stated he believed Root had been dealt a "dodgy hand" during his time as Test captain.

"Around the time he was appointed England were trying to win the 50-over World Cup and all the England eggs were put in the white-ball basket," said Vaughan.

"Then Covid struck. None of us would know how hard it would be to captain in a Covid time - Joe had to do that.

"That Caribbean tour where it came to an end, it looked like a job that was a little bit too far for him. He's a little bit older, a little bit wiser. I think Stephen Fleming will help out with a lot of the stuff that some captains get drained by - organising the dressing room and making sure the tactical side of the team is in good order.

"I just think in terms of his motivation and in terms of what is left for Joe Root to achieve in the game, of course there's a few runs to get past Sachin [Tendulkar's all-time Test run-scoring record] but if he can be an Ashes winner next year, a world leader in runs he's scored in Test cricket, you can't ask for a more perfect career."

Stumped podcast: New era for England as Stephen Fleming appointed Test coach

Stephen Fleming has coached Southern Brave in The Hundred and has coached in every season of the Indian Premier League (IPL) since 2010

Fleming has been appointed on a four-year deal that will mean he coaches England in the next two Ashes series, and Vaughan said managing director Rob Key has selected a "very experienced" option.

Former England Test coach Andy Flower was initially linked with the role, but Royal Challengers Bengaluru and London Spirit coach ruled himself out of the process.

Fleming joins after leaving Chennai Super Kings this month, having coached the Indian Premier League (IPL) franchise for the past nine seasons.

"Andy Flower, I think from what I've read is the one that they wanted. He turned that down so it was like 'OK, how do we get the next best?'" Vaughan said of Fleming.

"Some will say he's not coached in red-ball cricket but you've got a very experienced manager, very experienced coach who's been around the modern game with Chennai Super Kings over the course of the last few years.

"He was a very, very good captain back in the day, a very good tactician, renowned for being a really good man-manager.

"Having McCullum still as the white-ball coach and then having someone coaching the Test team who doesn't know McCullum, that could have been really tricky.

"I think Stephen Fleming has been brought in for that reason - he's obviously very close to McCullum.

"They needed someone who could work with McCullum because someone that doesn't know Baz and his style, I think it could have got very, very messy."

Fleming, who retired from playing in 2009, has a wealth of experience in Test cricket, making 111 appearances for New Zealand, scoring 7,172 runs with an average of 40.06 in the middle order.

McCullum was known for promoting an aggressive form of cricket, dubbed Bazball by fans and the media, but Vaughan said Fleming will have to make changes to England's style and technique.

"I'm kind of sick and tired of talking about England's style of play. The style of play I want to see is England winning," Vaughan added.

"Whatever that style is on that given day, session, hour, England have to play the right style of cricket that wins games of cricket.

"We can only talk about talent and the gulf of talent in English cricket for so long - they've got to start winning games of cricket and winning trophies now.

"The one thing this Test team needs is coaching the technical side of batting.

"How many of them can look themselves in the mirror and when Michael Neser, Matt Henry, Scott Boland bowls that good length just on or around that off stump, can play a controlled forward defence shot?

"They won't like saying it and they won't like talking about technique, but technique wins Test match cricket and the technical side of England's players and batting has been found wanting.

"So it's all right putting a good leader of the group, but I also think they need one or two changes in the backroom team to make sure these players are getting really well coached as well."

Burnham says he told Trump UK will be pragmatic about North Sea oil

BBC News Thu, 30 Jul 2026 16:19:08 GMT

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he told US President Donald Trump he would take a "pragmatic approach" to the issue of North Sea oil and gas.

Trump has long urged the UK to increase drilling and claimed that Burnham had pledged to "open up the North Sea" in their first phone call together.

Asked about the president's comments, the new prime minister said: "There is a resource there. When people are struggling - you can't ignore that and hence me indicating that to the president."

Burnham has faced pressure from some trade unions, industry figures and some of his own Labour MPs to back increased drilling in the North Sea.

In its 2024 general election manifesto, Labour promised not to issue new licences for drilling but said it would honour existing ones.

As energy secretary in Sir Keir Starmer's government, Ed Miliband was a staunch supporter of Labour's manifesto position. He has previously described the licence issued to Rosebank, Britain's largest untapped oil and gas field, as "climate vandalism".

Miliband is now the foreign secretary in Burnham's government.

Although the government has not made any announcements on the issue, Trump has praised what he perceives as a change of stance by the UK government.

In a social media post, published the day before Burnham became prime minister, Trump wrote: "The People of Aberdeen, in Scotland, are dancing in the streets because the new Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has stated that he will be opening up, all the way, the invaluable North Sea Oil!"

This week, when asked about his conversation with Burnham, Trump said: "He said he's going to open up North Sea oil.

"If he does that, you're going to be a wealthy country."

He later added: "You buy a lot of your energy, as you know, from the North Sea. You buy from Norway and Norway gets it from the North Sea... Norway's got trillions of dollars in the bank."

"Scotland has a better part of the North Sea."

Asked about Trump's comments, Burnham said: "I indicated in the phone call that we had a week last Monday that I would take a pragmatic approach when it comes to the North Sea, and that is my intention as we go forward from here."

In response, Green Party leader Zack Polanski said: "Our country is burning. Crops are failing. Thousands have been killed by extreme heat.

"Allowing new oil and gas drilling in the North Sea will worsen the climate breakdown putting more lives at risk and doing untold damage to our economy.

"It's not too late for Burnham to do the right thing and commit to leaving dangerous fossil fuels in the ground."

The Conservatives and Reform have urged the government to approve more drilling in the North Sea, arguing it would reduce energy prices.

Last year, Tory Party leader Kemi Badenoch said it would be "absurd" for the UK to leave "vital resources untapped".

Some Labour MPs have expressed unease about more drilling, with Rachael Maskell urging the government to "follow the climate science because we have got a climate emergency".

Simon Francis, from the End Fuel Poverty Coalition, said: "No household struggling with their energy bills will see a penny come off by drilling more from the North Sea.

"Gas is sold at the global market prices, so whatever is pumped out is sold to the highest bidder, not handed to British billpayers at a discount."

Sir Keir's government had already made concessions, allowing "tie-backs" - production in unlicensed areas close to or connected to already licensed areas.

Currently, the debate over North Sea drilling has focused on two oil and gas fields - Rosebank and Jackdaw, located in Scotland.

In 2022 and 2023, regulators approved drilling at the sites, but that was overturned in 2025 following a legal challenge.

The legal process is ongoing, but the government will at some point have to decide whether to permit companies to produce oil in the two areas.

Other oil and gas licences have been approved in recent years but remain largely undeveloped.

If he wanted to encourage more drilling in the North Sea, Burnham could also opt to scrap the Energy Profits Levy, also known as the windfall tax.

The levy is due to be replaced in 2030 by another windfall tax, which operators prefer because it's only triggered when prices are high and falls back when they are low.

Thousands evacuated in Crete as wildfires threaten tourist resorts

BBC News Thu, 30 Jul 2026 16:04:53 GMT

Thousands of people have been evacuated on the Greek island of Crete as wildfires fanned by strong winds menace tourist resorts and villages.

Two firefighters died on the island on Wednesday when they became trapped while tackling a fire near Krya Vrysi in the Rethymno region. A third firefighter died on the Greek mainland, near the port town of Gytheio in the Peloponnese.

As gusts reached 125km/h (77mph) on the island, around 8,000 people were evacuated from their homes overnight but were later allowed to return.

Greece is among many European countries facing devastating fires and drought.

Several fires have continued to burn in Spain and Portugal, although Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared an end to the national emergency for wildfires in the Ávila and Madrid regions.

In south-west France some residents have been able to return to their homes after a major wildfire in the Gironde region.

The fire raging in Crete broke out in the Rethymno region on Wednesday and has since spread rapidly, destroying homes and agricultural land. It remains one of the biggest fires currently active on the island and is still burning out of control.

There was no clear picture of the destruction so far, Rethymno's deputy regional governor Maria Lioni said, adding that containing the fire was the main priority.

Lioni described Wednesday as a "dark day" for the region and said gusts overnight reached up to 11 on the Beaufort scale - a wind force categorised as "violent" - fanning the flames and hampering containment efforts.

Some of those evacuated in Rethymno were moved into a temporary shelter.

"I was watching the fire and I just didn't know what to do. It was like a volcano down the side of the mountain," said Bianca Boorer, who was visiting the coastal resort of Agios Pavlos with her mother on a yoga retreat.

"The bar staff told us you need to get in cars and drive away but only two people had cars. Eleven people tried to get into one tiny car and the car my mum was in was nearer to the fire," she told the BBC's Your Voice.

"The place we had breakfast in has burnt down. Agios Pavlos hotel has burnt down, the place we did yoga in has also burnt down."

The fire broke out during one of Crete's busiest months for tourism. Hundreds of firefighters have been deployed to the region to battle the blaze.

Hellenic Fire Service chief Theodoros Vagias expressed his condolences for the two firefighters who died on Wednesday, naming them as 58-year-old Emmanouil Stratidakis and Pantelis Diamantakis, 25.

Both will be buried on Thursday, the statement added.

Meanwhile, wildfires have erupted in the north-western Spanish provinces of Zamora and León, not far from the border with Portugal, with more than 1,000 people evacuated.

Five people were injured in a fire in the eastern town of Valpaços in Portugal, according to local reports.

A major fire that consumed an area in excess of 66,000 hectares to the west of the Spanish capital, Madrid, and caused tens of thousands of people to be evacuated has stopped spreading, allowing some residents to return home.

As he ended the national emergency in the area, Pedro Sánchez urged "extreme caution" during the fourth heatwave of the summer in Spain.

The fire in Ávila, which has burned more than 43,000 hectares over the past week, is now considered the largest recorded wildfire in Spanish history.

A small amount of rain fell near Bordeaux in France on Thursday, raising hopes that the Gironde wildfire that has burned an area larger than the US city of Detroit and destroyed 240 homes might soon be over.

The region's fire service said it was "reasonably optimistic" given that the fire had not grown in size since the weekend.

Around 84,000 of the 220,000 displaced residents were allowed to return home on Thursday, according to French reports.

It is estimated that more than 90,000 hectares of land across France have burnt this year - higher than any other year on record, according to data from the European Forest Fire Information Service.

In Spain, more than 200,000 hectares have burnt in 2026 – roughly five times above the average for the time of year. The area of land ravaged in Portugal is also higher than usual for this point in July.

The European fire season typically extends into August and September – and with more hot weather on the way in the coming days, these figures are likely to keep rising.

Most wildfires are started by humans, whether deliberately or accidentally, but climate change is strengthening weather conditions conducive to fires spreading.

Last winter was mild and wet, encouraging vegetation growth, which has then dried out in successive heatwaves, generating tinder-dry fuel for wildfires.

Some researchers have also warned that the Mediterranean's forests and scrublands are not being properly managed – leaving plenty of vegetation as fuel for fires.

Forecasters say fire-prone conditions are expected to spread towards central Europe, with Greece and Turkey among the countries worst affected.

In Turkey, hundreds of homes have also been evacuated but the majority of fires that have broken out mainly in the south have been brought under control, authorities say.

Challenging times ahead for Newcastle - Shearer

BBC News Thu, 30 Jul 2026 15:10:54 GMT

Thank you, Eddie Howe. You gave me the best day of my life as a Newcastle fan.

Whatever the reasons are for him leaving the club, I think every supporter of my age or younger - and I am 55 - would say the same.

Eddie will always be a legend in the eyes of the Geordie public for ending our long wait for a major trophy with that epic day he gave us at Wembley when we won the Carabao Cup in 2025.

I had craved that moment for my entire life. I had been to Wembley before as a Toon player and I had been there before as a Toon fan, and we'd all had the same feeling of walking away empty-handed.

He will be remembered for changing that, and we have to say a massive thank you for everything else he has done since he took charge in November 2021, when the club were 19th in the Premier League, five points adrift of safety after 11 games.

Eddie kept us up that year, then finished fourth, seventh and fifth in the next three seasons, with some amazing nights in the Champions League along the way. He did a brilliant job.

The best way of showing how far we have come under him is that we finished 12th last season and it was a disappointment, but I would not blame him for that, either.

What happened last summer massively hindered Newcastle, with Alexander Isak leaving and the club missing out on their main transfer targets.

Unfortunately, that trend has continued this year. I would not be surprised if it influenced Eddie's thinking about whether to stay or go, and it also makes me worry about what will happen next.

Speaking purely as a fan, I think we have to get ready for a tough season and some very challenging times ahead.

Howe celebrates Newcastle's victory over Liverpool in the 2025 Carabao Cup final - the club's first major trophy since winning the Inter-Cities Fairs Cup in 1969 and first domestic success since the 1955 FA Cup

The timing of Eddie's exit is the biggest surprise for me - three weeks into pre-season, and with only three weeks to go until the Premier League starts again.

I don't know exactly what has gone on behind the scenes for this to happen now but I guess, from his point of view, he was seeing his best players being sold - first Isak, then Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali this summer - and with speculation over captain Bruno Guimaraes' future too.

He has probably thought it was a tough enough job anyway, but it is just getting tougher.

You cannot keep on selling your best players and then hope to be in contention at the top of the table - I hope I'm wrong but it is probably inevitable that Bruno will be next to leave.

Whatever Bruno's intentions were before, when Eddie was in charge, then he must look now and think well, we are selling our stars and now the manager, who he clearly had a great rapport with, has gone too.

It's not just the players leaving that is a bad look, it is seeing a series of attempted signings fail to get over the line as well.

Hugo Ekitike, Johan Manzambi and Victor Munoz all went to Liverpool or Aston Villa ahead of Newcastle in the past 12 months and now it also looks like James Trafford has chosen Leeds instead.

That's something else that Eddie has maybe looked at, because there has to be a reason why Newcastle are not getting so many of their targets.

Losing the manager on top of all this is a huge blow, especially a high-calibre one like Eddie who is going to get some huge job offers from home and abroad off the back of his achievements at St James' Park.

I think even someone really experienced would find the situation a difficult one and Matthias Jaissle, who is expected to get the job, is only 38.

While he has been successful with Al-Ahli in Saudi Arabia, you cannot really compare that to working in the Premier League, which is a completely different beast.

Matthias Jaissle has managed clubs in Austria and Saudi Arabia

Take a step back and, whether we like it or not, we can all see what is happening with all the ins and outs at Newcastle. Whatever statements come out of the club, it is clear the landscape has changed.

It is a changing football club - in terms of its owners' aims and ambitions and their transfer strategy, which all seem massively different to the way they were even three years ago.

Back then the sky seemed to be the limit, and the talk was about competing with the very best.

Now, the approach seems to be to sell their best players and replace them with younger, hungry and up-and-coming prospects. If it was that easy to do it successfully and still compete at the top of the table, then everyone would do it - but it isn't.

The club's spending always had to comply with the Premier League's profitability and sustainability rules but it still felt like the plan was to battle it out for silverware every season.

Go back to the summer of 2023, when Newcastle had just finished fourth and added Tonali, Harvey Barnes and Tino Livramento to a squad already containing Isak, Gordon and Bruno.

It felt like they were ready to challenge for everything, and capable of beating everyone. Howe had made them a horrible team to play against, in the nicest possible way.

Three years on, much of that team has gone and now the manager has too, but it is the whole model which feels the most different.

The goalposts have moved massively from where the club said they wanted to get to, compared to where they are now.

When we won the Carabao Cup, I was hoping it was just the start of something very special, but it seems a lot has changed since then.

Alan Shearer was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Why do parts of England and Wales keep falling into drought?

BBC News Thu, 30 Jul 2026 14:54:42 GMT

More than half of England and the whole of Wales has been declared to be in drought this week - the third such event over the past five years.

Farmers have described suffering from reduced yields and being forced to harvest earlier, and field fires increasing.

The drought comes despite winter bringing above average rainfall, and reservoirs still close to expected levels for this time of year.

So why are parts of the country struggling to get hold of water?

There is no single definition of drought, according to the Environment Agency (EA), it depends on who is impacted, the availability of water and its use.

A drought can affect things including the environment, farming, or the water supply - what response the government and industry take depends on what the drought is affecting.

Possible measures include rescuing and relocating fish, increased business checks on water usage, and redistribution of water supplies.

The sources of our water for drinking and farming vary significantly across the country.

The three main sources of water are rivers, reservoirs and from deep underground - groundwater.

Reservoirs have seen some decline during this hot weather period due to a combination of low rainfall and higher demand from households.

There are a number of temporary use bans - or hosepipe bans - in place affecting around 20 million people.

This is seen as a precautionary measure when reservoir levels are dropping but demand remains higher.

But currently, nearly all water companies are at drought level 1 - Anglian is the exception at 2 - out of a possible maximum of 4.

It is rivers and groundwater levels which have been significantly impacted by a sudden drop in rainfall.

South East England relies more heavily on groundwater - where rainfall is stored beneath the surface in pore spaces and fractures in the rock.

Chalk areas across the country - from the Yorkshire Wolds to the Wessex Downs - are all reporting levels either at expected or below normal for this time of year, with the Cotswolds particularly struggling.

But these groundwater stores "respond more slowly to changes in the climate than rivers, which is why they provide a useful buffer during periods of drought", said Prof Alan MacDonald of the British Geological Survey.

Wales has received just 8% of its average rainfall so far this month. England has received 7% of its average, with that figure as low as 1% across southern England. Therefore, groundwater levels are expected to drop even further still.

The low rainfall and high temperatures, which increase evaporation rates, have hit rivers hardest.

The EA said nearly 80% of England's rivers are seeing flows below normal or lower - the River Thames at Reading has recorded its lowest level on record.

Farmers source water for their crops and livestock over summer from a combination of stored winter rainfall on site, and by extracting it from natural sources - a process called abstraction.

This can be from groundwater or from surface water, like rivers and streams. So, as levels drop, this becomes a serious issue.

Eleanor Gilbert told Radio 4's Today programme that the hot weather has been "very tough" on her farm in Berkshire, which has recorded "less than 30mm of rain since the end of March".

Moisture content has to be at a specific level for harvesting different crops.

Gilbert said they have been harvesting at 03:00 BST to bring the moisture up, as at that time of day it's cooler and water condenses.

But the dry conditions caused by the hot weather have prevented the grain from swelling. It means the farm's yield is down to almost half of what it was the previous year.

The EA and Natural Resource Wales grant abstraction licences to farms, but when water levels drop they can impose what is called a "hands-off flow restriction".

This means farms are prevented from abstracting water, this is to protect the environment.

There are currently 1,353 of these restrictions in place. The EA has also warned that voluntary restrictions may be put in place next month - when farmers are asked to reduce their volumes of water use, only irrigate at night or on certain days of the week.

Ben Andrews, a mixed organic farmer in north Herefordshire, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he has had an abstraction licence restriction since the start of the month.

"We will have paid for the plants, paid for the labour, if we don't get to pick any of them then it's investment that's lost."

Even with these measures in place there have been 61 environmental incidents due to the drought, such as reported fish deaths which, although lower than last year, are rapidly increasing and thought to be underestimated.

Climate change is raising global temperatures, which in the UK is expected to lead to drier summers and more intense and longer lasting heatwaves - both of which could contribute to lower river and groundwater levels.

On Wednesday, the National Drought Group - which includes regulators, the government, the Met Office, water companies, farmers, the Canal & River Trust, anglers and conservation experts - held a briefing with Water Minister Emma Hardy.

The Department for Environment Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said the group reviewed the impact of the drought in England, the country's preparedness and response to it.

Hardy said: "We're delivering long-term change in the water industry and driving record investments in infrastructure, including nine new reservoirs.

"We expect water companies to follow their drought plans, to go further and faster to reduce leaks, and to ensure supplies are not disrupted even in the driest of weather."

In May, the Lords Environment and Climate Change Committee called on the government to undertake a series of measures, including investing in drought data collection and sharing, and increasing water storage by ensuring large reservoirs are built.

Baroness Sheehan, the committee chair, said: "England is at risk of sleepwalking into serious water scarcity if the government does not act now to safeguard the water system."

Meanwhile, the National Farmers' Union for England and Wales (NFU) has called on the government to change the planning system for water.

Scientists have said that climate change is likely to bring wetter and milder winters. The NFU said abstraction licences should be made more flexible to enable more water to be taken during these wetter winter months ahead of any dry summer spells.

It has also called for applications for building on site reservoirs to be sped up.

Alongside the current pressures on the system there is extra water demand expected in the coming years from new houses, data centres and other sectors which could further squeeze supplies.

"We need to invest for the long term, in new water storage facilities, whether it's at the local level supporting farmers or at a large scale with the water companies themselves being allowed to build reservoirs," Sir John Armitt, former chairman of the National Infrastructure Commission, told Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday.

He said for a long time governments have resisted building new reservoirs on the basis other solutions could be found, but the recent weather extremes the UK has been experiencing "have really caught people out".

There has been no major reservoir completed in England since 1992. Sir Jon Cunliffe, former Bank of England deputy governor, reviewed the sector last year and concluded that there had been "underinvestment" - blaming both the water industry and regulators.

Sir John Armitt also said that the industry must also tackle leakage and usage.

"That's beholden on all of us to try to reduce the amount we use, and we could save a similar amount if we could get down to the levels of Denmark who use about 100 litres per person a day."

The average use per person in the UK is around 140 litres.

Water UK, which represents the industry, said at the time, in response: "Everyone agrees the system has not been working.... fundamental change has been long overdue."

There are currently two reservoirs pencilled for completion in 2036 and the 2040s, and more set to be approved.

In May last year, the government said that water companies had committed to bringing nine new reservoirs by 2050.

They would be located in Lincolnshire, Cambridgeshire, Oxfordshire, Somerset, Suffolk, Kent, East Sussex, and the West Midlands.

The government said that these reservoirs have the potential to provide 670 million litres of extra water per day.

Additional reporting by Tom Ingham, Charlotte Hadfield and Ella Kipling.

Glen Hansard: A life in song and stories

BBC News Thu, 30 Jul 2026 14:41:50 GMT

The death of Oscar-winning singer-songwriter Glen Hansard in a motorbike crash in Dublin on Wednesday has been met with widespread shock and grief.

The 56 year old, who shot to prominence when he was cast in 1991 musical comedy film The Commitments, was long-time frontman of rock band The Frames.

From Bono to Bruce Springsteen, tributes have poured in from around the world with friends and fans sharing stories about his life and the impact he made.

His was a life in music, from first picking up a guitar as a teenager right up until the final hours of his life, when he was performing in a traditional music session.

Here's a look of some of the remarkable aspects of his life in music and film.

It all started with a guitar and a cassette tape.

In an interview with Irish broadcaster RTÉ in February, Hansard said he learned to play the guitar as a child after one was left in his home by an uncle who had gone to prison.

Ballymun was one of Dublin's most economically deprived areas in the 1980s, hit hard by unemployment, crime and drug addiction.

"I was on a kind of a trajectory of getting into the drugs - only gently - getting heavy into drinking, very young, beginning to kind of break into things, just getting into that slightly dodgy spot," Hansard said.

But a Bob Dylan cassette, given to him by his girlfriend's brother, changed the path of his life.

"I listened to Bob Dylan and everything, like my whole world just went into the opposite - flipped," he said.

"I stayed in the bedroom, I played Bob Dylan songs every day, I learned my craft, I decided music was all I cared about.

"So that was a real turnaround for me, it was a life changer and I suddenly had my path."

He said he was also fortunate that his headmaster at school encouraged him down the path of music.

Hansard said he told him: "I can't guarantee you'll be famous, but if you start now, then you'll always be able to live from your guitar."

He left school at 13, and went on to form The Frames and sign his first record deal in 1990, the same year he became part of the cast of The Commitments.

It's odd to say about someone who was a musician through and through, but - whether by fate or accident - Hansard ended up appearing in two of the biggest films in Ireland's history.

Alan Parker's 1991 film, The Commitments, tells the story of the rise and fall of a soul band made up of young working-class Dubliners.

Hansard played the role of guitarist Outspan Foster, despite not originally auditioning for the part.

"I just showed up with my friend, we had been up all night," he told the XS Noize podcast earlier this year.

"He went for the audition and I sat outside waiting for him."

Hansard said they were about to leave when he was asked if he wanted to read for a part.

"They said you've got red hair, you play guitar, you fit the bill for this character that we're casting.

"So I went in and I read a few lines and I'd no problem with the accent because I'm from the north side of Dublin - so I'm a northsider, I play guitar and I've got red hair, I kind of fit the bill.

"So they gave me a callback and much to my surprise I got the part."

The film was an unlikely hit, going on to achieve cult status.

He described the experience as "incredible, it was a beautiful experience".

"It's sad for me that people have said to me 'I've heard you didn't enjoy the experience with The Commitments' - I loved it, I had an absolute ball.

"I just sort of felt it didn't define me and that was my little bit of resistance."

Incredibly, the reluctant actor went on to star in another seminal Irish film.

Hansard won his Oscar for the song Falling Slowly from the 2007 film Once, which he co-wrote with his co-star Markéta Irglova.

Again, it was a role he wasn't originally assigned to play.

Director John Carney had earmarked Irish actor Cillian Murphy for the role.

"He's quite a good singer. I thought I'd do the usual thing where you get a good actor who can half sing and train that voice, but then it became clear to everybody on the film that we should do it the other way around," Carney said in an interview with American film news website CHUD.

"We should get somebody who could really sing and half act and I'll trust that I would be able to do something magical with that."

He turned to his friend Hansard, who had co-written the music for the film.

As well as Bob Dylan - who he would meet a number of times - another of Hansard's musical heroes was Belfast's Van Morrison.

Hansard said his first meeting with Morrison was a rather awkward one when he was 19 or 20 at the star's birthday party at a member of the Guinness family's home.

As Morrison jammed in the kitchen, Hansard said his request for one of his songs was met with a gruff response from Morrison.

Later, at his friend's urging, Morrison passed his guitar to Hansard to play then promptly walked out of the room.

"I'm thinking 'the only guy I want to actually sing to is gone'," Hansard told Kevin Pollak's Chat Show.

Morrison returned during Hansard's second song and then asked the Dubliner to play the song he had requested earlier, before joining in singing it.

The two then went upstairs and took turns playing their songs to each other.

"I'm getting to sit and observe a master at work up close," Hansard said.

"We passed the guitar back and forth and I ran out of songs after an hour and a half and Van kept going and going."

He said as Morrison was leaving at the end of their jam session he said: "Nice voice, nice songs, blah, blah, blah."

Speaking to BBC's Radio Ulster in 2023 Hansard talked about meeting other legendary musical figures.

"Up in the high sweet air of that universe, it's very small and there's very few people and they're all making contact with each other," he said.

"For example, I was at some of [former Pearl Jam singer] Eddie [Vedder's] sessions that were happening in Los Angeles and Ringo [Starr] came in and played drums, Stevie Wonder came in and played drums.

"Morrissey dropped in at one point and Iggy Pop dropped in.

"There's just this kind of place where there's never a question of how can I get that guy's phone number - everybody up at that level seems to have each other's contacts."

In the same interview, Hansard said his mother was a huge Beatles fan and came very close to meeting her heroes in the early 1960s.

"My mother climbed into the back of the Adelphi Cinema in Dublin - her and two of her mates - to see the Beatles," he said.

"They managed to get into the Beatles dressing room, they didn't know they were getting into the dressing room.

"And apparently they got up the corridor and [John] Lennon said: 'Hey mate, there's three more over here' and the girls all got kicked out.

"She always dined out on this story and she always called Paul McCartney Paul McCarty. But she adored The Beatles."

For the past 15 years, Hansard had organised an annual Christmas Eve busking gig to raise money for homelessness charities.

He persuaded many Irish stars, including Sinead O'Connor and members of U2, to join him in busking for cash in central Dublin.

Pat Green, of the Simon Community said the busk became "a tradition on the calendar" in the city.

He told BBC News NI's Good Morning Ulster programme on Thursday that Hansard had been motivated by a "sense of guilt and shame" during a city centre shopping trip at Christmas 2009.

"He was walking down Grafton Street himself with bags of presents and he passed a group of carol singers singing for the homeless and the Simon Community and they asked him to join in," Green explained.

"And he was busy, he was distracted and he said: 'No, I can't.'

"And he got home and it was then he realised there was no material value to the Christmas presents that he bought - that the greater value was out on the street, bringing joy and happiness to people over Christmas.

"So, he went back out and started to busk with literally the cap on the ground."

He said Hansard and other stars "have raised collectively – with Glen the leader – well over €2m (£1.7m) for homeless services that we provide here in Dublin's Simon."

Billy McGuinness, a guitarist in the Irish rock band Aslan, explained how Hansard was able to call in so many favours from his famous friends.

"Glen had this magical way of getting you to do something without making it feel like a job - he made you feel a part of it."

McGuinness also told the BBC's Good Morning Ulster programme that the singer was renowned for his kindness both on and off stage.

He cited the example of a young musician who had supported Hansard at a recent gig in County Cork.

"After the gig, Glen gave him a Takamine guitar and I believe that's not the first time that he did something like that," McGuinness said.

"That was the type of generous guy that he was."

Hansard was a long-time friend of Shane MacGowan, the late lead singer of the The Pogues.

Following MacGowan's death in 2023, MacGowan's widow Victoria Mary Clarke entrusted Hansard with the role of "musical director" of her husband's funeral.

Speaking to the Irish radio station Today FM on Wednesday, Clarke recalled how their friend stepped in to help.

"I said: 'Glen, would you be able to do something at the funeral?" she recalled.

"And he said: 'Look, if you don't mind, I'll do everything. I'll organise, I'll get all the music together, you don't have to worry.'"

MacGowan's send-off featured performances from Australian singer Nick Cave as well as a 'who's who' from the Irish music scene, including singer-songwriters Imelda May, Declan O'Rourke and Mundy, Hothouse Flowers frontman Liam Ó Maonlaí and Hansard's own band The Frames.

There were also readings from actor Johnny Depp, U2 singer Bono, Boomtown Rats singer Bob Geldoff and Irish actor Aidan Gillen.

"As people who watched it will testify, he did an incredible job, absolutely incredible, and in a short space – 24 hours – he pulled that together," Clarke said.

Drought declared across whole of Wales as conditions 'deteriorate'

BBC News Thu, 30 Jul 2026 14:15:09 GMT

A drought has been extended across the whole of Wales with the country on course for its driest July on record in 190 years.

Declaring the drought, the country's environment body Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said sustained high temperatures were causing the condition of the natural environment to "deteriorate".

The decision has been made in response to record-low river levels, dry soils, widespread wildfires and mounting impacts on wildlife, farming and forestry.

NRW had already announced a drought across the north and parts of mid Wales last week.

The nationwide announcement made on Thursday will trigger more monitoring of rivers and stronger advice for the public on use of water.

The declaration of a drought does not mean there is currently a threat to water supplies for homes and businesses, with Welsh water companies saying reservoir levels are holding up after a wet start to the year.

NRW said figures had shown Wales had received 8% of its long-term average rainfall for July, with most rivers in the country "exceptionally low".

Groundwater levels are also falling in Wales, with some lower than expected for the time of year.

The environmental body said its teams were dealing with reports of "wide-reaching impacts to the environment", and that "conditions across Wales' natural environment have continued to deteriorate".

This includes drying riverbeds, fish in distress, an accumulation of algae, wildfire risk and concern from farmers about crop growth, grazing conditions and water availability for livestock.

Rhian Thomas, from NRW, said the toll from the recent dry weather had been "clear to see", and teams were closely monitoring forecasts and river flows.

"With no strong indications for notable rainfall in the forecasts, and risks of further heatwaves over the summer, it's more important than ever that we all use water wisely," she said.

"Every drop we waste is less water for our rivers and wildlife when they need it the most."

The dry weather in recent weeks has also coincided with a number of wildfires across Wales.

A fire that broke out earlier this month in the Rhinogydd mountains in Gwynedd could be seen from space, with a firefighting helicopter deployed to tackle the blaze.

Residents were evacuated from their homes following a fire close to Conwy Mountain said they had heard the blaze, which had sounded "like popcorn", coming down the mountain.

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said he had organised a summit to look at the risks of fires from severe droughts.

Speaking to Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live, he said while there was no "immediate risk to the provision of drinking water", there needed to be "more resilience in our water supplies" across Wales and the UK.

George Tomlinson, 29, who runs Rossett Park Farming in Wrexham, said he had to sell 60 cows because the drought had killed off grazing land.

"There's nothing available for the cows to eat on the grazing platform apart from a little bit of dead grass some dry cows are eating," said Tomlinson, adding "you've got to make tough decisions in order to survive".

He said he was also worried about what the future might hold with warmer summers expected.

"If this continues a lot of farmers will be forced to close their gates and never open them again," he said, describing it as "depressing".

Richard Anthony, whose farm stretches over the Vale of Glamorgan and Bridgend county, said the ground on his land was as hard as a "rock" and had "no moisture at all".

The dry land has left Anthony unable to plant his crops, who added he had "never ever been in this situation" before.

"As soon as we've harvested the one crop, we plant in the next crop, but we can't do any of that now," he said. "I've never seen it as bad as this."

Our wheat deals are down between 20% and 30%. That is massive. we'll have to cope, we will survive, but the knock-on effect is huge."

Anthony said he is concerned that once the rain comes it will not stop, leaving him unable to plant next year's crops.

"It'll go from this to being too wet", he added.

National Farmers Union Cymru president Abi Reader has warned that the cost of the continuing dry and hot weather will have a financial impact on farmers.

"We're going to see costs for these farms rising, because they might be having to buy in extra feed for their livestock, or they might be spending a lot of money carting water," she said.

"We've been in this a long time now, and it's going to take a long time to recover, and absolutely everybody needs to remember that food security starts with water security," she added.

A drought occurs when a prolonged lack of rainfall and high temperatures causes severe stress to natural ecosystems.

NRW says it results in critically low river and groundwater levels as well as dry soils - which has an impact on wildlife, fisheries and protected habitats.

It also has impacts for farming and forestry - such as failing crops - while private water supplies like natural springs and boreholes can run dry.

A declaration of environmental drought triggers more monitoring of rivers and releases from reservoirs to help top up the flow.

Those who have licences to take water from rivers - from farms and canals to golf courses - will face restrictions.

There's a big communications element to this too - so it means firmer advice for the public on using water wisely.

There is a difference between NRW's drought announcements and those made by water companies.

Welsh Water already have a hosepipe ban in place for parts of west Wales as a result of unprecedented demand during the recent heatwaves, making it harder to process and deliver enough water around the network.

But they say there is currently no threat to drinking water supplies and reservoir levels are holding up.

Howe going as spending rules bite - troubles for Newcastle's Saudi owners

BBC News Thu, 30 Jul 2026 12:31:22 GMT

Newcastle's Saudi Arabian owners brought in Eddie Howe in November 2021

Seven months ago, Newcastle United's chief executive David Hopkinson said he could put them "in the debate about being the top club in the world" by 2030.

Right now, that ambition looks a long way off.

The departure of manager Eddie Howe on Thursday, and reported appointment of Matthias Jaissle, is the result of a poor Premier League season, where Newcastle finished 12th, and an uninspiring transfer window.

The latter is in no small part down to the club's need to sell players to generate income and so be able to spend more.

But does this latest development point to a bigger issue?

Newcastle have let go some of their biggest players in Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali while captain Bruno Guimaraes is also rumoured to be on his way out. That follows the £125m sale of striker Alexander Isak to Liverpool last September.

Transfers the other way have not exactly been flooding in either, with Newcastle missing out on Swiss midfielder Johan Manzambi to Aston Villa and Spanish winger Victor Munoz to Liverpool.

Newcastle's Saudi Arabia-backed takeover in 2021 - by the Public Investment Fund (PIF) - was supposed to lead to them becoming one of the world's top clubs.

But recent actions have raised questions about whether they are running out of steam.

Challenging times ahead for Newcastle - Shearer

The winner who played for Tuchel - potential Newcastle boss Jaissle

Newcastle captain Guimaraes expected to join Arsenal

Howe ended Newcastle's 70-year wait for a domestic trophy when his side won the Carabao Cup last year.

But rumours about the 48-year-old's departure have been circulating since the beginning of this year, when Newcastle sat 13th in the Premier League and securing Champions League football for next season was already starting to look highly unlikely.

That was exacerbated further in March when the Magpies were struck by a late Sunderland comeback in the Tyne-Wear derby, losing 2-1 at St James' Park, to extend their dismal league record against their local rivals to 15 years without victory.

They also went out of the FA Cup in the fifth round, exited the Champions League in the last 16 and made it to the semi-finals of the EFL Cup only to be beaten 5-1 by Manchester City over two legs.

Despite that, Howe's four-and-a-half-year stint as Newcastle boss will be looked back on fondly by Newcastle fans.

What supporters will perhaps be most perplexed by is the timing of Howe's departure.

The former Bournemouth boss could have left at the end of the season and would probably have been given a positive send off by fans.

Indeed, BBC Sport understands potential replacements for Howe were sounded out in July, including Kieran McKenna.

Instead, Howe got partway through pre-season before making his decision, the difficulties of building a squad he is happy with having become too much.

Although he understood the situation - saying in March "there's a limit to what we can spend" despite the ambition of the club - it is understood he communicated his intent to leave two weeks ago.

Selling three of your best players in the space of one year - Isak to Liverpool last summer and this year Gordon at Barcelona and Tonali to Tottenham - with another one possibly on the way in Guimaraes, is perhaps not conducive to becoming a top club.

Former Newcastle defender Steve Howey told BBC Radio Newcastle: "I'm shocked but at the same time kind of not.

"Eddie for a long time has basically had to put fires out. You are losing your best players.

"You can understand the frustration with him when he's trying to build something but you're having that semi-taken away losing your best players. It's always going to be difficult.

"You can understand his frustration."

So what are the rules that Newcastle have, at times, come close to breaking?

From the beginning of the PIF takeover, Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) have put the brakes on Newcastle's ambitions to spend.

Just because a club has wealthy owners does not mean they can spend big in the transfer windows.

After buying the club in 2021, PIF spent £404.7m in the first three years. But by bringing in only £50.4m from sales, Newcastle saw the stark reality of PSR hit home in 2024.

That led to them having to sell homegrown talent Elliot Anderson to Nottingham Forest and has snowballed since, with important players being offloaded every season.

The Magpies welcomed the new Financial Fair Play rules - the Squad Cost Ratio (SCR), which are now in effect - and, in short, mean the more you generate, the more you can spend.

But, when analysing their spending power against that of other Premier League clubs, Swiss Ramble, external found that the Magpies' SCR budget ranked ninth (£243m) in the Premier League.

On top of that, in April the PIF withdrew its multibillion dollar backing of LIV Golf after Yasir Al-Rumayyan - the fund's governor and chairman of Newcastle - confirmed the PIF was reviewing its deals and investments.

In turn, questions were raised about what that meant for the future of Newcastle - but senior club figures were informed at the time that the pullout did not affect the club. The fund is still viewed as being engaged.

In the club's most recent set of accounts from last season, Newcastle's revenues have more than doubled to £335.3m - from the £140.2m recorded in the final full campaign of Mike Ashley's ownership.

There are also plans for a new state-of-the-art training ground while Hopkinson has outlined a desire to revamp St James' Park or move stadiums to increase matchday revenue.

The potential appointment of former RB Salzburg boss Jaissle is also intriguing given he is currently in charge of Saudi Arabian side Al-Ahli - a club the PIF held a majority stake in until selling it in April.

It is understood that Howe communicated his intention to leave to the Newcastle hierarchy around a fortnight ago.

Newcastle initially asked him to reconsider to continue leading the club into next season.

Eventually, though, Newcastle accepted Howe's wishes but asked him to stay as they identified his replacement - a request the coach accepted.

Plenty has been made about the club's transfer policy this summer.

BBC Sport outlined in April how Newcastle would need to sell at least one of their top players during the current transfer window to comply with financial regulations.

Indeed, Howe leaves amid a backdrop of high-profile departures and in terms of incomings, Newcastle are going for younger, unproven talents – with the likes of relatively unknown Bazoumana Traore and Aladji Bamba arriving.

But while it is BBC Sport's understanding that the transfer strategy has prompted concern at how the squad is shaping up for next season and how competitive it may be, it is claimed that alone is not the only factor in Howe's decision to quit, and that the split between both parties is amicable.

Large rise in offenders sent back to prison, figures reveal

BBC News Thu, 30 Jul 2026 12:13:51 GMT

There has been a large rise in the number of offenders being recalled to prisons in England and Wales having been released on licence, new government figures show.

There were 51,419 licence recalls in the year ending March 2026, up from 40,259 in the previous year - a 28% increase.

Although recalls in January to March were slightly lower than the previous three-month period, they remain well above historical levels.

The figures follow government schemes to release a number of offenders early in an effort to ease prison overcrowding.

The Ministry of Justice (MOJ) said offenders released on licence face strict conditions "and can be hauled back to prison if they break these rules".

Cassia Rowland, from the Institute for Government think tank, said most recalls are for breaches of licence conditions, such as missed appointments, rather than offenders committing further offences or posing a serious risk to the public.

"The probation service is overwhelmed, with high caseloads and lots of vacancies putting often inexperienced staff under huge pressure," she said.

The most common reason provided for prison recalls between January and March was "non-compliance" (9,683), followed by "failed to keep in touch" (5,025).

There were 2,891 recalls because an offender faced further charges between January and March 2026, a 23% rise on the same period in 2025. More than one reason can be recorded against each recall.

Alex Hewson, from the Prison Reform Trust, said: "Many leave prison facing challenges such as addiction, poor mental health and unstable housing, making compliance with licence conditions difficult."

Responding to the figures, the MOJ said "public protection is our priority" and the statistics "show that we do not hesitate to recall offenders to prison when the risk escalates."

The increase in prisoner recall comes after the government introduced an early release scheme in England and Wales to help ease overcrowding pressure in September 2024.

The scheme meant eligible prisoners could be released after serving 40% of their sentence rather than half.

As of March 2026, 70,066 people had been released under the scheme.

Rowland says early release schemes have contributed to the increase in recalls.

"But these schemes have also made it harder for prisons and probation to prepare people for release effectively and give them support with basic things like finding accommodation, accessing job support and so on."

Despite the releases there were still 86,267 people in England and Wales' prisons as of 27 July, meaning the prison estate was 97% full.

In a further attempt to ease prison capacity pressure, Sir Keir Starmer's government had planned to release some offenders after serving just one-third of their custodial term.

The Sentencing Act release scheme was due to come into force from 2 September, but it has been paused by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham following criticism from survivors and victims' families.

The BBC understands around 700 prisoners would have been eligible for early release under the scheme's first phase.

Although the prison population has remained relatively stable since 2010, following rapid growth in the 1990s, government projections suggest it could rise to about 90,000 in 2028.

Using early release to manage prison overcrowding is not new.

Governments led by Labour and the Conservatives have each introduced emergency measures when the prison system has come under strain.

In October 2023, Rishi Sunak's Conservative government began releasing eligible offenders up to 18 days early. The scheme was eventually expanded to up to 70 days ahead of offenders' release date.

Nick Hardwick, the former chief inspector of prisons, says early release alone will not solve the problem, arguing "it's just going to slow the rate of growth".

The Starmer government announced a plan to add 14,000 new prison places by 2031, including four new prisons. It said it would acquire land if necessary and would "make sure the supply always keeps up with demand".

The MOJ previously told BBC Verify the government had delivered about 3,200 prison places so far - 1,600 for each of their two years in office. However, this figure only covers new prison places and does not factor in those taken out of use.

Hardwick says expanding the number of prisons is only part of the answer because "the one thing you can't do quickly is produce experienced staff."

The prison building programme is already costing billions of pounds, he adds, leaving it up to ministers to decide how much they are prepared to spend to keep more people in prison for longer.

"There's no perfect solution... it's a question of what's the least bad option."

Additional reporting by Isobel Cottam

US launches 'heavy' strikes on Iran after attempted attack on American troops

BBC News Thu, 30 Jul 2026 10:49:14 GMT

The US military says it has completed a "heavy wave" of strikes against Iran in retaliation for Tuesday's attempted ballistic missile attacks on American forces.

Centcom said it hit "dozens" of Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in response to Iran's firing on US bases in Jordan and at ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian state media said the latest strikes had killed three people, including a two-year-old child, on Qeshm island, while other locations were also hit in the south and west of the country.

The latest hostilities come on a week that has seen the conflict expand, with the first publicly announced joint US-Saudi strikes targeting Iranian proxies in Iraq.

Iran and the US have engaged in escalating strikes and counter-strikes since a ceasefire in April, aimed at pausing the months-long war, fell apart in June.

The US has blockaded Iranian ports and bombed Iranian sites, while Iran has fired missiles and drones at US assets in countries across the Middle East and targeted shipping in the economically important Strait of Hormuz, connecting the Gulf and Arabian Sea.

On Wednesday, news outlet Axios cited an unnamed US official as saying that Trump had met Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, who had conveyed that Saudi Arabia wants to de-escalate tensions. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Meanwhile, the Egyptian government said a fire at a port on Wednesday had been caused by a drone attack. Egypt, a US ally, has not previously been directly attacked during the war.

The US-Iran conflict has reignited after several days of relative calm.

For days, both sides halted strikes as talks apparently restarted in hopes of some type of diplomatic solution. Trump called them "very friendly negotiations", though Tehran denied any discussions were happening.

But following the Iranian missile attack on a US base in Jordan on Tuesday, Trump vowed to retaliate, telling reporters at the White House: "We're going to be hitting them very hard because it's our turn to hit them. They know it's coming. They asked us not to do it."

The latest wave of US strikes started at 20:00 ET on Wednesday (01:00 BST on Thursday) and lasted about an hour, with Centcom calling them a "powerful response to yesterday's attempted Iranian attacks on US forces based in the Middle East". All of Iran's missiles were intercepted, Centcom said.

The attack by the US targeted "military command centers, missile and drone facilities, coastal surveillance and defense sites, and maritime capabilities," Centcom wrote once the strikes were complete.

Iranian state media agency Irib reported that the islands of Qeshm and Abadan, both central to the oil industry, were among the areas hit.

"A US attack on a residential home in the Chah Tangu neighbourhood of Qeshm killed three members of a family: the father, the mother, and their 2-year-old child," Fars reported citing the Hormozgan University of Medical Sciences.

A man in his 30s living in the south of the island told BBC Persian he was heading to Tehran, because "things are becoming more dangerous here".

"Our internet situation has been a mess. The electricity has been cutting out several times since this morning," he said.

"There have been loud bangs since 03:40 this morning. We are helpless."

Meanwhile, Jordan's armed forces said that air defence systems had successfully shot down five Iranian missiles targeting the Kingdom's territory on Thursday.

On Tuesday, the IRGC said it had targeted a US air base and a command centre in Jordan "in response to the acts of aggression of the American child-killing army".

It also said naval forces had struck three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz after they "ignored warnings" and sailed along what it described as an "unsafe and illegal route" through the vital Gulf waterway.

Last Friday, Trump suspended an intensive bombing campaign that had lasted for 13 consecutive nights. The US said it had targeted Iranian weapons and military sites. Scores of people were reported to have died.

On Tuesday, Centcom said the joint US-Saudi strikes hit "multiple terrorist logistics and weapons sites across eastern Iraq in a strong response to over 30 IRGC-directed aerial drone attacks in the last 72 hours".

Iraq's paramilitary Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), which is dominated by Iran-backed Shia militias, said at least 20 of its members had been killed in US-Saudi strikes on its bases.

The Iraqi presidency said it denounced the bombing of the PMF bases, calling it "an unacceptable attack and a blatant violation of Iraq's sovereignty".

But Trump told Fox News the strikes had been "co-ordinated with the Iraqi government".

Saudi Arabia, which sees itself as the leading Sunni Muslim power, and Iran, the largest Shia Muslim country, have been locked in a struggle for regional dominance for decades.

With additional reporting from Ghoncheh Habibiazad, BBC Persian

How to do neon festival make-up without harming your skin

BBC News Thu, 30 Jul 2026 00:22:27 GMT

Festival season's here and neon make-up is everywhere.

Bright graphic eyeliner, vampy lips and holographic highlighter are some of this year's biggest beauty trends for the main stage.

But some of these make-up products, which are being sold by third-party sellers on online marketplaces such as TikTok Shop, can contain a host of toxic chemicals, warns the Chartered Trading Standards Institute.

So here's what to look out for – and how to stay safe while serving festival glam.

How to get the look: Dominic Skinner, make-up artist and judge on the hit BBC show Glow Up, came into the BBC's London offices to show us how to achieve the perfect festival look and make it dance and party-proof.

If you want colours to "pop", he says use a white eye pencil on the skin first and then press bright eyeshadows on top.

"It will make bold colours more intense, and last all night."

What to be aware of: Banned ingredients can cause bad rashes and allergic reactions, so check the label and avoid products that say they're "not for cosmetic use" - even if they say they're for the skin.

Also look out for banned colourants, like Solvent Yellow 172, CI 45161 (Basic Red 1:1) and CI 45174 (Basic Violet 11:1).

Be cautious of cheap products or sellers you've never heard of, says Skinner.

"There are some items that are UV reflective, glow-in-the-dark or neon that are made by cosmetics brands but are quietly labelled as a 'non-cosmetic paint'," he adds.

How to get the look: Fairycore-inspired make-up is in, which means sparkles, face gems and glitter.

Don't go for subtle, says Skinner. "The 'no make-up look' is gone. Clean girl is out!"

There's a child-like quality to festival make-up, he says, so embrace it - think playful colour and crystals.

To stand out, he suggests using glitter in hair partings or your shoulders.

"Personally, I say use gems as they're bigger and more impactful, plus you can peel them off at the end of night and reuse them in the morning."

What to be aware of: Skip near the eyes to avoid nasty scratches on your cornea, says the British Skin Foundation's Dr Emma Wedgeworth, and never use craft glitter.

Use biodegradable, eco-friendly products that are better for the environment and softer on the skin. Safe adhesives, like lash glue, will keep it in place.

How to get the look: Vogue says 2026 is all about juicy and blurred lips that play with texture more than colour. Think "your-lips-but-better", using stains and glosses.

InStyle magazine recommends dramatic, dark red vampy lips as a breakaway from summer-friendly pinks and peaches.

Use a liquid lip product, Skinner says, because it won't budge.

"You can do some drinking, you can do some snogging."

And he says leave that lip liner until last - it'll just "highlight how wonky your drawing skills are". Colour first, liner later.

What to be aware of: Whatever your look, don't share your balm or lipstick. That can spread nasty infections like cold sores.

Cross-contamination is real, and why make-up artists sanitise everything in between clients.

Use high-protection sunscreen - at least SPF 30 - as a base before the make-up and let it soak in like any primer, says Wedgeworth.

Skinner recommends matte or sweat-proof SPF to help your make-up last longer.

Reapply throughout the day, at least every two hours. Don't forget your hairline and any partings to protect your scalp.

Sprays let you layer over make-up, but can be difficult to apply thickly enough, so take shade breaks and bring a big hat for extra protection, says Wedgeworth.

How to get the look: Who, What, Wear says think about accessories - scarfs, crochet beanie caps or eye-catching hair clips, charms or cuffs.

InStyle suggests Mermaid waves or thin Baby Braids if your hair is long enough.

What to be aware of: If you want a colour change with a spray or dye, do a patch test first to check you are not allergic.

Put a small amount behind your ear or on your arm and wait 24 to 48 hours to check for a reaction, says Wedgeworth.

Skinner says you probably already own products that can give you a festival look.

"You just have to think creatively about how to play with it."

Smallpox DNA in ancient Inca mummies shows virus came from Europe

New Scientist July 30, 2026

DNA samples collected from Inca mummies have confirmed the presence of a strain of smallpox that first emerged in Europe.

“We interpreted this as the first direct molecular evidence of smallpox introduction into the Americas through European colonisation,” says Shigeki Nakagome at Trinity College Dublin, Ireland.

How a surge in ancient plagues 5000 years ago shaped humanity

Smallpox was the scourge of humanity for centuries until its eradication in the 1980s, through vaccination, from all but a few high-security medical laboratories. Severe strains of the virus had a mortality rate of up to a third and left survivors with scars from the blisters and scabs that cover the skin and fill with pus.

Advertisement

The disease was particularly brutal in parts of the world colonised by Europeans, such as Australia and the Americas, where Indigenous populations had no natural immunity, resulting in millions of deaths.

In the Americas, historical reports record that smallpox began devastating Indigenous communities in the early 16th century, after the arrival of European colonists.

Free newsletter

Matthew Ward at the University of Dundee in the UK, who wasn’t involved in the new research, says the waves of epidemics, including smallpox, that spread across the Americas were some of the most important events in history. “These diseases killed perhaps 95 per cent of the Indigenous population of the Americas and allowed for European colonisation,” he says.

Nakagome and his colleagues studied samples of bone from mummies found at an archaeological site known as Camarones 9 in northern Chile, discovered in 1957. Over subsequent decades, 41 mummified bodies wrapped in blankets and buried with grave goods were recovered from the site.

“While the original aim was to study the human DNA, we also searched for DNA from ancient pathogens,” says Nakagome. “That is when we discovered fragments matching the smallpox virus in two individuals.”

The first was a woman who was 30 to 35 years old at the time of death, and the second, an 18-to-20-year-old man, was revealed by carbon dating to have died between 1492 and 1631.

By reconstructing the virus’s genomes and comparing them with other ancient and modern smallpox viruses, the team found that they belonged to a lineage of smallpox that includes early medieval and early modern European strains.

Surprising skeletons prompt a radical rethink of Egyptian pyramids

The discovery adds weight to the possibility that small skin lesions on the trunks of the mummies, previously attributed to chronic arsenic exposure, may in fact have been the distinctive pustules that scar the skin of smallpox victims.

“This finding allowed us to identify a small group of people impacted by the virus for which no historical record exists,” says team member Constanza de la Fuente Castro at the University of Chile in Santiago. Before the new research, the pathogen was known only from historical accounts of large-scale outbreaks, she says.

The work was particularly sensitive because of the disturbance of the original remains and the loss of material during analysis, both considered extremely controversial subjects to Indigenous people and the scientific community. “We never forget that behind every DNA extraction is a person, not a data point,” says de la Fuente Castro.

Ward welcomed the new research. “Understanding exactly what was killing native peoples and why they were so susceptible to epidemic disease is a vitally important issue,” he says.

Historians are now trying to understand how Europeans deliberately or inadvertently fuelled the spread of epidemics like smallpox, he says. “Without these epidemics, colonisation of the Americas would have been very different.”

Science DOI: 10.1126/science. aee6957

The genome of a long-extinct ancient human is hiding within us

New Scientist July 30, 2026

Our ancestors interbred with at least two ancient human lineages in addition to Neanderthals and Denisovans, and now an improved method has given us a much better idea of which bits of our DNA came from them. In fact, it shows that nearly the entire genome of one of these “ghost ancestors” is preserved in small bits spread among all living humans.

In any person alive today, between 0.5 and 1 per cent of their DNA comes from this ghost ancestor, says Yulin Zhang at the University of California, Berkeley. But different people have different bits of DNA from them and, crucially, they are spread fairly evenly around the genome.

What made us human? The fossils redefining our evolutionary origins

“We find that almost all regions of the genome have ghost ancestry,” says team member Priya Moorjani, also at Berkeley.

Advertisement

This means that, if all the bits could be put together, it might be possible to assemble almost an entire genome of this ghost ancestor, though the team hasn’t attempted this.

Earlier research revealed that Homo sapiens interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans within the past 50,000 years. These studies have relied on the ancient DNA sequences from fossils.

Subscriber-only newsletter

While other work has also identifed ghost ancestry from human genomes, this team’s new approach is much more powerful, says Moorjani. It is based on constructing a “family tree” for parts of the genome, which has only recently become computationally possible. The researchers showed this approach works by identifying Neanderthal and Denisovan DNA from modern human genomes alone.

“I believe it is the next frontier of research in human genetics, because it allows us to even learn about our ancestors for whom we don’t have any fossil [DNA] evidence,” says Moorjani.

Only a small part of the Neanderthal and Denisovan genomes remain collectively preserved within us. “Long segments of the genome are devoid of, or have very low fractions of, Neanderthal or Denisovan ancestry,” says team member Arjun Biddanda at Johns Hopkins University in Maryland. “Yet we were able to find high-ish fractions of this ghost ancestry in these regions.”

The researchers think this is because the populations of Neanderthals and Denisovans were very small, and therefore were more likely to have detrimental mutations. “Most likely there was selection against Neanderthal or Denisovan ancestry in these regions,” says Moorjani.

But much more of the DNA deriving from one ghost ancestor appears to have been selected for, or it was at least neutral in evolutionary terms. This is probably because the population of this ghost ancestor was much larger, she says.

The remarkable tale of how humans nearly didn’t conquer the world

The team’s work suggests that the ghost ancestor split away from the main lineages leading to modern humans around 800,000 years ago. Then, some time later, the two lineages came back together and interbred.

“Because all modern humans carry signatures of the ghost ancestry, it’s most likely that the gene flow occurred in Africa, and that this population existed in Africa,” says Moorjani. Based on all these factors, this ghost ancestor could be a species known from fossils, such as Homo heidelbergensis, the researchers speculate.

The second ghost ancestor identified by their approach is much older. It split from the main lineage leading to modern humans around 1.8 million years ago. At some point later on, Denisovans in Eurasia interbred with this “super-archaic” ancestor.

“Modern humans have also inherited these super-archaic segments through the Denisovan gene flow, and now we can find blocks of this super-archaic ancestry,” says Moorjani.

This is important and innovative work, says Chris Stringer at the Natural History Museum in London.

He agrees that the more recent ghost ancestor could have been Homo heidelbergensis – fossil evidence shows this species was present in Africa as recently as 300,000 years ago. The most likely candidate for the super-archaic ghost lineage has to be Homo erectus, he says.

“These results are exciting,” says Stringer. “They provide indirect ways of reconstructing parts of the genomes of more primitive species like Homo erectus and Homo heidelbergensis.”

Science DOI: 10.1126/science. aef8874

Woolly mammoths butchered by humans were mostly female

New Scientist July 30, 2026

Twenty to thirty millennia ago, ancient human hunters and scavengers targeted mostly female mammoths, analysis of DNA from hundreds of fossils has revealed.

“The people weren’t just fooling around – they knew what they were doing,” says David Díez del Molino at the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, Sweden. “They probably had a structured way to interact with mammoths, one that we cannot really understand.”

How our ancestors invented clothing and transformed it into fashion

Many Palaeolithic archaeological sites include remains from dozens or even hundreds of woolly mammoths (Mammuthus primigenius), generally close to evidence of ancient human cooking. In some cases, scientists have found cut marks, unhealed bone fractures and embedded stone points in the mammoth bones.

Advertisement

Researchers have debated how much those sites differ from other places mammoths have been discovered, where the position of bones, tusks and teeth suggests the animals died naturally, perhaps caught in sinkholes, landslides or tar pits.

“It’s been suggested in the past that these were natural accumulations of skeletons, and that people deliberately set up camp next to such accumulations in order to collect bones, ivory and maybe meat,” says Natasha Reynolds at the University of Bordeaux in France, who wasn’t involved in the research.

Free newsletter

Díez del Molino and his colleagues sequenced specimens from 448 mammoths – mostly teeth – and analysed previously sequenced DNA data from another 73 mammoths found across Eurasia and North America to determine the genetic sex of 521 ancient animals. Combined, their dataset represented DNA from 100 mammoths at 11 human-related sites from 20,000 to 30,000 years ago, and 421 mammoths from natural accumulations, all across Eurasia and North America.

In the natural settings, male mammoths represented 67 per cent of the specimens. If they behaved like male elephants, they would have often roamed alone and more easily fallen into natural traps – a trend seen among male bison and brown bears, says Díez del Molino.

By contrast, 70 per cent of the mammoths in the human-related sites were female – suggesting people specifically targeted females. That might have been intentional, since females would have been smaller and, if accompanied by a calf, slower. But it is also possible that hunters were simply taking advantage of herds made up of adult females and their young, says Hannah Moots, also at the Centre for Palaeogenetics.

“Elephant herds move in a very predictable way, along seasonal routes, whereas males move more randomly,” she says. “So, if that’s true for mammoths, too, then these ice age sites might have been placed along mammoth migration routes. If the mammoth is really important to you – and they were – then maybe you’d want to make sure you’re somewhere where you’re sure mammoth herds will come through.”

“My reaction to this paper is, ‘Wow! This is amazing!’” says Pat Shipman, a retired anthropologist. “It never occurred to me that female mammoths were preferentially targeted, but if their behaviour is similar to that of living elephants, this pattern makes perfect sense. Female elephants make up the majority of herds and are protective of their babies, so will shield the babies with their bodies, making mothers easier to kill.”

“In several ways, female mammoths were the path of least resistance for Palaeolithic hunters,” says Audrey Rowe at the University of Alaska Fairbanks.

Surprisingly, Moots, Díez del Molino and their colleagues also discovered one mammoth with XX/X0 mosaicism, a condition in which some cells have only one sex chromosome, which is the genetic basis of Turner’s syndrome in humans. It is the first ever discovery of a sex chromosome mutation in an extinct species. The condition has been detected in modern domestic animals, but not yet in elephants.

“I was amazed,” says Julia Gresky at the German Archaeological Institute in Berlin. “But of course, we’re all mammals. So why wouldn’t they have genetic mutations like we do?”

While the findings are interesting, they paint a tragic picture, says Rowe. “The elephant in the room, so to speak, is a new line of evidence that humans contributed to the extinction of mammoths,” she says. “Sadly, they probably didn’t realise they were contributing to the thinning of their own resources over time.”

Advertisement

Olenik says the next step is longer-term animal studies. The rats in the current study had the device implanted for only about an hour, and while the procedure caused some inflammation, the negative effects of this were “minimal”, she says.
