Saudi Arabia is preparing for a major military offensive against the Houthis by sea and possibly by land in central Yemen, Yemeni sources believe, in a move to break the chokehold on its oil exports through the southern Red Sea.

Saudi forces have been seen withdrawing from the east of Yemen in what could be preparation for a land offensive. At the same time, Riyadh is trying to organise a naval coalition to protect shipping from Houthi attacks in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait.

The Saudi defence ministry said on Thursday that 14 states including Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt, Sudan and Djibouti had issued a joint statement supporting a multinational maritime defence coalition.

The Iran-aligned Houthis, who control Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, and much of its Red Sea coastline, announced on 20 July that they were implementing a blockade against Saudi ships, but they have denied they are planning to impose tolls on all ships.

The group says it will lift the blockade once Saudi Arabia lifts its blockade on Yemen, positioning the dispute as over the future of Yemen and not directly about Iran. Saudi Arabia intervened in the Yemeni civil war in 2015 in support of the country’s UN-recognised government against the Houthi rebels.

Riyadh has also asked the US and a group of European countries including Germany, France, the UK and Italy to join a Red Sea coalition.

The EU already has a naval protection mission, Aspides, operating in the Red Sea and it remains unclear if the Houthis are mounting a general blockade or one directed solely at Saudi Arabia.

Houthi forces said on 25 July they had hit “sensitive” oil transport sites inside Saudi Arabia linking eastern province oilfields to a Red Sea export hub.

If the Red Sea route is closed to Saudi shipping in addition to the strait of Hormuz blockade on the other side of the Arabian peninsula, the kingdom’s oil export will be severely constrained.

Up to 80% of Saudi crude exports were shipped through the strait of Hormuz before the Iran war began. The Red Sea has therefore grown in importance, with more than half of Saudi oil now transported overland to loading terminals at the port city of Yanbu.

Saudi strikes in Iraq on Wednesday killed at least 20 people as it hit back at Iraqi militia for striking its oil facilities. Donald Trump said the joint US-Saudi attacks had been mounted with the agreement of the Iraqi government, a claim that Baghdad did not confirm.

The Saudi defence minister, Prince Khalid bin Salman, held an urgent meeting with Trump and JD Vance on Wednesday to discuss the next steps. The Saudis are keen to show they will defend themselves and their industry, but are not willing to escalate the war against Iran, arguing that the disagreements between the US and Iran can still be settled by diplomacy.

The troop movements inside Yemen involve concentrating forces for what could be an attack on al-Bayda, a governorate in central southern Yemen captured by the Houthis in 2020-21, the sources said.

Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has erupted in the past fortnight with the Houthis mounting attacks against Saudi Aramco facilities. The strikes inside Saudi Arabia came hours after Saudi airstrikes targeted Houthi-controlled sites in the port of Hodeidah and a third Saudi commercial vessel was attacked in the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia and the Houthis have been vying for control of Yemen for more than a decade and an uneasy status quo has unravelled over the past month.

The tensions inside Yemen would be reduced if the Gulf states and Iran could reach an agreement for the reopening of the strait of Hormuz. Talks between Oman and Iran are continuing, with Iran demanding that all shipping enter the strait through a northern route close to Iran’s coast.

The outlook gets better and better at Rolls-Royce

Tufan Erginbilgiç, the chief executive of Rolls-Royce, seemed to be getting ahead himself when he said a year ago that the engine-maker had the potential to become the most valuable company on the London Stock Exchange.

Yes, everyone knows about the remarkable turnaround. Rolls was a corporate calamity during the Covid shutdown of global aviation, then a tenfold increase in the share price followed under Erginbilgiç. But it still required a leap of imagination to think the firm could challenge the very top of the capitalisation charts one day.

And it still requires work. Today’s valuation of £120bn puts Rolls roughly neck and neck with the miner Rio Tinto for fourth place in the Footsie, but there is still a big gap to Shell (£185bn), AstraZeneca (£198bn) and HSBC (£274bn), none of whom intend to stand still.

Erginbilgiç’s long-term bullishness, however, sounds less fantastical with every set of results. Thursday’s half-year numbers came with the usual upgrade to financial forecasts. Cashflow over the full year will be £200m better than previously predicted at £3.8bn-£4bn; for operating profits, the increase was £700m to £4.7bn-£4.9bn. Those upgrades suggest there is still mileage in Erginbilgiç’s efforts to invest in the reliability of the engines to allow a “win-win” renegotiation of contracts with airlines.

The long-term growth projections, however, rely on many other things – way beyond widebody-aircraft engines – going well. Defence looks a safe bet, naturally. The sight of the prime minister at Barrow-in-Furness on Thursday served as a reminder that Rolls makes the nuclear propulsion systems for the UK’s submarines. The rest of the country’s defence investment plan, whatever the wrangles over the precise budget, is unambiguously good news for Rolls too. There are possibilities in propulsion systems for uncrewed aircraft and much more.

The division that is suddenly getting most attention, though, is power systems. It used to be seen as a maker of boring old-tech diesel systems for marine vessels and military tanks. But AI datacentres in the US also want the equipment. And they also want Rolls’s gas-fired turbines for primary power as they struggle to get hooked up to an under-invested US electricity grid. Rolls’s order book for power generation was up 55% in the half.

after newsletter promotion

It looks, too, as if there will be spillover AI benefits for Rolls’s small modular reactors (SMRs). At 470 megawatts, SMRs were originally intended only as sources of low-carbon power for national grids, but some hyper-scale datacentre projects in the US are so huge and power-hungry that they have become potential customers. It gives Rolls a foot in several AI power camps: diesel for back-up; gas for primary power; and SMRs when they arrive in the 2030s.

The very big possibility is Rolls’s intended re-entry into the market for engines for narrowbody aircraft. That is a slower story because Airbus and Boeing have yet to commit formally to new single-aisle models. Nor it is guaranteed that Rolls would win a place as an engine supplier given the competition from incumbents.

But the potential market is enormous – many times the size of the widebody one – which is why Rolls’s requests for financial support from the UK Treasury will almost certainly be granted, never mind that corporate welfare for a company awash with cash-for-share buybacks sounds an aberration. In reality, subsidies are a fact of life in the international aerospace business, a point that will surely not be lost on a reindustrialising prime minister. Think of the potential for 40,000 jobs in UK advanced manufacturing, runs the corporate pitch.

If it all comes together, then, yes, Erginbilgiç’s projections for Rolls’s potential are not as wild as they seem. The company is positioned squarely at the centre of “major global trends”, as he puts it: defence, AI and energy transition via nuclear. One of these days, something will go wrong, just as it did regularly at Rolls for about two decades. But it is also impossible to name another major UK company with huge opportunities on various fronts.

In retrospect, the Treasury missed a trick in 2020. Instead of granting loan guarantees to help Rolls out of its Covid financial hole, the UK state could have made a few billion quid by insisting on bonds that converted into shares.

The co-founder of Palestine Action has won permission to challenge the ban against the group at the UK’s highest court.

The direct action group was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July last year but its co-founder, Huda Ammori, has been fighting to have the ban overturned amid a mass civil disobedience campaign.

In February, the high court ruled that the ban was disproportionate and unlawful but its decision was overturned by the court of appeal last month.

On Thursday, the supreme court said Ammori could appeal against the court of appeal’s decision and that the case would be heard in the final quarter of this year.

It means the fate of more than 3,500 people who have been arrested for alleged support of Palestine Action since the ban remains in limbo as their cases are on hold until the legality of proscription has been definitely resolved.

Ammori welcomed the supreme court’s decision, saying: “The proscription of Palestine Action has become a vehicle for a far broader crackdown on expressions of solidarity with the Palestinian people.

“This unprecedented attack on free speech and the right to protest in this country is already having a chilling effect at a time when speaking out about Israel’s crimes could not be more urgent.”

She appealed directly to the supreme court to hear the case after the court of appeal’s decision refused permission to appeal against its own decision within hours of the application.

The court of appeal review was comprised of five judges, which is unusual as it normally consists of two or three. It included the country’s two most senior judges: the lady chief justice, Sue Carr, and the master of the rolls, Geoffrey Vos.

The supreme court said it was arguable that the ban represented a disproportionate interference with articles 10 and 11 of the European convention on human rights, which protect the rights of freedom of speech and protest respectively.

Ammori has pledged to challenge the ban, which has been widely condemned by civil liberties groups, as well as by UN experts and politicians from across the divide, at the European court of human rights if it is upheld by the UK courts.

As the supreme court’s decision was published, dozens more people were arrested for allegedly supporting, being a member of and/or encouraging others to join Palestine Action.

In a demonstration outside Westminster magistrates court in central London, protesters took turns to stand up and declare their support for or membership of Palestine Action.

Many of the mainly elderly protesters lay down after speaking and were carried away by officers. Among those arrested was an 87-year-old woman in a wheelchair.

Porritt, 76, is a former director of Friends of the Earth and was an adviser to the Prince of Wales – now King Charles – for more than 30 years.

Dick Scroop, 79, from Wolverhampton, was one of those who was there to be arrested.

He said: “There’s a genocide in which the British government is deeply implicated by its diplomatic efforts and the continuing supply of weapons to Israel, and the attempt to suppress legitimate protests by the wielding of anti-terrorism laws is simply unacceptable. It’s an assault on free speech.”

By inviting support for Palestine Action, and expressing membership of the group, the protesters risk up to 14 years’ imprisonment in trials before a jury, a significant escalation from most of the previous arrests for holding placards which will be dealt with by magistrates and risk a maximum of six months in jail.

Many arrested on Thursday had previously been arrested for holding placards allegedly supporting Palestine Action.

The Metropolitan Police said 117 people were arrested, most for “expressing support for a proscribed organisation”.

The Guardian view on ‘kidulthood’: Britain prices young adults out of independent life

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 17:30:50 GMT

More young people live with parents as low wages, insecure work and unaffordable housing turn family support into another source of inequality

In Britain, young people are expected to become independent in their 20s. Yet the UK’s economic model increasingly denies them the means to do so. Analysis by the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS), commissioned partly for the BBC, finds that the proportion of 25-year-olds living with their parents has risen from 25% in the 1990s to 42% today. The research says “co-residence” among those in their 20s and 30s has increased by more than a third over two decades. The rate in Britain remains well below Italy and Spain, where leaving home is frequently more about finding a partner than turning 18, going to university or starting work. But that is scant comfort: Britain appears to be slowly drifting towards a southern European experience without the family culture that makes this feel normal.

Young Britons struggle to move out of “the hotel of mum and dad” for obvious reasons. Employment for those aged 25 has fallen for both women and men. Real earnings have barely progressed beyond the level reached around two decades ago. Hardly a surprise, then, that home ownership at 25 has dropped from 43% in the mid-1980s to 15% today. As the IFS notes, the changing age, educational, ethnic or migrant composition of the population might have been expected to reduce rates of co-residence. Instead, the “declining affordability of housing” has driven them up. In short, young adults are not just opting for a cheaper domestic arrangement to save money. They are submitting to it because they have less control over their lives as the options narrow for housing and work.

Britain’s economy risks turning a generation’s 20s into a depressingly prolonged “kidulthood”. Having your own home provides privacy, the ability to establish adult relationships and the space to experiment with identity. The dilemmas that not having a place of one’s own can create were highlighted by a 26-year-old man who moved back to live with his parents. He told the BBC’s Today programme: “I’m not going to bring a girl back to my parents’ house. So it would have 100% affected that part of my life, which does get me low.”

Richer parents often help their adult children to become independent; among the wealthiest fifth of households, about 15% gave or lent money to their children in 2018-20, compared with under 5% among the poorest fifth. Lower-income families help by keeping their adult children dependent in the home. The latter may save rent, but it can also mean less privacy and autonomy for young adults, and greater housing and living costs for their parents. The evidence is that the trend reproduces inequality not only in wealth but in the ability to establish an independent life.

These financial outcomes are not the result of neutral markets. They reflect institutions that suppress wages, let landlords capture housing scarcity and allow the wealthy to buy opportunities denied to others. A social democratic programme should build more social housing, strengthen wages and job security, and shift taxation away from work towards rent extraction. “If you don’t give people a good home, what chance have they got of having a good life?” Andy Burnham has argued. Before becoming prime minister, he promised “the biggest council housebuilding programme since the postwar period”. Without bold change, the government will keep subsidising the consequences of social and economic failure while leaving the causes intact.

The Guardian view on sporting fair play: it was never quite cricket

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 17:25:50 GMT

Saltburn’s alleged trickery caused outrage, but cricket’s moral code conceals a rich history of cheating and convenient national myth

One incident has dominated this week’s sporting headlines, garnering even more column inches than Gianni Infantino’s apparent desire to sell the football World Cup to the highest bidder. It occurred in a second XI cricket match last weekend between Saltburn and Norton in the North Yorkshire and South Durham League. A fielder at first slip was alleged to have clicked his fingers as the ball passed the batter’s bat, in an attempt to con the umpire into thinking that there had been an edge. The ball sank into the wicketkeeper’s gloves; bowler, keeper and fielder erupted in a full-throated appeal; and the umpire sent the disbelieving batter on his way for a duck.

There the matter might have ended, but these days even second XI matches are recorded and there was footage of the alleged finger-clicking. Over the past few days, this footage has been analysed in minute detail. One writer on The Athletic bathetically likened the interrogation of the video to the decoding of the Zapruder film of President John F Kennedy’s assassination. What precisely does it show? Could the sound have emanated from behind a grassy knoll at the Saltburn ground?

The club and league have opened investigations, but, even without those inquiries being concluded, Saltburn have suspended the alleged clicker – 38-year-old Brian Devine – and said that he will not play for the club for the foreseeable future. Sleepy Saltburn, worried about critics labelling it the “Argentina of village cricket”, are taking no chances. But is the footage really definitive? What will Devine’s teammates say? The story could run and run.

“It’s not cricket” has been the hackneyed phrase rolled out in almost every iteration of this gloriously clickbaity story. But what is cricket? It’s one player hurling a dangerous projectile at another. An odd activity on which to base a moral code. Yet, at the same time as parroting “It’s not cricket”, pundits have been enumerating the sport’s numerous other falls from grace (and indeed the great WG Grace was a noted rule-bender) over the centuries. There was bribery and corruption in the early days, which led to games that both teams were trying to lose; numerous incidents of doctoring the ball to get it to behave in peculiar ways, the Australian “Sandpapergate” in 2018 being the most notorious; the time-honoured reluctance of batters to walk for catches even when they know they are out; and a host of modern-day match-fixing scandals. The “spirit of cricket” is a fragile flower.

We have an especially rose-tinted view of village cricket, insisting that amateurs “Play up! Play up! And play the game!”, in the words of Henry Newbolt’s poem Vitaï Lampada. We imagine village cricket as the bucolic dreamworld described in Siegfried Sassoon’s recollections of prewar games (the idyll before the nightmare of the trenches), Hugh de Sélincourt’s 1924 classic The Cricket Match and AG Macdonell’s 1933 England, Their England. Endless summer days, resplendent rural grounds, sumptuous teas and pastoral rivalry.

But even if that vision once shimmered, it does so no longer: the beautiful old cricket ground is now a supermarket car park, English summers increasingly Saharan, and the winning-is-everything mentality that has seeped into amateur cricket all too often ends with volunteer umpires being abused and rival players exchanging jibes – or worse. It’s just not cricket, but then it probably never was.

‘Outstanding leader’ Fleming backed to find calm among the chaos for England

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 17:18:47 GMT

New Zealander has won the County Championship and makes those around him better but is also not averse to mind games

With two games of the 2005 season remaining Nottinghamshire, under the captaincy of Stephen Fleming, were sitting precariously at the top of the County Championship, still needing to visit their two main rivals. First up was Kent: Notts were 397 for five after the first day, but rain washed out most of the second and at the end of the third Kent were only five down. A draw looked inevitable, and with a Shane Warne-inspired Hampshire – Notts’ final opponents – on their way to victory at Glamorgan the title chase seemed to be turning. But Fleming had other plans.

“He called a meeting of the senior players on the fourth morning to say he had an idea,” says Darren Bicknell, his Notts teammate. “If Kent didn’t win the game against us, they were dead, they’d have no way to win the title, so he recognised that he had them over a barrel a little bit.” Fleming offered Kent the chance to chase 420 in 70 overs, an unlikely target – but also the best they were going to get. “To take a calculated gamble in that game was a stroke of genius,” Bicknell says. “Some of the senior players were a bit anxious, thinking we didn’t need to take any risks because the draw was still a good result. But people went with him.”

On that final day Kent duly declared their first innings; Notts motored at seven an over until the agreed total was reached then declared also; then Kent, with no choice but to attack, were bowled out for 205. Notts won the title with a game to spare.

England’s interim captain when New Zealand played them the previous year – Marcus Trescothick, now back in charge of England’s Test side in an interim role – had admitted his opposite number was “regarded as the best captain in the world”, and here was more proof. Kent’s first man out in that forlorn run chase? Rob Key, the man who has just appointed him England coach.

“He was just very calm all the time, very unruffled,” Bicknell says of Fleming. “He worked out the game really well, worked out people very well, but overall he was just calm, even in the hottest of moments. Everyone trusted him to be on everything. I think in moments when things weren’t going well, there was a reflection from him that everything was still all right: just be patient, stay calm, and it will come right as long as we’re doing the right things. He was just a really good man and the sort of person you felt like you wanted to play for. I think he’ll be very good and he’ll bring a sense of common sense and calmness to the whole England set-up.”

Fleming has not always been calm in hot moments. There is another widely quoted example of his cricketing cunning: in the fifth of six ODIs in South Africa in 2004 the hosts, needing to win to keep the series alive, came out to chase an achievable, rain-affected target of 178 in 29 overs. As their captain, Graeme Smith, approached the crease Fleming unleashed a stream of invective.

Just three days earlier Smith had described Fleming “changing his game plan against me in every match so far … I’m sure he’s just trying to get into my mind”. But as this normally gentle man showered him in abuse, that was all forgotten. Smith responded in kind and then, distracted, scored 15 off 33; New Zealand won by two runs. “Graeme is an emotional guy. That was one chink we thought we might explore and he took the bait,” Fleming later said. “It was never personal. I made it personal in one game to get the edge.”

Those who have worked with Fleming describe an empathetic man, a skilled reader of people – skills he can use to build you up, but perhaps also to destroy you. “He was quite simply an outstanding leader of men,” says David Alleyne, another member of that Nottinghamshire side. “He had a great way of communicating, and finding the right time and the right space to really empower you as an individual, and get you to think about your game in a way that was going to help the team. I found him quite remarkable in that sense. He was very calm, very calculated.”

Praise for Fleming has not quite been universal, and most notably Hemang Badani, currently head coach of Delhi Capitals and Southern Brave, said the success he achieved at Chennai Super Kings in the Indian Premier League – where he reached 10 finals and won five titles – was all down to his long-time captain, MS Dhoni. “He’s never won anywhere outside the IPL,” Badani said in 2024. “If someone says he’s a great coach, I wouldn’t agree. Dhoni is the winner.”

Chris Jordan, having played under Fleming at CSK and Southern Brave, disagrees. “He comes with a lot of empathy. He has a very relaxed aura about him but he’s still very, very detailed in his planning and his messaging. And he’s very, very good at creating role clarity within a team,” Jordan says. “One thing he identified about the Hundred, he was astute enough to realise that it can be quite chaotic. So he found a way of getting us to find simplicity within the chaos, just with his messaging and his tactical awareness. He’s just a very well-rounded coach, and when you start to spend time with him you really get the feeling that you not only want to do well for yourself, but you want to do it for him as well.”

Jordan is one of just a handful of people to have played under Fleming and alongside Joe Root, who has returned as England captain. “I definitely think Joe and Flem as a combination will be quite excellent, and I actually think Flem could take Joe Root’s captaincy to the next level,” Jordan says. “He really has that knack of bringing out the best in players and making you really believe in yourself. I find the debate about the purported conflict between academic and technical education baffling and somewhat amusing (Burnham to tell schools in England to adapt teaching to local business needs, 28 July).

In the 1950s, I attended Northampton technical high school. I studied the sciences plus English, French and technical (engineering) drawing to GCE level. I also did hands-on workshops in woodwork, metalwork and leatherwork (Northampton being a traditional shoemaking town). At A-level, I passed physics, chemistry and double maths, and studied physics at Leeds University. I also sang in choirs.

My subsequent career in international business systems took me through manufacturing companies, consultancy and ultimately university teaching. I also sang in a cathedral choir for 50 years. I never found the academic, practical and artistic worlds mutually exclusive.

So a useful model that we’ve perhaps lost: back to the 1950s!Graham WarrenCoventry

Andy Burnham’s desire to revive vocational education is very welcome and long overdue (Andy Burnham’s plans for technical education build on coalition’s UTC roots, 29 July), but has no chance of long-term fulfilment without a complete overhaul of the 14-19 curriculum and, crucially, the abandonment of the deep-rooted cultural assumptions that underlie the current desiccated model, with its dreary apparatus of nonstop tests and examinations.

Chief of these assumptions is the idea that technical and vocational education are for “other people’s children” – an idea that can be traced back to the late 1860s, when industrial magnates began sending their children to be gentrified at public schools, and which will persist as long as technical and vocational education is presented chiefly as a solution to the problems posed by “non-academic” pupils.

Burnham’s desire to establish parity of esteem between hard hat and mortar board is wholly admirable, but that parity has to be established while children are still at school and, in this regard, he could do worse than revisit the recommendations of the 2004 Tomlinson report, which the then Labour government sadly lacked the courage to implement. Gary NethercottWoodbridge, Suffolk

Offering vocational and technical courses aligned to the job market makes sense. However, the root cause of why many young people are disengaged is what needs addressing.

The skills needed in the workplace are generic: team building, creativity, resilience, flexibility, independent thinking, work ethic, communication, self-belief, cooperation and empathy. These skills not only provide readiness for work but also enjoyment of learning and, importantly, relevance.

The demise of teaching in the performing arts has demoted these very skills that are paramount to the development of young people and readiness for the workplace.

Come on Burnham, Powell et al … this is the chance to redress the balance in teaching and meaningful learning, not just to attempt to ready young people for the job market. It is how to enable young people to become fully rounded adults that is crucial. Helen ElliottRetired deputy headteacher, Taunton, Somerset

Be good to know if Andy Burnham’s advice to state schools, “teach pupils for local jobs”, applies to private schools. Dr Mike SquiresLondon

I’m a mum of two. Since my first pregnancy, I have grappled with the endless advice and contradictions on health. Should I use glass bottles of non-organic milk, or plastic bottles of organic milk. Organic broccoli wrapped in plastic, or plastic-free non-organic broccoli.

As I read the article, I also processed the solution: “Mothers can take some steps to protect themselves, including using water filtration systems that remove Pfas, buying organic, avoiding waterproof clothing, and avoiding stain guards.”

My immediate reaction was of despair and rage. How can these huge, systemic issues be just another thing for us to solve? How many working families can afford to eat only organic food? How many of us can afford to fit water filter systems? How many of us can avoid getting wet during school pick ups?

It is outrageous that these issues are now so commonplace and uncontested that the burden of solving them gets shunted on to the shoulders of parents.

It is not our responsibility. It is the government’s responsibility to legislate. It is big agriculture’s responsibility not to cover our food in chemicals. It is the water companies’ responsibility to ensure we have clean water. As if these things even need to be said.

I cannot read another article about how I am irreparably damaging my child’s long-term health, with the solution just to “buy x or y”. The solution is bigger and harder than this. And it is not our responsibility to shoulder it. Kendal ArcherExeter

Homelessness crisis starts at the prison gate

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 17:03:01 GMT

No government can credibly promise to end rough sleeping while one public institution keeps releasing people straight into it, writes Gary Teper

We should all applaud Andy Burnham’s commitment to end rough sleeping (‘It’s generations of decline’: can Andy Burnham really end rough sleeping?, 24 July). The ambition is right and overdue. But he set the same goal in Greater Manchester in 2017 and found, as anyone would, that you cannot clear people off the street faster than the system puts them there. Much of rough sleeping is manufactured upstream.

Take prison. In 2024-25, around 1,000 people a month left prison in England and Wales homeless and went on to sleep rough. Homelessness feeds reoffending, reoffending feeds custody, and release feeds the street. No government can credibly promise to end rough sleeping while one public institution keeps releasing people straight into it.

We run accommodation for prison leavers under the Ministry of Justice’s transitional community accommodation service tier 3 (Cas3) scheme and house more than 1,400 ex-offenders a night. What we see is simple: a bed alone is not enough. Many people leaving custody need housing alongside trauma-informed support, life skills and help to sustain a tenancy. Give them that continuity and the cycle can be broken. Without it, homelessness becomes a revolving door.

The £340m to be spent at the street end will not fix a pipeline that starts at the prison gate. Until the government treats prison release as homelessness prevention, not homelessness management, the promise will stay a promise. Gary TeperManaging director, The Housing Network

Desmond WhymsFormer senior health adviser, Department for International Development

‘It was a big shock’: new border rules left couple stuck in Kraków after living in UK for 80 years

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 16:59:20 GMT

Maria and Czeslaw Krupa, who arrived as children of displaced Polish veterans, told they have no post-Brexit rights to return home to Bury

Two Polish citizens who have lived in the UK for nearly 80 years after their parents fled the second world war have spoken of their terrifying experience after being told they did not have post-Brexit rights to return to the UK.

In May, while visiting Poland, they learned that although they had been welcomed as refugees after the war, they now needed special post-Brexit paperwork to return to their home in Bury, Greater Manchester.

Maria Krupa, 85, and her husband, Czeslaw, 92, who met in the UK and went on to marry and settle in Bury, were issued with “aliens’ registration cards” and have travelled extensively as adults without anyone asking them for their immigration status.

Czeslaw, who came from Lviv which was then part of Poland, and Maria, who left her home town in what is now Belarus as an infant, had travelled to Poland in May to meet surviving family members.

But Ryanair refused to allow them to board the flight for their return journey on the grounds that they had neither proof of the right to live in the UK nor the new electronic travel authorisation (ETA) now required for foreign tourists entering the UK.

“It was a big shock,” said Maria. “We were very, very disappointed and a bit upset because my husband takes a lot of medicine because of a stroke to his spinal cord.”

They had arrived in Southampton in 1947 and 1948 as the young dependants of displaced Polish service members who had been evacuated from their homes in 1940 and later became part of Gen Władysław Anders’s Polish army that served in Persia, India, the Middle East and Africa.

Anders’s army played a key role in the defeat of the Third Reich and had integrated into the British military command structure after friction with the Soviets in 1942.

“We tried to explain to Ryanair that our fathers fought for Poland and England in the war, but they refused to let us on the plane because they said they would have to pay a big fine,” said Maria.

“My husband was really upset,” she said, explaining that Czeslaw used a mobility scooter and was on a lot of medication after the stroke. He has difficulty getting in and out of cars and “just wanted to get home”, she said.

They are speaking out to help others who might be in the same position. “It was a big, big shock because we never heard of this and we never thought for one minute that after nearly 80 years someone would tell us we couldn’t go home,” said Maria.

Kate Smart, the chief executive of Settled, who helped the Krupas, said the charity was seeing “thousands of cases” like the Krupas’. “It is a really common occurrence, almost on a daily basis,” she said.

The EU settlement scheme was launched in 2019 to give EU citizens living in the UK the documentary evidence needed to travel as they had done under the pre-Brexit, free-movement rules.

Many of the people seen by Settled are elderly people who have British children and grandchildren. “They have nobody in their family circle who thinks like immigrants so they don’t talk about things like ‘settled status’,” said Smart.

after newsletter promotion

Maria said she had never thought to get a British passport as she had never needed it in the previous 80 years and it had never crossed her mind. “It was really important. I didn’t think of it as sort of weakening my identity. I love England. I mean, I always say, I’m very grateful to England, you know, to have taken so many people, you know thousands after the war. But I just thought it was important that we stay Polish,” she said.

After being forced to leave the airport late on a Sunday night in May, they returned the next day with an ETA but the couple had to pose as tourists, claiming they lived in Poland as the online form would not accept their British address.

Maria said: “When we arrived in England we were terrified. We had to be careful about what we said. We were terrified because they started asking questions and we thought we are not going to lie again and have to tell the truth.”

After going to Citizens Advice in Bury, they were connected with Settled. Smart commended the Home Office resolution centre for its swift action after the charity submitted a no-time-limit application that resulted in settled status for the Krupas last week.

She appealed to the government to take note of the issues with the EU settlement scheme, arguing “a process should have kicked in at the airport” when an issue such as this one arose.

A spokesperson said the Home Office would encourage people to check their immigration status before they travel, but anyone in a similar situation to the Krupas should make a no-time-limit application to get the paperwork they needed to travel in and out of the country.

“Anyone settled in the UK without up-to-date evidence of their status is encouraged to make a no-time-limit application. This will give them access to an eVisa and facilitate seamless future travel,” they said.

FA raises minimum ban for racism and other forms of discrimination to 10 matches

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 16:34:53 GMT

Discrimination ‘continues to be challenge’

Current minimum ban is six matches

The FA is to increase the minimum punishment for discriminatory behaviour to 10 matches, in an attempt to counteract behaviour it says “continues to be a challenge across the game”.

The changes will come into force at the start of the new season and will apply to players and other football participants who are found guilty of an “aggravated breach” of the FA’s disciplinary rules on improper conduct, effectively actions that included discriminatory behaviour against any protected characteristics. Currently the minimum suspension for such a breach is six matches.

Across the 2025-26 season 10 individuals were found guilty of aggravated breaches, with their punishments, decided by independent Regulatory Commissions, ranging from six to nine matches. Under the new rules a punishment of fewer than 10 matches will only be allowed if sufficient mitigating factors have been presented, and the individual themselves has pleaded guilty to the charge.

Among the cases heard involved the Preston’s Milutin Osmajic, in which the Montenegrin was found to have made racist remarks to the Burnley player Hannibal Mejbri during a Championship match. Osmajic, who denied making the remarks, was served with a nine-match ban and given a minimum fine of £20,000. There has been growing concern that the behaviour of players in the professional game has trickled down the pyramid, creating greater problems in the grassroots game.

“We are committed to delivering a game free from discrimination. While significant progress has been made in recent years, discriminatory conduct continues to be a challenge across the game,” the FA said in a statement. “Enhanced measures are necessary to tackle this abhorrent conduct, and our updated sanction guidelines will now require regulatory commissions to impose a standard suspension of at least 10 matches in these circumstances.”

The new rules do afford commissions some flexibility. Cases that involve aggravated breaches “in writing only or via any communication device” – ie comments made online – could receive a punishment as low as three matches in the event of mitigating factors being accepted. If, however, an individual found to have breached the rules then commits a second offence, bans of over a year could be applied.

More prisoners in England and Wales are recalled than released for first time

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 16:31:07 GMT

Returns for breaches of licence conditions rose 31% in the first quarter of 2026, adding to pressure on prison places

More people were recalled to prison than were released during the first three months of 2026, the first time on record the “recall rate” has surpassed 100% in England and Wales.

Between January and March 2026, 12,977 people were released from prison while 13,193 people were returned to prison for breaching their licence conditions, up 31% from last year, new Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data showed.

This means that for every 100 people released, 101 people were recalled to custody, creating a “recall rate” of over 100%.

This rate has increased rapidly from about 30% a decade ago. Between January and March 2016, 17,923 people were released and 5,185 were recalled, meaning about 30 people were recalled for every 100 prisoners released.

Prisons in England and Wales are close to capacity, and the government has recently paused its plans to release about 6,000 prisoners early to ease the crisis.

Andy Keen-Downs, the chief executive of the Prison Advice and Care Trust, said: “The prison population crisis will not be solved if as many people are being sent back to prison as are leaving it.”

He warned that if current circumstances don’t change, prison places may run out by Christmas.

“Hundreds of people are recalled every month not because they have committed new offences, but because they have fallen foul of licence conditions,” he said. “This makes little sense at a time when the government is doing everything it can to reduce pressure on the prison system.”

In total, 51,419 prisoners were recalled to jail in the year to March 2026 after breaching the terms of their licence, up 28% from the previous 12 months and the highest number since current records began in 2015.

Of all recalls, 22% involved a further charge of offending, while the vast majority were for breaches of licence conditions, which have risen sharply over the past decade.

Breaches include failing to keep in touch with probation services or failing to reside at an approved address.

The figures also showed 70,066 prisoners have been freed early since September 2024, when the government brought in emergency measures in response to the overcrowding crisis.

Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said the number of recalls were “piling further pressure on an already overcrowded prison estate” and showed “a system that simply isn’t working”.

“Thousands of people are being sent back to custody each year for licence breaches rather than new crimes, and we know from our work that many of these recalls are linked to homelessness after leaving prison, addiction to drugs and alcohol, and mental health issues,” he said.

Almost 13,000 people left prison homeless or as rough sleepers in the year to April 2025, a 39% rise from the previous year.

Pavan Dhaliwal, the chief executive of the charity Revolving Doors, which works with people who are in repeat contact with the justice system, said the system needs reform so recall becomes a “genuine last resort”.

“Sending people back to prison when they are struggling to rebuild their lives is costly, counterproductive and keeps the revolving door turning,” she said.

The MoJ said the increase was probably due in part to early release schemes, under which more prisoners have been released on licence earlier in their sentences.

Alex Hewson from the Prison Reform Trust said more people on short sentences being released on licence was creating “more opportunities for recall”.

“We are now using recall far more frequently than in the recent past, and it is reasonable to ask whether every return to custody is necessary and proportionate,” he said. “Given the pressure on both prisons and probation, that question deserves serious attention.”

Gunther von Hagens obituary

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 16:15:40 GMT

German anatomist who devised a system of ‘plastination’ to preserve cadavers that were exhibited all over the world

The German anatomist Gunther von Hagens, who has died aged 81 of a cerebral haemorrhage, following nearly two decades of living with Parkinson’s disease, was the creator of the international exhibition Body Worlds, which generated plaudits and revulsion in equal measure whenever and wherever it toured. Frequently accused of showmanship and self-aggrandisement, the theatrical Von Hagens, always seen wearing a black fedora, was known by some sections of the media as “Doctor Death” thanks to his use of a technique called “plastination”, which he had invented to preserve human corpses. Bodily fluids, fats and organs that usually decay after death were replaced with plastics, so tissues remained intact. The corpses could then be put on display, usually with the skin peeled away to reveal skeletons, organs and muscles.

Plastinated corpses remain flexible, meaning they can be manipulated into lifelike poses – a basketball player or a trapeze artist – or sliced into cross sections. But Von Hagens often trod a fine line between scientific exposition and the macabre. Other exhibits included a dead expectant woman with her foetus still in her uterus and a man who had deliberately killed himself by driving into a tree at the place his wife had died previously. Both had donated their bodies for plastination and were exhibited along with the objects that caused their deaths.

Unsurprisingly, Von Hagens and Body Worlds – which first went on display in Japan in 1995 – were considered somewhat contentious. Religious leaders denounced him. Churches in his native Germany held requiems for the corpses. The chief rabbi of Haifa described plastination as a violation of the Jewish principle of kavod adam, or human dignity, while the Catholic archbishop of Miami deemed Von Hagens would, when arriving at the gates of hades, be treated as he had treated his subjects, unaware that the anatomist had already expressed a wish for his own body to be plastinated on death.

He was also disparaged by secular critics who simply found his work repugnant, with the Nobel laureate Günter Grass reported to have compared him to the Nazi eugenicist Josef Mengele. The journalist Jasper Gerard wrote a particularly caustic article in the Sunday Times in 2002, concluding that “the moral problem is not how Von Hagens treats the dead, it’s what [his exhibition] says about his view of the living”.

Others acclaimed Von Hagens as an emancipator and normaliser of the human physique. The Akron Beacon Journal in Ohio said he “illuminated physiology and helped us grasp the anatomical elegance of our species”. One visitor to Body Worlds, who had tried to take her own life, declared that the exhibits convinced her never to consider harming herself again. At the time of Von Hagens’s death, it was estimated more than 20,000 people had pledged to donate their bodies to him – including family members and his employees – while more than 58 million people have visited Body Worlds. The exhibition even featured in the 2006 James Bond film, Casino Royale, in which Von Hagens played a cameo role.

Over the years many legal challenges were brought against him and Body Worlds in various countries over both his acquisition of cadavers and the morality of his exhibitions, including accusations that he received corpses from Kyrgyzstan without the permission of family members or the authorities. He insisted that all corpses in his possession were donated with full consent. However, in 2002 Von Hagens was accused of accepting 56 corpses from a Russian pathologist who had apparently passed them on to him without approval. The bodies were impounded by German officials and returned to Russia. Von Hagens was not charged with an offence.

Meanwhile, in 2002 Von Hagens held a public postmortem of one of his subjects – the first public autopsy in the UK since the 1830s and broadcast in part by Channel 4 – in the Atlantis art gallery in east London before a sold-out audience of 500. This, it was argued, breached the Anatomy Act of 1832 introduced to regulate educational use of cadavers. Once again charges were never filed.

Born in Alt-Skalden, which was then part of Germany, but is now in Poland, where the town is known as Skalmierzyce, Gunther was the third of five children. His father, Gerhard Liebchen, formerly a bank clerk, was a wartime sergeant in the Nazi SS, his mother, Gertrud, was a homemaker. Having fled the advancing Soviet army towards the end of the second world war, the family lived in Berlin before settling in Greiz, a town in what would become communist East Germany.

Gunther was a haemophiliac – once given only days to live – and spent much of his childhood in and out of hospital. This stimulated an interest in medicine, specifically anatomy, and after leaving school in 1965 he studied medicine at Jena University, having witnessed his first human autopsy at the age of 17. While at university he began questioning the orthodoxy of communism and participated in protests against the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968.

The following January he made attempts to escape eastern Europe, twice failing to cross the Czech border into Austria. He was arrested and spent almost two years in prison.

On his release, the West German government bought his freedom, alongside other political prisoners, and he continued his degree at Lübeck University, later earning a doctorate from Heidelberg University in 1975. This was where he met Cornelia von Hagens, another medical student, who became his wife that year, and whose surname he took. They had three children, Rurik, Bera and Tona, before divorcing in 1989.

After graduating, Von Hagens became a lecturer at the Institutes of Pathology and Anatomy at Heidelberg where, between 1977 and 1982, he developed and patented the technology for infusing anatomical specimens with plastics. The technique had obvious practical medical uses. Students could view damaged hearts or scarred livers without waiting for somebody to donate their body, while entire corpses could also be sliced into slabs for study.

Von Hagens subsequently set up a company to supply plastinated body parts to medical institutions and eventually began to realise his technique might have commercial value via exhibitions and practical demonstrations of his methods. In this he was aided by his second wife, Angelina Whalley, a German anatomist whom he met after she attended his anatomy classes, and whom British tabloids typically nicknamed “the Bride of Frankenstein”. She managed his Heidelberg-based business and later curated his exhibitions after they married in 1992.

Despite being accused of unnecessary dramatic flair, Von Hagens, an avowed agnostic, insisted his sole intention was to educate the public about human anatomy and to end the squeamishness often associated with it. “It’s an honour to cause this controversy,” he told the Guardian in 2002 at the opening of his London exhibition. “Yes, some specimens are difficult to look at. But it has helped people discover new respect for their bodies.”

In later life he divided his time between Berlin and Guben, on the Polish border, where he had set up a plastination laboratory. Beyond his medical and business life, his interests were limited, although he enjoyed playing and listening to violin music.

Angelina and his children from his first marriage survive him.

Gunther Gerhard von Hagens, anatomist and businessman, born 10 January 1945; died 24 July 2026

Uefa agrees to boycott Fifa competitions if World Cup sell-off plans proceed

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 15:35:09 GMT

Uefa agree stance at emergency meeting on Thursday

Boycott would begin with Under-20 Women’s World Cup

European countries have agreed to boycott all Fifa competitions if Gianni Infantino pushes forward with his proposals to sell chunks of the World Cup to US-based private investment.

In an extraordinary development all 55 Uefa members resolved not to participate in future World Cups or other Fifa-run events, saying in a statement that they “unanimously and unequivocally reject” the proposals. An emergency meeting that lasted just short of two hours ended with a united front despite earlier fears that smaller countries, attracted by the money on offer through Infantino’s scheme, would be swayed in favour.

European FAs are expected to write to Fifa this week with a formal notification of their threat to boycott future tournaments unless the planned World Cup sell-off is withdrawn.

It means Infantino faces an uphill battle to push his plan forward. Countries had been given until 19 September to sign up but there will now be significant pressure to drastically revise his scheme or withdraw it completely. While the majority of European FAs had submitted letters of support in favour of his re-election next March, such a decisive line in the sand from Uefa weakens his position dramatically.

Uefa’s statement confirmed the decision. “As a result of today’s discussion, no Uefa national teams will participate in any Fifa competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that Fifa will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” it read.

Thursday’s meeting was introduced by the Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, with executive committee members and Uefa’s Fifa council representatives also addressing delegates. Those early speeches are understood to have set the tone, with around 20 further FA heads taking the floor and multiple sources describing an atmosphere of “unity”. Among those to offer their view was Debbie Hewitt, the president of the FA, who one attendee said gave a “very tough” exposition in favour of a boycott.

That was backed up in a statement by an FA spokesperson that read: “We stand shoulder to shoulder with our European colleagues and fully support the collective view. We oppose Fifa’s plans – the Fifa World Cup belongs to football and always will.”

Along the lines spelled out by Uefa, at senior level the proposed boycott would begin with next year’s Women’s World Cup, while the first age-group Fifa tournament to be boycotted is likely to be the Under-20 Women’s World Cup. It is due to take place in Poland from 5 September with six of the 24 competitors, including England, due to represent Uefa countries.

England’s women’s team also have a two-legged World Cup qualifying playoff tie against Greece in October, which would be a major test of the FA’s resolve if Fifa refuse to back down.

The European governing body invited other confederations to follow their lead. Uefa are understood to be confident that a number of Asian countries, in particular, are similarly minded. Infantino’s strongholds traditionally lie outside Europe and a collapse in support elsewhere could have severe consequences for the Fifa president.

“National associations around the world are now presented with an ultimatum: accept the irreversible capture of football’s greatest competitions or bear the consequences,” Uefa said. “This is not a ‘democratic decision’, but governance by intimidation – an act of coercion unworthy of an institution entrusted with the stewardship of the global game.”

Sources within European football believe Uefa’s decision increases the chances of a Europe-backed candidate running against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, which he had been expected to sail through without opposition.

North American confederation Concacaf also unanimously rejected Fifa’s proposal after an emergency meeting chaired by the president, Victor Montagliani, who is seen as a potential successor to Infantino, but stopped short of following Uefa’s lead by announcing a boycott.

Despite this however, it is understood that the majority of Concacaf’s 41 members are losing confidence in Infantino’s leadership of Fifa, raising the possibility that his own position could be in serious doubt for the first time since he took office in 2016.

A number of European national associations are understood to have held talks with their respective governments over the matter, many of whom have backed a boycott in private.

The new UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, was the first politician to criticise Fifa’s plan on Tuesday evening, writing on X that the World Cup “was never anyone’s to sell”.

“This is a principled decision that we strongly support. Football belongs to the fans, not billionaire investors. Enough is enough. It’s time to take a stand to protect our game.”

Child pedestrian casualties are almost five times higher in England’s worst-off areas

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 15:01:10 GMT

Official figures expose widening gap in road deaths and injuries between poor and wealthy postcodes

The number of children killed or injured crossing roads is almost five times higher in England’s most deprived areas than its wealthiest, official analysis suggests.

Department for Transport figures show a widening gap over the past 10 years in road casualties between those living in the poorest 10% of postcodes and the most affluent 10%.

The number of people reported killed or seriously injured across Great Britain’s roads went up to 29,918 in 2025, 2,432 of whom were under 16. The total was 3% above the 2022-24 average while fatalities fell 4% to 1,538.

DfT analysis of where the most serious accidents in England occurred showed stark differences in the proportion of casualties from poorer and wealthier areas, particularly among younger people.

More than 20% of child pedestrians killed or injured lived in the most deprived 10% of areas, compared with 4% living in the least deprived, according to the DfT report on deprivation and road casualties in England.

It found strong links between casualties and deprivation for all pedestrians and bus users. The difference is less stark for car occupants, but mileage is higher in wealthier postcodes, which the analysts said “suggests that the risk for car occupants is much higher for the most deprived income deciles even though they have less exposure”.

The overall British figures released by the government showed fatalities continued to rise for motorcycle users, countering the falling death toll for car drivers.

Campaigners said the 14% rise – from 325 deaths in 2024 to 372 last year – needed a response.

Rebecca Guy of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents said: “It is particularly concerning that the gap between the most and least deprived areas has widened over the last decade.

“If the government is serious about reducing road deaths and serious injuries, tackling inequality must be at the heart of its approach.

“That means targeting investment and prevention efforts toward the communities at greatest risk, ensuring everyone has access to safe roads, safe infrastructure and safe journeys.”

Motorcyclists were one of the most vulnerable groups on the roads and the figures reinforced the need for targeted action to improve their safety, she said.

after newsletter promotion

Speeding was a factor in 52% of recorded deaths on Great Britain’s roads last year. More than three-quarters of those killed across all types of accidents were male, the figures show.

Motorways were statistically the safest roads per mile travelled in 2025 – accounting for only 6% of fatalities despite carrying 21% of traffic.

A DfT spokesperson said: “Everyone should feel safe on our roads, no matter where they live.

“Our road safety strategy, the first in over a decade, recognises that people from deprived areas can face higher risks on the road. That’s why it aims to reduce deaths and serious injuries for all road users. We will keep track of the strategy’s impact, including how it affects people in more deprived areas to make sure measures are fair to all communities.”

The headline on this article was amended on 30 July 2026. An earlier version said that child pedestrian deaths were almost five times higher in England’s worst-off areas; it should have said casualties.

Even GB News cringes as Reform turns dementia patients into a political football

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 14:58:28 GMT

Honest Bob was rattled at the idea of joining cross-party talks on social care. Why bother behaving as a serious opposition?

When you’ve lost the trust of GB News, when you’re too deranged, too extreme and too outright mendacious for your biggest fan, then you know you are in trouble. You can almost sense the panic beginning to set in at Reform HQ.

No longer topping the opinion polls. A new prime minister resetting the dial, the public increasingly choosing optimism over grievance. A party mired in financial sleaze. A leader turning into a laughing stock in his head-to-head with a dustbin. It was never meant to be this way for Reform. They thought they were the winners.

With Nigel Farage locked away on a self-imposed witness protection programme, Richard Tice on an Accountancy for Dummies summer course and Zia Yusuf on a never-ending anger management retreat, the Reform front-of-house recess duties have been left to Robert Jenrick. Which is just the way Honest Bob likes it.

No one rates Honest Bob higher than Honest Bob. He believes himself to be a winner. Someone who connects with the ordinary people. Which, to be fair, he does. Because Honest Bob has the unique ability to get people to dislike him on sight. It saves time that way. Why waste time getting to know him before you find you can’t bear him? He is a man who radiates inauthenticity. An establishment politician through and through who poses as the voice of forgotten Britain. Who believes the rules don’t apply to him. Who can’t help patronising everyone he meets.

Thursday morning brought Honest Bob’s latest exercise in self-destruction. Giving a speech in a large hall, rammed with about … er … eight people. The only person in the room who actually wanted to be there was Honest Bob himself. Sometimes you have to wonder if it’s all a game on his part. As if he knows just how hopeless he really is and has devoted his life’s work to parodying himself. Reform’s ultimate enemy within. The former Tory politician who switched allegiance merely to bring down Nige, one day to be acknowledged as a hero to the Conservative party.

There again, that would assume a level of self-awareness and intelligence that Honest Bob has never previously shown. So best to work on the basis that what you see is what you get. A not-very-bright opportunist who has bounced his way through life from one bad choice to another. A man with nothing very much to say, who still needs a teleprompter to say it.

What Honest Bob wanted to talk about today was Andy Burnham’s “death tax”, which doesn’t even exist yet other than as a vague possibility to be considered among other options. But for Bob it was as if it had already been implemented. Already HMRC inspectors were hovering around hospices, terrifying dying patients by stealing their wedding rings, confiscating their debit cards and laughing as they emptied their houses and their bank accounts. This was Honest Bob’s wish fulfilment. There’s nothing that excites him more than misery porn.

Then a rare moment of honesty. “I want to level with you,” he said. It would only be the least well-off who would end up paying a death tax. The rich would find ways of avoiding it. And by the rich, he meant himself, Nige, Dicky, Zia and Posh George Cottrell. “That’s what offshore accounts are for,” he boasted. You wouldn’t find any of the Reform elite being dim enough to pay for someone else’s social care.

Dementia and disability were for other people’s families, not his. What was it to do with him if someone got Alzheimer’s and needed full-time care for seven years? In Reform World it’s every person for themselves. Unless they happen to be a party donor and pornographer. Under those circumstances, Honest Bob was sure he would find a way of saving that person £45m in tax by granting an unlawful planning permission. The rich look after each other.

Honest Bob droned on like this for the best part of 20 minutes. Making specious argument after specious argument. Knocking down countless straw men. Lacking the insight to realise he was embarrassing himself. When he finally stopped, not a single person in the room bothered to applaud. Not even the Reform press person who was there to control the complete lack of interest.

The first question came from GB News, more in sorrow than in anger. Why had Honest Bob made such a fool of himself? Why not actually try to join in the cross-party talks to find a solution to such a serious problem? Why the scare tactics of a death tax that isn’t even government policy? If the Tories and the Lib Dems could behave as grownups and engage with Andy Burnham, why couldn’t Reform? Instead, Reform ended up looking like a deeply unserious party. One that didn’t even have a health and social care spokesperson.

For the first time, Honest Bob looked rattled. It hadn’t occurred to him that GB News might desert him. He had believed them to be on the side of grievance and division. What was in it for Reform to behave like a proper opposition? After all, its leader isn’t even currently an MP. Far better to invent a government policy it can then attack than to try to reach a consensus. That was clearly the way forward. Dementia patients were best used as a political football.

It was all downhill from there. Few other media organisations could be bothered to engage with the half-arsed grandstanding. They were more interested in following up the Guardian’s story of Posh George transferring £2m to his mum, moments before she sent money to Thicky Dicky. Why were all the financial dealings of the Reform elite so opaque? Why the need to deal in crypto and offshore accounts? What was wrong with ordinary bank transfers? It was almost as if there was something to hide.

Now Honest Bob got genuinely snappy and tetchy. Why couldn’t people ask him the questions he wanted them to? Where was the respect he deserved? He had nothing to say on the money other than he was sure everything was above board. Of course it was. We had his word for it. Daddy had just been indulging George. Much more of this and the wheels will come off entirely.

Four crashes and a disqualification: chaotic Commonwealth Games race to be replayed

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 14:27:44 GMT

Scotland’s Melanie Woods was originally awarded gold

Women’s T54 1500m final will now be restaged on Friday

It turned into Glasgow’s version of Wacky Races. After four crashes, three overturned wheelchairs, three appeals and a disqualification, the women’s T54 1500m final is to be rerun 39 hours after it first took place.

The controversial decision was taken on Thursday after the extraordinary scenes at the Scotstoun track on Wednesday – and despite the medallists doing a lap of honour, posing for photographs together and going to bed thinking they were part of Commonwealth history.

The drama started on the first bend when Canada’s Nandini Sharma cut across Noemi Alphonse of Mauritius, who then flipped spectacularly in the air.

Moments later Australia’s Eliza Ault-Connell, who had also been impeded, was knocked to the floor. The chain reaction then led to Scotland’s Joanna Robertson skidding on one wheel across the Mondo track, while England’s Ellis Kottas crashed into a wall.

While all this was happening, Scotland’s Melanie Woods took gold in a Commonwealth record of 3min 33.39sec. But it turned out the drama was just getting started.

Shortly afterwards, Sharma was disqualified for causing the crash, leaving Kottas to take silver, having finished 50 seconds back, and Australia’s Mikaela Dingley to claim bronze.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

However, after appeals from Australia and Mauritius, and a counter-claim from Canada, Para-athletics chiefs have now decided to run the race again at 10.24am on Friday - more than 39 hours after the official race began.

Six of the seven athletes will be allowed to compete again. However, Sharma’s disqualification will stand. The ceremony was not due to be held until Thursday, so none of the athletes were actually presented with medals.

In an Instagram post on Thursday Kottas said she accepted the decision. “While I really don’t want to rerun the race (lowkey traumatised) if I’m going to medal I want to do so on my own merit, so I will go out and give it all I’ve got,” she said. “If I don’t medal, so be it. I’ll still have the incredible memories of lifting that England flag.”

However the decision was criticised by Jonny Riall, chef de mission for Team England, who said: “We are incredibly disappointed by the late decision to rerun the T54 1500m tomorrow morning.

“While there is no formal protest process available to us, we have strongly challenged the decision,” he added. “The race officials did not halt the race at the time of the incident, nor was any immediate decision made to declare the race void or order a rerun.”

Team Scotland also released a statement, which was rather more prosaic. “We note the decision of the Jury of Appeal regarding the Women’s T54 1500m final,” it said. “Melanie Woods and Joanna Robertson will now prepare to compete again on Friday in the rerun.”

Fifa’s sales pitch revealed: more tournaments, more debt … but no mention of women’s game

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 14:19:35 GMT

Fifa’s 25-page sales deck produced by JP Morgan

Reference made to doubling global tournaments

Fifa’s sales pitch to persuade members to approve the sale of the World Cup’s commercial rights clearly states that its plans for financial growth will be achieved by staging more tournaments, having higher ticket prices and debt financing.

A 25-page sales deck titled “Fifa Forward Enterprise Member Materials”, that has been seen by the Guardian, makes the case for the creation of a new company to run Fifa’s commercial operations, 20% of which would be sold to Joshua Kushner, a US investor who is the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

The prospectus has been produced by JP Morgan, the US bank that was also behind the failed European Super League breakaway five years ago.

In addition to the previously reported $20m (£15m) sign-up payment Fifa has offered to all 211 member associations, which could be made available as soon as January, the document projects that the four-year Fifa Forward payments would increase to $24m for each member by the 2035-39 cycle.

JP Morgan makes clear in the sales deck that such growth will come from “a growing tournament portfolio”, “third party sources of capital and debt financing”, and prioritising “high yield” partnerships and events.

There is also a reference to more than doubling the number of global tournaments held each year, from 200 to 450, which if followed through would put a huge strain on player workload.

Staging the World Cup more frequently would be the most obvious way of raising revenue, with Gianni Infantino having previously proposed making it a biennial tournament five years ago.

The bank also raises the prospect of TV coverage of the biggest events such as the World Cup being sold to subscription channels or streamers, by referring to a lan to “expand and optimize media rights monetization”.

JP Morgan claims that Fifa is “undermonetized” but significantly makes comparisons with other sports leagues with the revenue figures based on club or franchise earnings, rather than with comparable governing bodies.

Fifa’s stated annual revenue of $3.6bn therefore compares unfavourably with the NFL’s compared revenue of $21.2bn, Major League Baseball’s $13.1bn and the NBA’s $12.5bn.

The document was sent to all 211 member associations on Wednesday night and immediately provoked a strong reaction.

One senior figure queried why Fifa, which has cash reserves of around $4bn and accumulated revenues of $15bn over the current four-year cycle, would need to take on debt.

Another highlighted the odd comparison of a world governing body with private, member-run leagues, while JP Morgan’s proposed timeline for completing the deal was also questioned.

According to the document “Investors will be given access to a term sheet and select materials” in August before a vote of Fifa members has taken place.

Significantly there is little mention of the investor group elsewhere in the prospectus, with no reference to its identity, projected returns or exit terms.

There is one more major omission in the document, as there is not a single mention of women’s football anywhere across the 25 pages.

Fifa was approached for comment.
