A meat thermometer transformed my cooking – here are nine of the best for roasts and barbecues

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 14:00:48 GMT

Stop guessing and start probing with our writer’s pick of the top thermometers, including smart Bluetooth and leave-in models

Readers’ favourite barbecue tips and tricks

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

While fewer of us are eating meat regularly – I refer you to the rise of “beef days” – if you’re going to cook it, it needs to be done properly. Overcooked beef with the texture of shoe leather, or undercooked poultry with a side of food poisoning, will put off even the most devoted carnivore.

The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

A reliable meat thermometer solves both problems. It takes the guesswork out of cooking, helping you achieve melt-in-the-mouth steak and the best of any cut, with no special skills required.

As a bonus, it can even help you make modest energy-use savings by preventing overcooking. Buying one of the best meat thermometers isn’t about adding to a pile of gadgets – it’s about making the most of the meat you choose to eat. Personally, I’d choose a cheaper piece of meat cooked perfectly over a pricey one that’s dry and chewy.

Best meat thermometer overallNinja ProChef wireless thermometer WP100EU

Best budget meat thermometerSalter Heston Blumenthal Precision indoor/outdoor meat thermometer

Best wireless smart meat thermometerTyphur Sync Gold dual two-probe wireless meat thermometer

Best wireless Bluetooth meat thermometerMeater Pro

Best leave-in meat thermometerETI Dot digital oven thermometer

I grew up believing that I didn’t like meat – I was vegetarian through my teens. Turns out, I just didn’t like how it was cooked. As an adult, I’ve always kept a meat thermometer at hand and have been testing them since I bought my first Meater wireless probe nine years ago. Since then, I’ve upgraded as the tech has improved. I test a lot of air fryers, multicookers and ovens, so for me a meat thermometer isn’t just a nice-to-have – it’s an essential tool for assessing how well an appliance cooks.

There are unexpected side effects to testing meat thermometers. One is cooking so much meat that a slightly greasy fug lingers in the house for days. Another is temporarily altering my App Store algorithm, after downloading five meat thermometer apps in succession. That’s a lot of cooking, says the store. Would I enjoy these 10 grocery shopping apps? Or how about some hiking and cycling apps to balance out your burger binge?

I tested 12 thermometers, but only nine made the cut. The first two tests used hot and cold calibration methods. I took the temperature of boiling water in a pan and ice water in a glass, alongside a thermocouple thermometer, and compared the readings. This was repeated three times for each. Since meat thermometers are designed for solids, liquid readings may not be degree-perfect, but they provided a guide to accuracy at the upper and lower limits of the scale.

I started the cooking part of the tests by pan-frying thick beef burgers on a medium-to-high heat, noting when each thermometer said they were done, when I was advised to flip (if applicable), and if the burgers were still pink in the middle. Burgers were placed in a preheated pan straight out of the fridge, with just a small amount of oil. They were then fried for about six to seven minutes on each side with a three-minute rest, until cooked through and measuring a peak of 70-72C in the centre.

This was followed by roasting chicken legs in a preheated air fryer at 190C. It normally takes about 25-28 minutes for the chicken to reach an internal temperature of 75-78C, with a three-minute rest. For each thermometer, I noted when it read that the chicken was done, then checked it by slicing open the leg to see if there was any pink remaining. I also noted whether the juices were running clear and whether the meat remained moist.

Finally, I evaluated how easy each thermometer was to set up, use and maintain, and its battery life. All samples have been returned to their supplier or donated to charity.

Compared with other wireless thermometers, this Ninja unit has plenty going for it. First, if you’re looking for a brand you recognise, then price-wise, only Meater’s entry-level SE and the Plus are in the same ballpark. Its app is easy to use – particularly for smart meat thermometer newbies – even providing guidance on when to flip food. But where it stands out is its integration with Ninja’s other appliances. The app includes cooking charts and appliance-specific guidance, making it especially useful if you already own a Ninja air fryer, grill or outdoor oven.

Why we love itThe probe connected to the app first time – not always a given with connected devices – and was easy to navigate. It can handle temperatures up to 370C, so it was no surprise that it did well in the hot-water test, reading only a degree lower than the thermocouple, but it was out by a few more degrees with ice water.

It’s a thicker probe than the Meater Pro, so it can be tricky to insert, but it handled cooking well. Although there was a slight fluctuation in the estimated cooking time (dropping from 15 to 10 minutes in only two minutes), barbecue cooks that get easily distracted will welcome its alert to flip and that it factors in rest time, which resulted in a thoroughly cooked burger. Placement in chicken was problematic, playing havoc with the estimated cooking time and alerting me that it was cooked before it actually was – but reinserting solved the issue.

It’s a shame that … it’s better for bigger items than small pieces of food.

Water resistance? YesProbe length: 8.5cm (6.5cm from tip to insertion line) Battery life: up to 30 hours (AAA battery supplied for charging case)Recycling and longevity: the Ninja ProChef comes with a two-year warranty, and the brand advises that all its electrical products should be recycled at dedicated recycling points. It doesn’t offer a repair service

Equally at home in the kitchen as it is by the barbecue, this versatile instant-read thermometer can withstand temperatures from -45C to 200C. Unlike others, it’s also suitable for making jam and caramel and checking the temperature of deep-frying oil, while its silicone casing and probe cover keep it protected from the elements. It’s the long probe you’ll love most, though, letting you check bangers on the barbecue without reaching for the oven gloves.

Why we love itIn testing, the Heston Precision was fantastically accurate, matching up with the thermocouple in the boiling- and ice-water tests most of the time. The probe was easy to use and insert, too. Salter’s Precision meat thermometer is practically identical in spec and similar in price, and put in a similar performance in my testing – but the Heston made the list because of its extra cooking guidance.

The slim probe made it easy to check multiple spots in burgers and chicken, ensuring they were cooked through with no pink remaining.

It’s a shame that … at 30cm long with the cover on, it’s awkward to fit in a cutlery drawer – a hanging hook would be a useful addition.

Water resistance? Yes, to IPX5 Probe length: 18cmBattery life: approximately one year (2xAAA batteries supplied)Recycling and longevity: the Heston Blumenthal thermometer comes with a one-year guarantee that can be extended to two if registered within 30 days of buying. It can be recycled at a local e-waste collection point or household recycling centre in the small WEEE container once the battery is removed

Typhur is in the process of making a humanoid kitchen robot, Athena, so I was expecting great things from its Sync Gold Dual meat thermometer. And for the most part, it lived up to expectations. Its two probes live in a sleek base that not only charges them but also acts as a monitor and control hub, so you can track cooking without reaching for your phone.

It also uses a stronger, longer-range signal (sub-1GHz for those radio frequency aficionados out there) – making it ideal if thick walls or a robust barbecue disrupt smart probe connections.

Why we love itThe Sync Gold can withstand up to 500C and is waterproof, too, making it suitable for almost any type of cooking, including sous vide. Having said that, I was surprised to find it struggled during the boiling-water test, coming in 3C lower than the thermocouple, and read 0C in the ice-water test, when the thermocouple read 4C. Fortunately, its cooking performance was excellent.

The app was easy to set up and use, while the base took more getting used to, although it’s useful if you’re avoiding your phone. I liked the cooking graph and frequent alerts, although it doesn’t remind you to turn the food. Both the burger and chicken were perfectly cooked without drying or overcooking. Great performance, then – as you’d expect at this price.

It’s a shame that … the base is set with arrows to scroll through and a button to select, rather than being a touchscreen.

Water resistance? Yes, probes to IPX8; base to IPX2 Probe length: 8.5cm (7.5cm from tip to insertion line) Battery life: 24+ hours on a single charge/rechargeable baseRecycling and longevity: the thermometer’s sealed design means it’s not intended to be repaired, although it is covered by a two-year warranty. Typhur doesn’t offer a take-back or recycling scheme

My fridge sits behind my kitchen door – but if yours is in a more visible location, you’ll appreciate that the Meater Pro’s magnetic bamboo base can be affixed to the fridge door for storing the thermometer, so it’s within easy reach when you’re next cooking steak. There’s plenty more to like, too.

The probe is waterproof, dishwasher-safe for cleaning, and suitable for deep-frying or sous vide. It’s also heatproof up to 550C, and slimmer than most at just 0.5cm in diameter – making it easier to use with smaller cuts of meat. Meater claims its app is so friendly, you can leave it to your kids. While they’d probably rather be playing Pokémon Go, I did find it genuinely easy to use.

Why we love itI use a Meater Plus in my kitchen, but it’s not as whizzy as the Pro, which charges rapidly and lasts a long time (a 15-minute charge will buy you about 12 hours of cooking), making it perfect for spur-of-the-moment meat feasts. In testing, I appreciated the ability to specify not only the meat being cooked and the level of cooking, but also how you’re cooking it – there’s an option for air fryers, for example.

It didn’t perform so well in the water tests – fluctuating between 92C and 97C when the thermocouple read 99C, and 1.3C when the thermocouple was at 3C – although it did offer guidance for frozen meat. Cooking performance was better, although the burger was drier as a result of the preset being 2C higher than what I’d normally choose, and the chicken was a little pink. This could have been down to probe placement or the leg being thicker.

It’s a shame that … estimated cooking time takes a while to appear. I was over halfway through cooking the burger by the time this popped up.

Water resistance? YesProbe length: 9.8cm (6.7cm from tip to insertion line) Battery life: 24+ hours from a 30-minute charge, estimated two years of charging based on one steak a week (AAA battery supplied for charging case)Recycling and longevity: the Meater Pro isn’t recyclable at the end of its life, but it does come with a two-year warranty should it need to be replaced or repaired

I enjoy the name of the Dot – both short for digital oven thermometer and a nod to its round shape – but it’s more than an appealing moniker that made me like this thermometer. Equipped with a wired probe, magnets for convenient placement on an oven door, and a light to brighten the LCD screen, this is a simple bit of kit, executed well.

The stainless-steel braided lead is a generous 1.2m, and the probe will measure temperatures from as low as -50C up to 300C. There’s no ignoring its 70dB alarm for when it hits temperature – great for easily distracted cooks who have wandered off to another room.

Why we love itIf you dislike apps or fiddly setup routines, the Dot will appeal. It has just three buttons: one on the back for power and adjusting screen brightness, and two on the front to set the target temperature. And that’s it.

It did well in the water tests, only usually a degree out from the thermocouple, but pan cooking and air frying proved more awkward. Positioning the probe in smaller items was tricky, and the cable often got in the way, meaning I had to reinsert it for an accurate reading. Eventually, I got a juicy well-done burger and thoroughly cooked chicken, but it took some effort. That said, for its intended use in the oven, it’s better designed, more robust, and slimmer than Lakeland’s in-oven model below.

It’s a shame that … its fold-up stand is flimsy and popped off in my hand. It didn’t break, but a more substantial structure would be an improvement.

Water resistance? Yes, to IP65 Probe length: 11.4cmBattery life: 5,000 hours (2xAAA batteries supplied)Recycling and longevity: it comes with only a one-year guarantee, but ETI offers a repair service and will recycle returned products

Best for: barbecuing

Designed to work either as a probe or a grate sensor with any barbecue, the Weber Connect smart probe is one for the alfresco cooks. It’ll withstand temperatures of up to 420C, attaches to your barbecue via magnets, has a 0.91m cable, and comes with a clip so it can measure ambient temperature. If you want to dip your toe into app-monitored cooking, the Smart Probe could be one of the most affordable ways to do it.

Its performance in the water tests was mixed, coming in at 99C when the thermocouple read 100C, and 1C when the thermocouple read 3.7C. Indoors, it’s tricky to use, but not impossible. For example, the ambient heat of the pan tended to skew the reading when cooking the burger, registering it as cooked before it actually was, while the cable was too thick for the air fryer drawer to close properly. I had to reposition the probe a couple of times in the chicken, but once it was in the right spot, the readings were what I’d expect. Used in an oven or, as it’s intended, on a barbecue, it worked well for larger cuts, but it’s far from being an all-purpose meat thermometer.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the choice for app-assisted cooking is limited – for example, chicken leg wasn’t listed.

Water resistance? Weather resistant, but not waterproof; probe length: 8.89cm; battery life: one year (1xCR2032 battery supplied); recycling and longevity: two-year limited warranty; no recycling or repair programme. The stainless steel probe is recyclable, while the electronic components and battery should be processed through suitable recycling facilities

after newsletter promotion

Best for: beginners

Lightweight, compact and easy to use, the Oxo Chef’s Precision is brilliant for those new to using a meat thermometer. It has a big, clear digital display, a button on the back flicks between celsius and fahrenheit readings, and the probe protector offers suggested temperatures for different meats and levels of doneness, along with resting advice. The display pivots 90 degrees so you can read it from any angle.

It’s less versatile than some, though. While it has a temperature range of -40 to 150C, it was confused by the ice-water test, reading 1C when the water was actually at 4C. It was spot on for the boiling water, though. During cooking, it was slower to climb up to temperature than other units on test, although it got there in the end. Both the burger and chicken were well cooked, but not before the screen had become splashed with fat – a combination of waiting time and a short probe.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s powered by a button battery, which you’re less likely to have to hand for replacement – and the one supplied was almost flat.

Water resistance? No; probe length: 11.5cm; battery life: two years of moderate use (1xCR2032 battery supplied); recycling and longevity: the probe cover and battery can potentially be recycled, but the thermometer can’t, and Oxo doesn’t have a policy in place for recycling its products. However, it does offer a “better guarantee”, a lifetime warranty that promises to replace or refund products with material or manufacturing defects

Best for: an easy-to-read display

It’s unwieldy and won’t be for everyone, but I liked the simplicity of this affordable meat thermometer. There are just two buttons for scrolling through what you want to cook – meat and taste – plus you have the option to easily switch temperature readings between celsius and fahrenheit under the battery cover. An anti-slip handle, easy-to-read backlit LCD panel, safety caps for its menacing prongs, one-year guarantee, and presets for six meats complete the package.

Its temperature range goes from -5 to 250C – although, like many others I tested, it did better with boiling water than cold. It was only one degree off for boiling water, but for ice water, this increased to two or three degrees. It worked well for the chicken leg in the air fryer, but I had issues with the burger. Not only did it leave a pair of large holes in the meat, but it also tended to hit the base of the pan when inserted from the top, throwing off the reading. I had more success piercing the burger from the side – awkward, but accurate. As such, it’s probably better for use with larger cuts of meat and joints.

It didn’t make the final cut because … there are no real instructions for getting started or guidance on how far the probes need to be inserted.

Water resistance? Yes, to IPX3; probe length: 8cm; battery life: one to three years depending on batteries bought and frequency of use (2xAAA batteries, not included); recycling and longevity: one-year guarantee. At the end of its lifespan, ProCook will recycle it for free when you buy a new electrical item from it via its trade-in/WEEE scheme

Best for: multifunctionality

If you like your kitchen gadgets to do more than one thing, Lakeland’s digital in-oven kitchen thermometer should please you. When it’s not working as a thermometer, it doubles as a kitchen timer – just change it using the switch on the back. It also comes with a decent three-year guarantee, a handy leaflet of cooking guidance, a temperature range from -20C to 250C, and presets for different meats and doneness. It even has a fold-out stand on its rear, plus a small notch so you can hang it. However, the screen is hard to read – on a bright day, I found myself having to tilt it to see the display.

Performance was mixed: it did well with boiling water, reading the same temperature as the thermocouple, although it was several degrees out with ice water. I struggled to position it in the chicken, and it shifted during cooking and needed reinsertion to get an accurate reading. The cable was too thick to use easily in the air fryer, too. It was awkward in a pan and slipped out of the burger when I flipped it, so it’s definitely one that’s just for the oven.

It didn’t make the final cut because … a dim screen, even on full brightness, makes it almost impossible to read unless positioned at just the right angle.

Water resistance? No; probe length: 15cm; battery life: should last past the three-year guarantee depending on the batteries bought and frequency used (2xAAA batteries, not included); recycling and longevity: three-year guarantee. Lakeland doesn’t offer a repair service, and advises that the thermometer is thrown away in line with local waste disposal guidelines

Those that didn’t make the cut in my testing include the Salter analogue meat thermometer (doesn’t require batteries or charging, but its dial didn’t offer as much information as others here, and it briefly malfunctioned in my test); plus Salter’s Precision meat thermometer, which performed brilliantly, but is identical in price and similar in spec to the Heston Blumenthal Precision meat thermometer above. The Heston put in a similar performance but came with more guidance.

Also missing is the ETI RFX wireless. On a positive note, it uses radio frequency rather than wifi for a more stable connection, but it’s lacking in features compared with other wireless meat thermometers. The app is basic – there are no guided cooks, for example – and I didn’t find it especially user-friendly. It also requires exact placement in small items, or else it can give misleading data – I had to reinsert it mid-cook. I have included ETI’s Dot digital oven thermometer, though, and would always recommend its Thermapen, which is the thermometer I use for general cooking at home.

The type of meat thermometer you choose will depend on what you might cook with it and how.

Analogue or traditional meat thermometers will be fine for infrequent users, or those who mainly cook joints of meat in the oven or on the barbecue. They’re durable, affordable, and don’t need to be recharged or have their batteries replaced. That said, they’re less precise than others and can be slow to respond to changes, which can lead to overcooking, plus the dial can get in the way under a grill or in a pan. They’re better than no meat thermometer at all, but could prove frustrating for a keen cook.

Digital meat thermometers are more accurate than analogue, quick to respond to temperature changes, and may also come with extra features, such as a timer, alarm, or presets for different meats and levels of cooking. They’re available either as a stand-alone, instant-read probe or wired to a base, so that the probe can stay in an oven, pan, grill or barbecue – just always check the maximum temperature, particularly with wired models. Most cost less than £40 and are a good choice if you don’t need all the bells and whistles – and extra cost – of a smart wireless probe.

Smart, wireless meat probes are designed to be used with a companion app for checking the temperature remotely. There may also be a separate base for monitoring, so you don’t always need to have your device to hand. They’re often pricey, but if you cook meat frequently, you’ll love the convenience of not being confined to the kitchen or grill. They’re the most versatile of the lot: many fit in smaller food items more easily; they work well in pans, grills and ovens; and apps will usually offer guidance for achieving the best results. Great for beginners and more confident cooks aiming to up their game.

Correct placement of a meat thermometer will return the most accurate reading, but this depends on what you’re cooking and the type of thermometer you’re using. Smart probes usually need to be inserted fully into the meat, up to a marked insertion line, while instant-read probes often only need the thin tip inserted so it reaches the centre of the food. Analogue meat thermometers typically need to be inserted deeper than instant-read models. Check the insertion guide for your particular model.

The aim with most meats is to insert the probe into the thickest part, avoiding bone or gristle. For example, for a whole chicken, this would be through the thigh into the centre of the breast. While multiple insertion holes allow juices to leak out, don’t be afraid to take the meat thermometer out mid-cook and reinsert if the temperature looks too high too soon.

It’s important to clean your meat thermometer when switching between pieces of meat to avoid cross-contamination. Wipe the probe with a hot, soapy cloth (don’t submerge), then rinse and dry with a kitchen towel to prevent bacteria growth. An alcohol wipe will do in a pinch.

For stuck-on mess, soak the probe tip in hot soapy water to soften the residue before cleaning. Resist the temptation to scrub with harsh cleaners or pads – scratches on a probe create more places for bacteria to grow and can affect sensory accuracy.

It’s advisable to clean a probe after every session: dip it in diluted bleach or distilled white vinegar (avoiding any electronic parts), then rinse under hot running water. Don’t forget to clean protective sheaths or covers since these can harbour bacteria, too.

Yes, but not all foods. If you don’t have the budget for a cooking thermometer and a meat thermometer, the latter can be used for foods such as quiche, casseroles and desserts.

However, they’re not usually suitable for liquids. Meat thermometer probes tend to be thicker and slower to react, which can lead to imprecise readings in liquids. In addition, they may not cover the temperature range.

It’s also best to opt for a specialised thermometer for high-heat cooking, such as jam or caramel, or deep-frying. A meat thermometer may not have the upper range, plus high heat can damage sensors.

Rachel Ogden has worked as a consumer journalist for decades, becoming an expert unboxer before it was a thing, although she is less successful at repacking. Her home has hosted hundreds of small appliances, from air fryers and slow cookers to meat thermometers, while outside, you’ll find her messing about with barbecues and pizza ovens. It takes a lot to impress her – many appliances have tried and failed

‘It’s the Meryl Streep of the orchestra’: why cinema loves the cello

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 14:00:16 GMT

From Audrey Hepburn to Pedro Pascal, cellists have become a movie shorthand for sensitivity, intensity and emotional depth. But why has Hollywood turned one orchestral instrument into a character in its own right?

There’s a throwaway line in 2012’s The Avengers, after a character’s death, when his partner is alluded to. “There was a cellist, I think,” muses Robert Downey Jr’s Tony Stark. It’s a spot of pathos amid the punch-ups – but also rather telling. Because when even a superhero blockbuster reaches for the cello, you know the instrument is carrying more than just a melody.

Earlier this month, a trailer dropped for the upcoming Pedro Pascal drama Behemoth!, in which he plays a celebrated cellist returning to Hollywood to score films. Real-life cellist and film composer Hildur Guðnadóttir says the instrument “is definitely having a moment right now. But it’s always been present.”

It’s true. And this cinematic love affair first found its rhythm almost 70 years ago, when Audrey Hepburn played a witty young cellist in Love in the Afternoon. In the decades since, the instrument has become a marker for a certain type of character: cultured, intense, romantic, haunted. Think Alan Rickman in Truly, Madly, Deeply – or the titular cellist in the 1996 Czech drama Kolya, which won the Academy Award for best foreign language film. Even Woody Allen toyed with the stereotype; in Annie Hall, Carol Kane’s leftwing, liberal intellectual played the cello in a deleted scene.

But why, out of every option in the orchestra, did the cello become the instrument of introspection? “It’s the cliche, but it’s probably because the cello comes closest to the human vocal range,” says Guðnadóttir. “It has this ability to play around with notes, too, like human intonation. Press a note on a keyboard and it’s straightforward, definitive. The cello – like our voices – can play with this intonation for expression.”

Put an actor in a scene playing the cello, then, and they can deliver dialogue without words. Guðnadóttir says the only other instrument with this human timbre and “fluidity of intonation” is the bass clarinet. But you’re unlikely to see a protagonist reaching for one – nor a prestige biopic being made of a famous bass clarinettist. In fact, the cello has cornered the market on tragic orchestral stories – perhaps most notably in the Emily Watson-starring Hilary and Jackie.

“That film, the story of cellist Jacqueline du Pré, is the cello film that has stuck with me most,” says Guðnadóttir. And it’s not the only cellist biopic to reach the screen. In 2009’s The Soloist, Jamie Foxx was cast as musician Nathaniel Ayers, but the narrative was restrung, swapping his primary instrument – the double bass – for the cello.

You can see why. Not only does the cello have that uncannily human register, it’s also visually dynamic. A cellist’s bow strokes are physical and expressive, and the performer’s face is rarely obscured – making it a perfect screen partner.

It’s probably why cellists tend to be the beating heart of musical dramas. Guðnadóttir also scored Cate Blanchett’s tour-de-force Tár, in which a cellist becomes the catalyst for the drama. Christopher Walken’s cellist, struggling with Parkinson’s, is the centrepiece of 2012’s A Late Quartet, and Dermot Mulroney (a real-life cellist who played on the scores of multiple Mission: Impossible films) frequently guest-starred in Prime Video series Mozart in the Jungle.

But cellist characters are not confined to musical dramas. The cello’s emotional shorthand has been transcribed across almost every genre: from Chloë Grace Moretz in sci-fi romance If I Stay, to Maryam d’Abo in 007 adventure The Living Daylights, to cellist love interests in sitcoms from Frasier to New Girl. And then there’s the darker side of the cello, whether channelled by Michelle Pfeiffer in supernatural thriller What Lies Beneath, Uma Thurman in neo-noir Jennifer 8 or Jenna Ortega in Netflix’s smash series Wednesday.

“There is a gothic connection to the cello,” says Guðnadóttir, who won her Oscar for scoring Joker, a soundtrack that features the instrument prominently, with its neck being “choked”. “When it’s played in an ugly way – because we yearn for it to be this beautiful instrument – it feels uncomfortable.”

Director Richard Shepard took that darker side one step further in 2018 with The Perfection, a horror set inside a prestigious music academy. When choosing the instrument his two leads would play, he wanted something both sinister and sensual.

“I remember growing up on the Upper West Side of New York City, near Lincoln Center,” he says, “and seeing these young cellists on the subway, lugging these huge cases. It stuck with me. How big it is. How much effort it takes to not only play it, but just move it. When writing The Perfection, we felt that physicality could make a statement. It’s sexy. It’s a sexy instrument.”

The film-makers behind the Allison Williams-starring horror film were determined to make the cello playing as convincing as the scares. “It was really hard work,” says Shepard, “but I’m proud there are only two shots of musicians’ hands rather than actors’ hands in the entire film.”

The cello is an instrument actors can’t bluff their way through – it’s harder to fake than hiding your hands behind a piano or overdubbing a singing voice. Ortega trained for Wednesday and earned Golden Globe and Emmy nominations. Watson trained for Hilary and Jackie and got an Oscar nod. Pascal recently told Vanity Fair that taking on the cello was “literally the hardest, hardest, hardest thing I’ve ever had to learn to do.” If he’s angling for awards, there are few better bets than a deep, introspective stringsman.

And that perception extends beyond the screen. David Cohen, the principal cellist of the London Symphony Orchestra, says that “there’s definitely a stereotype that cellists are the orchestra’s empaths – warm, thoughtful and just a little bit intense. I’m not sure it’s entirely true, but it’s amusing that film-makers so often cast cellists as the emotionally intelligent ones. You rarely see the villain saying: ‘Just let me finish my Bach Suite …’”

Cohen adds that the cello’s versatility often shapes the characters written around it. “It can sound noble, lonely, hopeful or quietly heroic – often within the same phrase,” he says. “It’s the Meryl Streep of the orchestra. And, because it has the depth to suggest sadness without wallowing in it, the cello is also film music’s favourite therapist.”

Catherine Warner is a music therapy practitioner who has long watched the cello play its introspective, insular part on film. But she also points to the instrument’s role in memorable cinematic dialogues. In The Witches of Eastwick, a devilish Jack Nicholson seduces Susan Sarandon’s cellist during a duet, which Warner says “seemed to symbolise Sarandon’s character’s sexual awakening, as well as her discovery of authentic emotional expression – she had previously struggled to bring that into her playing”.

In Master and Commander: The Far Side of the World, Paul Bettany plays a cello bass line under Russell Crowe’s virtuosic violin flourishes. Warner says this “symbolises a close supportive working relationship whereby the soloist can be freer to express their brilliance”. The cello, then, is a literal baseline: a “straight man” that performs whatever emotional function the story needs.

Warner also returns to something she once wrote in a collection of essays: “Symbolically, the cello can evoke the sense of the instrument being rather like a person.” And this gets closest to explaining Hollywood’s obsession with the instrument. More than any other member of the orchestra, introducing a cello is like casting another actor in a scene. Guðnadóttir even says that “there’s something about the size of it being quite close to the human body – not to mention the shape of the cello almost looking like a torso.”

Pair its resemblance to the human body with its similarity to our vocal range, and it’s no wonder cinema loves the instrument. It’s a character actor in and of itself. It can be embraced, fought, comforted or strangled. Now we just need to wait for the inevitable Oscar category: best bowed string instrument in a leading role. It’s either that, or Pascal runs the risk of having his cello nominated ahead of him.

The future of AI hinges on openness and cooperation. China and Britain can gain much by working together

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 14:00:16 GMT

There is no point competing in isolation. There are so many benefits to be had, in manufacturing, healthcare, research and governance

Zheng Zeguang is the Chinese ambassador to the UK

Artificial intelligence is widely regarded as one of the defining technologies of our time. Like the steam engine, the harnessing of electricity and the internet before it, it has the potential to transform how we work, live and interact.

But every technological revolution brings challenges as well as opportunities. As AI systems become more capable, people are asking legitimate questions. How can AI remain safe, accountable and under human control? How should its development be governed? How can its benefits be shared more widely?

These questions were at the heart of the 2026 World AI Conference, held last week in Shanghai. Representatives from more than 100 countries and international organisations gathered to discuss how AI could better serve humanity, and how a more inclusive and effective global governance framework could be built. I am glad the UK also sent a delegation to the conference.

China’s president, Xi Jinping, delivered an important address calling on all countries to “boost innovation-driven development”, in a spirit of openness and mutual benefit, to strengthen risk-awareness and ensure that AI is secure and controllable. We must, he said, encourage inclusiveness and promote mutual learning between civilisations. He also stressed the importance of improving global AI governance together.

Things are moving quickly. To further support global AI development, China has announced that in the next five years it will provide developing countries with 5,000 opportunities in AI training and seminar programmes. We will also develop international AI-application cooperation centres with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, the League of Arab States, the African Union, the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and our fellow Bric countries. Thirty nations will also be able to use the AI-powered, early-warning weather system, Mazu.

To ensure that AI is a trustworthy tool for humanity, legitimate concerns over data security, privacy protection and responsible use must be taken seriously. These challenges transcend national borders. They obviously require international collaboration, especially in areas such as developing common standards and practical governance. At the same time, security considerations should not become a blanket justification for restricting normal technological cooperation or fragmenting global innovation.

China’s own experience reflects this approach. Through the AI Plus Initiative, AI is being integrated into manufacturing, healthcare, logistics, energy and consumer services, helping to build one of the world’s most dynamic AI ecosystems. In 2025, China’s core AI industry exceeded 1.2tn yuan (about £130bn) and a large number of AI companies are growing rapidly.

Another notable feature of China’s AI development is its emphasis on open-source and open-weight models. The success of models such as Qwen, DeepSeek and Kimi demonstrates that advanced AI capabilities can be developed at lower cost and made accessible to a much wider community of developers and users. Lowering the barriers to innovation allows more countries, researchers and smaller enterprises to participate in the AI revolution instead of being left behind.

It is important to say that no country has a monopoly on innovation. Different nations bring different strengths to AI development, and lasting progress will depend on how well those strengths complement one another rather than compete in isolation.

after newsletter promotion

This is where China and the UK have much to gain from working together. The UK has a competitive edge in frontier research, life sciences, financial services and AI innovation. China has well-recognised strengths in advanced manufacturing, engineering and large-scale industrial deployment, plus one of the world’s largest markets for AI applications. These advantages are highly complementary.

In healthcare, combining British strengths in biomedical research with China’s capacity to deploy AI at scale can accelerate drug discovery, improve medical imaging and enhance healthcare delivery. In manufacturing, pairing British innovation with China’s industrial capabilities can speed up the adoption of smarter, cleaner and more efficient production. Joint research can also contribute to internationally applicable standards for AI safety, testing and evaluation, supporting innovation while strengthening public trust. Such cooperation would not only benefit our two countries but also generate solutions with wider global value.

Policymakers, researchers and business leaders from China and the UK need to increase exchanges and translate dialogue into joint research, commercial partnerships and closer cooperation on AI governance.

For China, for Britain and for the wider world, cooperation is not simply desirable. It is the right way forward to ensure that AI develops in a way that benefits us all.

Zheng Zeguang is the Chinese ambassador to the UK

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 13:59:32 GMT

State department ‘takes full responsibility’ for erroneous, widely shared chart displayed at Aids conference in Brazil

A US government map of Africa mislabeled every country during a state department presentation at a ⁠global conference in Brazil ⁠this week, ​causing a stir among attenders who took screenshots and posted them online.

Reuters viewed a video of the presentation given at the Aids 2026 conference in ⁠Rio de Janeiro, which shows the errant map displayed halfway during a presentation about the state department’s new health agreements.

A Reuters analysis found the image of the map included ⁠in the presentation contained an artificial intelligence watermark that signals it was made with OpenAI tools. The company did ​not respond to a request for comment.

The state ‌department said it took “full responsibility” ‌for the confusion caused and that the map had been produced by a team member who hastily changed ‌the slide deck before the event.

The map showed Nigeria, where the US currently has several hundred troops deployed, as landlocked in the Sahara desert. Mozambique, which is in south-eastern Africa, was relocated to the Horn of Africa, while Côte d’Ivoire in west Africa was placed on the other side of the continent.

Screenshots of the map first appeared in a Substack post by the Aids expert Emily Bass and were widely ‌shared on LinkedIn, with one post garnering about 40,000 views.

“Whoever created and approved this slide did not know where countries in Africa are and did not care to ​check their work,” wrote Matt Petit, who focuses on AI and geopolitics at the Atlantic Council, in the post.

In a statement, the state department said: “We take full responsibility for the confusion and misrepresentation it caused for attendees, including our African partners.” The speaker at the conference was Jeff Graham, the ⁠top US health envoy who oversees the initiative known as the President’s Emergency Plan ​for Aids Relief, or Pepfar. He ​did not reply to requests for comment.

The ​state department said the discussions at the conference were “substantive and constructive” despite the map ​and that it remained ‌committed to fighting Aids ​with real results. The ​Trump administration’s decision last year to pause funding pending a review disrupted aid programs worldwide but Pepfar’s core work such as the provision of life-saving drugs has largely resumed. The US is scaling back other areas of its spending including on prevention and surveillance, and plans to fully phase out the program in South Africa.

The US public is fed up with RFK Jr. To really ‘make America healthy again’, it should look to Europe

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 13:00:15 GMT

Americans are dying younger than Europeans, despite being the wealthiest people on the planet. Wellness fads won’t change that

I’m just back from my home country, the United States. I always enjoy visiting, but every time I go between the US and my adopted home of Europe, I’m keenly aware of disparity in health: Americans live much shorter lives and spend more of their lifetime in poor health. This is despite Americans earning some of the highest salaries per capita in the world and spending twice as much as comparable countries on healthcare.

A recent study in the New England Journal of Medicine of 74,000 adults found that even the wealthiest Americans had higher mortality rates than the wealthiest Europeans – and that the richest Americans had mortality rates comparable to the poorest residents of northern and western Europe. Across every wealth category, Americans were more likely to die younger than Europeans, suggesting that even wealth doesn’t insulate from larger factors that impact life expectancy.

That the US has a health problem isn’t controversial. The Make America Healthy Again movement, led by US health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, has highlighted soaring rates of obesity, diabetes and chronic disease. The movement’s public face isn’t scientists or doctors, but influencers posting videos from saunas, gyms and parks talking about better choices and individual discipline. Eat more red meat. Do more push-ups. Drink raw milk. Avoid vaccines and boost your natural immunity. Sweat more. This health advice is given, while month by month, public health agencies are gutted, research is not funded and experts are sidelined and dismissed from advisory groups.

Of course, the public aren’t stupid. Polling consistently finds that scientists remain among the most trusted sources of information in the US, compared with politicians and influencers. RFK Jr himself isn’t popular, 60% of voters disapprove of the job he’s doing. People might enjoy following entertaining social media accounts, but when Americans want reliable health information, they still largely turn to doctors and scientists.

Why are Americans dying younger than Europeans? If we look at the data, several factors pop out. I’ll pick up a few here.

The US is a uniquely violent high-income country, with guns the leading cause of death for children and adolescents, followed by road traffic collisions. For example, the firearm death rate among American children (age 0-17) is 72 times higher in the US than in the UK, with one mass shooting taking place per day, on average.

Why? Because the US doesn’t regulate guns as tightly as the UK (which effectively banned handguns after the Dunblane shooting) and hasn’t addressed road safety as a government issue. No amount of cold plunges or protein shakes will prevent you from getting shot or being killed on the roads. Those are policy decisions that have to be addressed by government.

Additionally, the US is the only high-income country that doesn’t guarantee healthcare: around 26 million Americans remain uninsured while millions more carry insurance plans with loopholes or deductibles so high that it’s financially risky to access care. According to a Commonwealth Fund survey, an estimated 57% of underinsured adults delayed or avoided medical care because of cost. Diseases that could have been detected early become more serious and more expensive. Think of waiting with your asthmatic child outside an emergency room, hoping their breathing stabilises because otherwise you’ll face a $20,000-30,000 bill. As a result, Americans have substantially higher levels of preventable and treatable mortality than Europeans.

How to solve those challenges? Looking to the UK and European countries helps. While these nations differ politically and economically, most share universal healthcare, strong regulation of guns, investment in public transport alongside road infrastructure and safety, and through EU legislation an emphasis on food quality and safe ingredients.

In contrast, rooted in libertarianism and “freedom”, the Maha movement pushes individual solutions to the US’s health challenges. Of course, personal behaviour matters in health. Diet, exercise, smoking and alcohol consumption affect how long we live. Yet many of the largest contributors to premature mortality in the US cannot be solved by individual discipline. They require policies and institutions capable of reducing collective risks across society.

What does freedom even mean? It depends who you ask. I would define freedom as the ability to live a long and healthy life, and in that regard, public health policies can bring more freedom. People in the UK have given up their freedom to easily own a gun to gain the freedom for children to go to school safely without shooter drills. The UK has not had a school shooting since Dunblane – and not because individuals haven’t planned to carry one out. They just haven’t been able to find a gun.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Maha is right: Americans need to become healthier and live longer. But this won’t happen with influencers telling people to do pull-ups or increase sunlight exposure. Otherwise, the wealthiest Americans would be outliving us all. What the US needs is public policy that makes daily life healthier and less dangerous. Unfortunately, the Maha movement, through its leader RFK Jr, has done the opposite in diminishing key US public health agencies such as the CDC, the FDA and the NIH, and removing the US from the World Health Organization.

How your community looks affects your health profoundly. Less me, more us. That’s the key health lesson the US could learn from Europe.

Prof Devi Sridhar is chair of global public health at the University of Edinburgh

Dedicated followers of passion: the Kinks’ 40 greatest songs – ranked!

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 13:00:14 GMT

To coincide with a new exhibition in London about the Davies brothers, we rate the best of a band who brought a sociologist’s eye to hard rock, gentle pastoralia and so much in between

The quality of Kinks albums declined precipitously from the late 80s: you sensed their hearts weren’t really in it. Even so, Ray Davies couldn’t stop himself writing the occasional gem: from their final studio album Phobia, Scattered is a sweet, sad reflection on the Davies family’s complexities, powered by jangling guitars.

The decision of Davies’s older sister Rose to emigrate to Australia “devastated” him: it lurked in the background of Arthur (Or the Decline and Fall of the British Empire) but took centre stage on this track from Face to Face: evidently heartfelt, it twists and turns, deploying everything from pleading to mockery to secure her return.

Originally the soundtrack to a Ray Davies TV special, Soap Opera nearly broke the Kinks: some members assumed it would be their last album. There’s certainly a sense of finality to its closing track, impressive though it is: despite the title, it sounds like a eulogy for rock’n’roll, spiked with personal bitterness.

As an example of how out of step the Kinks were with the burgeoning counterculture in 1967, the harpsichord-led Two Sisters is hard to beat. Loving domesticity and parenthood trumps free-spirited bohemia: formerly jealous of her unencumbered sibling, the married sister ends the song delightedly running “round the house with her curlers on”.

Never released by the Kinks – a demo version is on the deluxe version of Kinda Kinks – the fraught ballad I Go to Sleep was the most sophisticated song Ray Davies had written by this time. The most famous cover is by the Pretenders, but the best is the 1967 version by German singer Marion Maerz: lushly orchestrated, echo-laden, girl group-adjacent, magnificent.

Belatedly excavated for the 2013 deluxe edition of Muswell Hillbillies, Lavender Lane’s failure to make the cut in 1971 seems baffling. It’s fantastic, a broadside against what would now be called gentrification that pivots between nostalgic sadness and fury, aimed at “the old school tie and all the la-di-do-dahs”.

In the hands of the Chocolate Watchband, who covered it in 1968, I’m Not Like Everybody Else is a classic screw-you garage band sneer. The Kinks’ original has a menacing power, but feels more complicated and personal, its emotional temperature shifting from defiant to faintly distraught.

From the largely ho-hum Word of Mouth, this is an atmospheric, ominous and pessimistic survey of Thatcher’s Britain from the pen of Dave Davies – “there’s no England now,” he dolefully concludes – subsequently rescued from obscurity and brought to the wider audience it deserved by its inclusion on the soundtrack of The Sopranos.

At their height of Britpop, it was common to compare Damon Albarn’s brand of social satire to that of Ray Davies, a fairly obvious influence. More bizarre is how much this impressive single from 1979’s Low Budget sounded like Blur’s Girls and Boys: disco beat, slashing guitars, mannered Cockney vocals.

Easy to overlook amid the waspish character studies and social satires of Face to Face – the Kinks’ first entirely superb album – Too Much on My Mind feels like Ray Davies’s most personal song of the era: a plaintive depiction of a man teetering on the verge of a breakdown. Understated, but quietly devastating.

The last of the Kinks’ riff-heavy garage rock anthems – although the fantastic She’s Got Everything belatedly slipped out as a B-side in 1968 – is more sophisticated than its predecessors: check the harmony vocals. But it’s just as thrilling, and – curiously for the Kinks – snottily optimistic in tone. But if you flipped the single over …

… you got the first – but definitely not the last – example of Ray Davies in contrarian mode. The 60s are fully swinging, the Kinks are at the centre of the action, and yet he’s riven with angst, complaining that things ain’t what they used to be, suggesting his parents had it better.

Not all of Davies’s scabrous music business satire Lola Vs Powerman and the Moneygoround Pt 1 has aged well, but This Time Tomorrow still rings out: detached from the album’s concept, it ceases to be a song about touring, and instead becomes a hugely affecting study of a life turned aimless.

Dave Davies’s aborted late 60s solo album was doomed by the Kinks’ gradually declining commercial fortunes rather than a lack of strong material, evidenced by Death of a Clown, rhythmically jaunty but hauntingly eerie: a compelling solo hit that wound up on 1967’s Something Else By the Kinks.

Songs in which rock stars complain about life on the road seldom elicit much sympathy from the listener – there are, far, far worse jobs, after all – but Sitting in My Hotel is among the few exceptions: a heartbreaking piano ballad that perfectly expresses a sense of homesick dislocation.

Sometimes, Ray Davies could sound like a grumpy reactionary, sometimes like a revolutionary, seething with class rage. It isn’t entirely clear what Mr Pleasant has done to incur Davies’s wrath, beyond being middle class, but his downfall is brilliantly, wittily depicted, to a jolly music hall-inspired backing. The evident delight in Davies’s voice is quite unsettling.

As Ray Davies’s theatrical ambitions got more elaborate, his songwriting genius seemed to flicker more fitfully: the Kinks’ 70s concept albums can be a longwinded slog. But persevere and you’re occasionally rewarded with a song like the gorgeous Sweet Lady Genevieve, entirely up to the standards he’d set himself. Perhaps the Kinks’ great lost classic.

It isn’t entirely clear if the character in 20th Century Man is a character, or an expression of Ray Davies’s increasing alienation and the precarious state of his mental health. “I don’t want to be here,” it offers. He would attempt suicide two years later. Ironically, the music that misery is set to is utterly charming.

Victoria deals in the sort of ambiguity that had become one of Davies’s most striking trademarks. Is it a nostalgic celebration of a bygone era, or a biting satire on empire? Probably both. Whatever it is, it’s a great song, blessed with a wonderful middle eight and an exultant brass arrangement.

Depending on who you believe, the sound of See My Friends was either inspired by a brief stopover in Mumbai, or the raga-influenced playing of folk guitarist Jon Mark. Either way, it was a hugely innovative pop single, both for its droning sound and its (admittedly oblique) lyrical treatment of homosexuality.

The Kinks’ only UK hit in the final 22 years of their career concerned their fraught origin story – the death of Ray Davies’s sister Rene in a dancehall, the same day she gave him his first guitar – and featured a sound that recalled their mid-60s hits: the synth hasn’t dated well, but the song itself is sweet, sad nostalgia.

Sixties London not as the swinging epicentre of the world, but a dark, forbidding nightmare, ready to swallow the unwary, including the song’s increasingly speed-addled protagonist. Ferociously performed and emotionally complex, as empathy for the girl’s frantic mother battles it out with a certain native Londoner’s relish at her grim fate.

The Kinks’ unexpected early 80s elevation into hard-rocking, arena-packing stars in the US sailed over British audiences’ heads. If their albums from that era aren’t up to 60s standards, they have their moments, of which Better Things’ unexpectedly optimistic – and richly melodic – reflection on a collapsing marriage is the most stellar.

Kinks fans can argue all night over whether 1972’s Everybody’s in Show-Biz represents their last soup-to-nuts classic album. Less contentious is how great its highlights are, as evidenced by Celluloid Heroes, an impossibly weary rumination on celebrity and posthumous reputation, provoked by a visit to Hollywood Boulevard’s Walk of Fame.

Outside of the world of folk, mid-60s British pop wasn’t big on social realism or protest, which made Dead End Street’s depiction of working-class poverty, complete with mournful french horn and shouted chorus, all the more striking. It had more in common with contemporary TV dramas than it did the rest of the charts.

Arthur (Or the Decline and Fall of the British Empire) was a much thornier exploration of Britishness than the preceding year’s The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society. The lengthy, episodic Shangri-La’s melody barely conceals a lyric livid about conformity, limited aspirations and social mobility, a country “too scared to complain”.

It’s hard to pick out individual tracks from The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society – it works best taken as a whole – but Picture Book’s interrogation of memory (“those days when you were happy, a long time ago”) is particularly great: sentimental but irreverent, and genuinely affecting.

Muswell Hillbillies is a curious, fascinating album, packed with great songs drenched in Americana but lyrically rooted in north London. Oklahoma USA is its highlight: its tune among Ray Davies’s prettiest, the lyrics both wistful and sharp – its dreams of a more glamorous existence in Oklahoma are fuelled by the Hollywood musical rather than reality of life there.

The subject of some controversy in recent years, Lola’s depiction of a brief, confused dalliance with a trans woman was more or less uncharted territory for pop in 1970, a topic no one other than Lou Reed had ventured to touch. It seemed to energise Ray Davies, pulling one of his greatest tunes out of him.

Partly inspired by the Kinks’ encounter with a gay Midlands promoter, this story of schoolboy rivalry is liberally sprinkled with homoeroticism. Does the narrator envy Watts’s wealth and accomplishments or is his fascination sparked more by Watts’s lack of interest in girls? The music fits perfectly: relentless, agitated, but deliberately mannered.

The Kinks, Marianne Faithfull subsequently opined, were “creepy and silent” and seemed “fearful of everyone”. Perhaps Ray Davies was taking notes, which would explain how perfectly he skewered the affectations of 60s hipsters here. Best moment: when the lyric slips into contemporary journalese: “This pleasure-seeking individual always looks his best.”

If you want an example of Ray Davies’s contrarian nature, consider God’s Children. Easily one of his finest early 70s songs – spellbinding melody, intriguing lyrics about the advance of technology – and he stuck it on the soundtrack to a sex comedy about a man rendered irresistible to women after a penis transplant.

The song that introduced a sharp brand of social satire into 60s British pop and inspired a legion of contemporary imitators – Semi-Detatched Suburban Mr James, et al. But no one else was as nuanced a lyricist as Ray Davies: listen to the verse about the protagonist’s ghastly mother, and you can virtually see her.

After 60 plus years, You Really Got Me is so familiar, it’s hard to picture the jolt it must have delivered in the summer of 1964, its distorted riff, unhinged guitar solo and Ray Davies’s vocal – alternately impassioned and slightly camp – sounding nothing like anything British pop had thus far produced. It still rocks.

That rarest of things: an attempt to follow up a huge hit with something similar that improves on the original. Cut from the same cloth as You Really Got Me, it succeeds by dialling everything up: it’s tougher, heavier, more exhilarating, and the mid-chorus key change is a masterstroke.

The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society flopped on release: perhaps a rock band singing in praise of the George cross and virginity was too confusing amid 1968’s revolutionary tumult. It was correctly reassessed as their masterpiece. The opening track demonstrates Davies’s songwriting firing on all cylinders: funny, sharp, provocative, warm.

How good a writer was Ray Davies at his zenith? Good enough to draw a pen portrait of a dissipated, abusive aristocrat and somehow manage to elicit a sense of empathy from the listener, helped by the irresistible melody and the song’s timelessness: its story could have been written in the 1920s but it’s not a nostalgic pastiche.

At the close of the summer of love, Ray Davies was to be found lovingly hymning the mundane life of a suburban gardener. Far more than a mere dry run for The Kinks Are the Village Green Preservation Society, Autumn Almanac is a lovely song: no snark or cynicism, just warmth and empathy.

That Days failed to make the UK Top 10 tells you everything about the Kinks’ waning commercial fortunes and nothing about the song itself. In a just world, anything blessed with a tune this beautiful, so suffused with equal part sadness and reflective warmth, would have been No 1 for weeks. A masterpiece.

Critic Robert Christgau called Waterloo Sunset “the most beautiful song in the English language”: certainly it’s among the greatest singles of the 60s, quite possibly one of the greatest pop songs of all time and a remarkable example of the songwriter’s art. On top of an extraordinarily beautiful melody, the lyrics are perfectly balanced between love for London, affection for the lovers meeting outside Waterloo Station and aching sadness: ever the outsider, Davies looks on at it all from a distance, and complains about the cold. It’s his best song, but it isn’t head-and-shoulders over everything else he wrote, which says a great deal about his brilliance.

The Kinks: Brothers, by Ray Davies, Dave Davies and Christian Furr, is at the Gibson Garage, London, until 6 September

Fifteen elephant deaths at Kenya park may be due to cyanide poisoning

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 12:46:50 GMT

Analysis of samples collected from carcasses found traces of toxic chemical compound, says Kenya Wildlife Service

The recent deaths of 15 elephants near a park in southern Kenya in the past month were likely caused by the animals ingesting pesticides used on nearby tomato farms, the Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) has said.

Erustus Kanga, the agency’s director general, told Citizen TV that analysis of samples collected from the carcasses had found traces of cyanide, a chemical compound used in farming as a predator control poison and a pest fumigant, which has also been used by poachers.

“Cyanide is a highly toxic chemical,” he said. “If elephants consume cyanide, they cannot survive a day or two.”

The deaths occurred in the Kimana sanctuary and Kuku Group ranch areas around Amboseli national park, an area covering 392 sq km (96,865 acres) and that, together with other neighbouring conservancies are home to more than 1,600 elephants.

Kimana town is a leading tomato producer and a place where researchers at the Route to Food Initiative, a food rights programme, have previously reported the use of a cyanide substance on the crop.

Isaac Lekolool, the head of veterinary and capture services at KWS, told Citizen TV that the stomach contents of one member of a herd that roamed Kimana sanctuary included “lots of tomatoes,” suggesting agrochemical poisoning.

Kanga warned that the effects could reach a wider population, as livestock may also eat from farms in the area.

“We have the goats, we have the cattle that are there. Eventually, if this cyanide is truly the one that is in the system, then we are going to see a bigger impact.”

On Tuesday, KWS announced it was investigating the deaths of the elephants from 24 June and 24 July in Amboseli. It said 10 of the elephants had shown signs of partial paralysis before dying and that preliminary tests had detected a potential toxic substance.

Benson Leyian, the CEO of Big Life Foundation, a conservation organisation that operates in the area surrounding Amboseli national park, said the elephant deaths were a cause for concern.

“Thanks to decades of community-centred conservation, the Amboseli elephant population is one of the best protected in Africa, and elephant poaching has been virtually eliminated here. Aside from losses during periods of severe drought, we haven’t seen a cluster of elephant deaths like this for some time,” he said.

In a statement, the International Fund for Animal Welfare described the deaths as “deeply alarming”, adding the incident “reinforces why we must continue investing in science, monitoring, and collaborative conservation efforts”.

“Every elephant lost is significant – not only for the species, but for the health of the ecosystems they help sustain and the communities that live alongside them,” it said.

Farmers and herders in Kenya have in the past poisoned wildlife in retaliation for eating their crops and livestock.

In Zimbabwe, poachers have killed dozens of elephants by lacing watering holes and salt licks with the chemical compound.

The Amboseli ecosystem is a major source of tourism revenue, but tensions have been building in recent months as local leaders demand the handover of the park’s management and operations to the government of Kajiado county, where it is located. Earlier this month, a court suspended the county government’s takeover.

Shaboozey: The Outlaw Cherie Lee & Other Western Tales review – a striking addition to the rich canon of country concept albums

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 11:00:13 GMT

(American Dogwood/Empire)Beneath the Hollywood narrators, Pink Floyd-y interludes and accompanying comic books lies songwriting that proves the Tipsy singer’s breakout success was no fluke

It’s fair to say that if Shaboozey never released another note of music, his place in history would still be assured.

He wasn’t the only Black country-leaning artist brought to a wider audience by a guest appearance on Beyoncé’s 2024 album Cowboy Carter, but no one else capitalised on the exposure quite so remarkably. Released two weeks after his guest appearance on that album’s Spaghettii, his single A Bar Song (Tipsy) unexpectedly eclipsed Beyoncé’s success, becoming the biggest-selling country single of the year – more than 1.75bn streams and counting on Spotify – and for a time, the joint longest-running US No 1 of all time. He’s received three nominations at the Country Music awards, an event traditionally resistant to artists of colour. The accompanying album, Where I’ve Been, Isn’t Where I’m Going, was by far the most successful sustained attempt to fuse hip-hop and country, two genres that have been warily circling each other for some time, spawning the occasional novelty hit such as Nelly and Tim McGraw’s Over and Over Again, the Ludacris-featuring 2010 remix of Jason Aldean’s Dirt Road, and Lil Nas X’s Old Town Road; the baleful, rap-influenced spectre of bro country; and the deep underground sub-genre of hick-hop, a hidden world of Maga politics, confederate flags and festivals held at Georgia mud holes. The album is still on the US chart, 112 weeks after its release.

Understandably, its success has led Shaboozey to swing for the fences two years on. The Outlaw Cherie Lee & Other Western Tales is a 20-track concept album, accompanied by a three-issue comic of the same name. It features scene-setting interstitial tracks: cinematic and orchestral, ambient and Pink Floyd-y, with weeping pedal steel subbing for David Gilmour’s trademark mournful string-bends. There’s narration by actors Jamie Foxx, Teyana Taylor and Sam Elliott, the latter going some way to ameliorate the traditional problem with concept albums: that the listener quickly loses the thread of the narrative and spends most of the album listening without a clue what’s supposed to be going on.

Country got to concept albums long before rock did. Marty Robbins’ thematically linked Gunfighter Ballads and Trail Songs were released in 1959, Johnny Cash’s Bitter Tears in 1964 – and they loom large in the genre’s history. Willie Nelson’s Red Headed Stranger, the 1975 saga of a murderer on the run, is regularly voted the greatest country album of all time; many major artists, including Emmylou Harris, Kenny Rogers and Dolly Parton, have at least one in their catalogue. You could thus view The Outlaw Cherie Lee as a concerted effort to pivot away from pop into country’s heartlands, albeit while still featuring a heavily Auto-Tuned guest appearance by rapper Gunna on High Noon (“spent a hundred thou on clothes / I got bad hoes,” he offers, presumably not referencing farming equipment). Cowgirl and Born to Die are two obvious – and, it has to be said, remarkably charming – attempts to replicate the success of Shaboozey’s biggest hit: “Got another bar song for you,” he notes by way of introduction to the former. Bullets and Blades, meanwhile, is a big and strikingly beautiful ballad with Shaboozey duetting with R&B star Kehlani.

Elsewhere, The Outlaw Cherie Lee is more purely country: If I Was an Outlaw has saloon-bar piano, Sweet Revenge goes country rock, while the closing track is a burst of the traditional cowboy ballad Streets of Laredo sung by Orville Peck. The album’s predominant mode is stark and brooding, driven by fingerpicked acoustic guitar and decorated with fiddle. At their best, these tracks are darkly atmospheric and powerful – as on Drunk – although it’s occasionally hard not to feel that part of Shaboozey’s USP has gone with his decision to dial down the rap influence in his vocals. He can certainly croon with a glowering power, but there’s a distinct leap in excitement when he reverts to a hip-hop-inspired delivery, the better to inhabit the character of a swaggering outlaw on Til Sunday.

Still, as a demonstration of his eclecticism – or, if you prefer, a desire to be all things to all people – The Outlaw Cherie Lee works well. The pop-facing tracks hit, the strike rate when he diversifies is higher than his naysayers would suggest, and there’s an impressive boldness about his evident desire to draw R&B, soul and hip-hop artists into his world – aside from Gunna and Kehlani, there’s an impressive turn from Leon Bridges on Burn It Down. The overarching storyline is tight and well handled. Perhaps most importantly, the album never feels like the work of an artist whose career has been destabilised by a huge, unexpected and unrepeatable hit, but rather the work of an artist digging in for the long haul.

Mr Wa7t – Secrets (Richard Norris Fitness Mix)

The original is great soulful, deep pop, but Richard Norris’s remix turns it into delightfully smooth, hot-afternoon Balearic: very much what is needed at the moment.

‘We have to become warriors’: the fight to save the world’s only women’s sculpture park

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 10:13:26 GMT

With most monuments in London made by men, Claire Mander envisaged the Artist’s Garden as a way to redress the balance. Now, she says, it could be turned into a generic space for VIP events and cocktails

Ten years ago, when Claire Mander was studying for an art history MA at the Courtauld Institute in London, she stumbled upon the neglected roof terrace of nearby Temple underground station. She found herself strangely drawn to the overgrown expanse with its stunning views of the Thames and the London Eye.

“It was dirty, abandoned and a magnet for antisocial behaviour,” recalls Mander, now director and curator of theColab, an arts charity and incubator specialising in large-scale outdoor sculptures. She researched the history of the abandoned space, which was built as part of the Victoria Embankment in 1870. Before that, the ground beneath the site housed a 17th-century sculpture garden created by the Countess of Arundel.

“It inspired me to visualise how the roof terrace could become a really special women’s sculpture garden,” says Mander. “The ‘hidden in plain sight’ nature of the location felt to me like the perfect place to redress some of the gender disparity that we see in public artworks.”

A survey by Art UK revealed that of almost 1,500 monuments in London, more than a fifth were dedicated to named men and only 4% were dedicated to women, half as many as those that celebrated animals. And of all the public sculptures in London, only 13% were created by women.

Mander kept badgering Westminster council until eventually they gave her the go-ahead. With funding from donations and over £500,000 to date from the council, the Artist’s Garden opened in October 2021. It is the world’s first and only public sculpture garden devoted to the work of female artists. Since then they have attracted 100,000 visitors a year, commissioned 18 major works, and collaborated with 24 different emerging and established artists.

But now, theColab has been informed by Places for London, Transport for London’s property arm, that their licence to occupy the site will not be renewed on 1 October and they must clear the garden.

A Places for London spokesperson said: “The terrace and station roof may now require essential repair and safety works, and the space needs to be cleared for the assessment of the extent of the works required. We are working with Westminster city council and local stakeholders to explore alternative locations nearby for the Artist’s Garden, while also developing future plans for the terrace at Temple. As a legally protected space, it will always remain accessible to the public.”

Mander disputes this, stating that the repairs relate to upgrading the commercial property below the terrace, and that according to the scope of works, no large-scale overhaul of the roof is mentioned. She believes the space is at risk of being handed over to a private developer. “It’s a prime location with incredible views of the river, ideal for VIP events selling overpriced cocktails. They don’t understand that this is a landmark project. Their perception seems to be that we’re a small, pathetic female-led charity that’s doing some sort of nice little sculptural things. But we are prepared to take this to court if it comes to it.” They have launched a campaign and petition to save the garden.

Alexandra Hodby, head of programmes at Yorkshire Sculpture Park and a trustee of the gardens, points out that such spaces are of vital cultural and economic value, both to artists and to the cities they inhabit. “Look at the High Line in New York. It wasn’t even a public space, then it was made public through art. Artists activated it. Now it’s one of the most visited places in the city.”

Hodby believes that sculpture has a particular power to engage the public in a way that art on gallery walls does not. “There’s an immediacy about it, there’s no separation between the work and the world.” This is true. On the day I visit, London is in the grip of a heatwave. Office workers, builders on an early lunch, bemused tourists, all throng the space. A toddler crawls towards Mexican artist Adeline de Monseignat’s pebbled Croissant, no doubt spying a potential see-saw. In the distance, I spot people posing for selfies beside Alice Wilson’s Savoy, a giant forest of technicolor timbers.

“Obviously, seeing art made by women inspires other women who want to make art themselves. But it goes far beyond that,” says Hodby. “Representation is about being part of a public space and being seen. Visibility allows visitors to see themselves, be it the Artist’s Garden or Yorkshire Sculpture Park where we endeavour to show a broad range of artists including non-binary, queer practice and younger artists.”

Lakwena Maciver created the site’s opening exhibit, a kaleidoscopic mural titled Back in the Air: A Meditation on Higher Ground. It unfurled across the entire 140 sq-metre space. For the British-Ugandan artist, the site holds particular emotional significance. “When I was a teenager, we would get the train up to town and I remember sitting in Embankment Gardens eating Skittles with my sister. I’d be thinking about my future but also feeling that, as a minority, London didn’t belong to me. To be asked to do the mural was very special because I was being invited to contribute something so monumental. It was like, I do belong! It has never occurred to me not to work on a large scale but I had so many positive interactions with visitors at that site, it gave me a lot of confidence.”

Artist Florence Peake created work for the site’s current show Sculpture in Three Acts. “It’s rare these days in London to find a public space that is free and doesn’t have a commercial agenda. It’s a place to reflect, take a breath and be with artworks that may draw you in, and hold space for a state of reflection.”

She believes the garden has provided a much-needed space. “It allows visitors to see that women can make huge monolithic work. Of course we can! It’s just that so often we’re not trusted to be ambitious and do things to scale. Our visions are often rejected and considered naive. This is what I’ve encountered in my 30 years of being an artist anyway. A man comes along and says ‘I want to build a big steel thing sticking 18 metres up in the air’ and he’s hailed as a genius. A woman suggesting the same thing, there are anxious sideways glances.”

At the heart of the garden is the artist’s hut, currently featuring a wraparound photomontage created by feminist artist Linder Sterling. “The Artist’s Garden is situated in Temple, once the province of the Knights Templar,” she says. “It seems that women have to become warriors now and defend our right to take up space there.”

Presiding over the back wall of the montage is a portrait of the Countess of Arundel, reminding us of the lineage of women who have gone before. “On one of the walls of the hut, you can see the phrase ‘She Is Here’, the title of the work, writ large,” adds Sterling. “Now that the site is under threat, She Is Here has become a rallying cry - we’re not going anywhere.”
