I’d never cried during a live broadcast – then three poignant words had me sobbing

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 10:00:11 GMT

I couldn’t help choking up when the writer Katriona O’Sullivan told me her life story. Now I’m on a mission to get everyone to read her memoir

In more than 30 years of live broadcasting, I’ve only once sobbed on air. This was the other week, during a radio interview with a professor of psychology called Katriona O’Sullivan. That’s what she is now, a professor at Maynooth University in County Kildare. Before that, she was at Trinity College Dublin, where she also got her PhD. Before that, she was to be found on the access programme through which she got into Trinity. Before that she was living a life of chaos in Dublin, a single mother with next to nothing.

She was in Dublin escaping an even more chaotic life in Birmingham, which had followed a childhood in Coventry, growing up in harrowing, grinding, distressing, miserable, terrifying poverty. No single adjective feels adequate here, so I’ve thrown in as many as I can think of.

She’s better with words than me, as you’ll find if you read her memoir, which is called Poor. I’m buying so many copies of her book to give to people that she may soon have to write one called Rich. I’m on a mission to get everyone in the country to read it.

O’Sullivan and her siblings were parented, if that’s the right word (it isn’t), by two heroin users. She went hungry, for food and for love. Her first real taste of either came at primary school. It was there she came across Ms Arkinson and Miss Hall. If Coventry can manage a statue of Lady Godiva atop a horse, I suggest it should also find a spot for one of Ms Arkinson and Miss Hall.

Ms Arkinson, a teacher, was Irish and knew O’Sullivan’s heritage. “An Irish girl in my class – what a treat.” To have an adult pleased to have her in the room was a new sensation for O’Sullivan. “I loved Ms Arkinson and I knew she loved me,” she writes. “Her eyes said so. The way she helped me said so.”

Miss Hall was the teacher’s assistant who, like Ms Arkinson, like every kid in the school, was aware that poor Katriona smelled. “Pissy pants”, some of her classmates called her. As children often do when they are in crisis, she wet the bed, every night. And she didn’t know how to wash. “There were no towels in our bathroom, barely any toilet paper. Never any soap. None of us owned a toothbrush.” Miss Hall took her to the toilets, locked the door and taught her how to wash. And she gave her clean pants that had the days of the week stamped on them. Words fail me.

In a fairy story, this would have been the moment that things started to get better. Well, they did, but mainly they didn’t. Years of disarray lay ahead, horrific stuff I can’t bear to relate here. And even stuff, she told me, that she couldn’t bring herself to write. What that concerns I dread to think.

She tells an uplifting, if brutal, story so well. It helps that I love her voice, which is a mashup of my two favourite accents: my, erm, own accent, West Midlands, and Dublin. Listening to her, it struck me how much we know about the lives of all manner of ordinary and extraordinary people. Celebrities afford us blow-by-blow accounts of their every move. Athletes, actors, musicians, politicians; you name it. Some of their accounts are better than others, some more honest than others. But we have that insight. Important work is also done by film-makers, endeavouring to show what life looks like in far-flung corners of planet Earth.

This is all to the good, but it’s bizarre that we know more about what it’s like to be Taylor Swift, or Cristiano Ronaldo, or what it’s like to live in Bangladesh or the Amazon basin, than we know about what life is like for millions of people in this country with childhoods like Katriona’s.

Most of us probably have a clearer idea of what it’s like to live on the International Space Station than what it’s like to live in a tower block in the wrong part of Coventry, existing – just existing – as a member of the underclass. Underclass is a ghastly word, I know, which is possibly one reason we don’t like using it. More likely it’s just another excuse to look away and pretend that world doesn’t exist. There’s a good chance you haven’t even read this far.

O’Sullivan’s story, in a turn of events that is nothing less than thrilling, has a happy ending. She landed in Dublin before the 2008 crash, when the Celtic tiger was still alive and kicking. There was money about – money to help people in her world. Help with childcare, treatment for addiction, counselling, access courses to higher education for those whose trajectories were never going to fly them close to any such thing. It all worked out wonderfully in the end. And it’s joyous to join her on that ride.

Then the epilogue, her afterword, is a thump to the solar plexus. It amounts to a stern bollocking from her to you if you happen to be drawing the wrong conclusions from this story. It’s fine to love the rags-to-riches ride – who doesn’t? – but if you’re taking it as proof that, if you just try hard enough, you can do it, you can be anything you want to be, then that, she says in so many words, is balls.

Most people who start out in the world she knew never make it out. She insists she did so only because political decisions were made in a time of relative plenty to fund the kind of social services that were there to help her. Many of those services, in Ireland and the UK, have since been cut.

As for the bit that had me choking up on live radio, it was talking about three words that jumped out of a sentence in her book describing her love, her need, for school dinners. It’s not her reference to the food that got me – it’s how, almost as an aside, she refers to her classmates: “Other kids, the loved ones, they sometimes complained, but I didn’t give a shit what was served. I’d have eaten anything.”

The loved ones. What it must be like to think that everyone but you is loved.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

‘Grey lump with orange wings’: hummingbird hawk-moths descend on UK gardens

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 08:00:01 GMT

Boom in migrating moth sightings put down to hot weather, strong winds and food scarcity in Europe

He had just sat down to dinner in the garden when a speedy visitor whizzed by – a “grey lump with orange wings”, recalled Luke Burstow, from Sussex. It was a hummingbird hawk-moth, a flying insect that migrates to the UK from continental Europe and north Africa.

“I was like: ‘Wow!’,” said the software project manager. “I didn’t even know they existed.”

Burstow is one of many UK wildlife watchers who have described seeing the moth on social media lately. “This made my day,” wrote one Reddit user after their sighting.

Butterfly and moth experts told the Guardian that 2026 could be a bumper year for hummingbird hawk-moths in the UK after a boom in sightings during recent weeks. Hot weather and strong winds appear to have brought many of the insects here from more southerly climes.

Burstow, who, along with his wife, spied the hummingbird hawk-moth enjoying buddleia flowers on 30 June, said: “It was just so different to everything else you normally see.” After quickly Googling the species, Burstow ran inside to grab his camera and managed to take some photos of the creature. He marvelled at how, even with a very fast shutter speed, the moth’s wings – which beat roughly 80 times per second – still appeared slightly blurry in his photos.

“We’ve had a big increase in sightings and inquiries about the hummingbird hawk-moth sent to us this year,” said Richard Austin, a recording schemes officer at the charity Butterfly Conservation. “We expect it is going to be a great summer for them.” Austin cautioned, however, that it was too early to compare their numbers with previous years.

Hummingbird hawk-moths may be spotted all around the UK, including in Northern Ireland and even northern Scotland. Warm southerly winds associated with recent heatwaves could have helped bring high numbers of the moths to the UK, said Richard Harrington, an honorary fellow of the Royal Entomological Society. “It may also be that their food plants are drying out in their Mediterranean breeding areas,” he added.

Sunny weather in the UK has perhaps encouraged people to spend more time than usual in their gardens, raising the chances that they will spot one of the moths, said Ray Barnett, a council member at the British Entomological and Natural History Society. “I’m in Bristol and there’s lots of people recording it locally,” he said.

There’s a chance the hummingbird hawk-moths could stick around, should the UK continue to experience milder winters due to global warming, Barnett added.

Hibernating adults that make it through the British winter may go on to reproduce in the UK on a regular basis. Hummingbird hawk-moth larvae feed on plants including lady’s bedstraw and hedge bedstraw, which are common wildflowers in the UK.

“If these weather patterns continue, then [the moth] is going to survive winters regularly,” said Barnett. “It’s almost becoming a resident species rather than a purely migratory species.”

You be the judge: should my brother stop hogging the living room while staying in my flat?

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 07:00:55 GMT

Daniella doesn’t want to go to bed early. Seamus says she shouldn’t offer the sofabed if she doesn’t want guests. Who has room for improvement?

Find out how to get a disagreement settled or become a juror

double quotation markIt’s not that I don’t want him here, but he needs to understand that I am giving up my space to host him

My younger brother Seamus is staying with me in my flat for six weeks. He’s a teacher and lived with me for a bit last year, before moving to Dubai.

When he lived with me before, we split the bills and mortgage, which was a great help as I was in a tricky spot as a freelancer. He needed somewhere to live after our parents sold their house, so I turned my living room into a bedroom for him.

After he moved out, I used it as a living room again. Now, he’s come back to see friends and family. I bought a sofabed for his stay, which set me back £400. While I like having him here, there has been some tension.

Seamus immediately started changing things around in the flat. He turned up the temperature in the shower and I burned myself. He moved the chopping boards back to where he used to store them. He took the spare keys I was using, so I got locked out.

I like going to bed around midnight, but Seamus wants to go to sleep at 10.30. On the first night, he asked to go to bed at 9.55pm, which meant I had to leave the room and stop the show I was watching. I kicked off. He said: “I’m tired and deserve my own space too.” But it’s not really his room any more. And he wasn’t fresh off the plane – he’d been staying with friends.

It’s not that I don’t want him here, but he needs to understand that I am giving up my space to host him. I do appreciate Seamus helping out around the flat when he’s staying with me. He waters my flowers and does odd jobs. He’s not messy, but I have to ask him to pack away the sofabed every morning so I can use the room in the evenings.

He’s no longer a lodger, but he’s not quite a guest either. I don’t feel it’s fair to ask him for a financial contribution, but I wouldn’t say no if he offered. He has no bills or outgoings and his rent abroad is paid for.

Going back to living with someone 24/7 is a big adjustment. I’m single, and I’d started to enjoy spending time on my own. Am I being selfish or is my irritation reasonable?

double quotation markIf you say someone can be a guest in your home, you can’t take it back when it doesn’t suit you

I need somewhere to stay when I’m back and I’d rather stay with my sister than our parents, who have moved to the country. I think Daniella was a bit put out because I originally said I would move between the two homes, but it’s easier for me to stay in one place.

I understand she is giving up her living room, so I make sure I leave it as I found it and put away the sheets and sofabed every morning. I’ve tried to make myself useful around the flat. I have cooked, bought food and done the gardening. I’ve bought things too – for example, I put up some shelves.

I guess she wouldn’t be stressed if things were less tight for her financially, and as I don’t have any outgoings or bills I understand why she might appreciate a contribution. I don’t mind chipping in towards the bills, but she hasn’t said how much she wants.

Last year, moving in made sense for both of us: I didn’t have anywhere to go and she needed a flatmate to help pay the bills. I paid about £900, which was just under half of her monthly outgoings of £1,875 for her mortgage and bills.

I didn’t mean to change things when I came back. I adjusted the water settings on the shower because I prefer it hot, then forgot to turn it back down – it was accidental. As for moving the chopping boards, I didn’t even think about it. How was I to know she had moved things about since the last time I was here?

When she got upset with me for kicking her out of her living room so I could go to sleep, I was confused because she had said the room was mine during my stay. She either wants me here or she doesn’t. If you say someone can be a guest in your home, you can’t take it back when it doesn’t suit you.

I have adjusted my bedtime to around 11pm, which works better. And Daniella has said that if she wants to watch something that goes on later, she will give me advance notice. I think that will help us live harmoniously for the next six weeks.

If Seamus wants his own space, he should pay for somewhere else to stay. Letting Daniella watch her TV shows is a small price to pay for free accommodation. He should make the effort to fit around her lifestyle – including finding out where the chopping boards live! Phoebe, 24

I’ve seen what can confound Farage on his home turf: optimism. People need a politics that offers them that

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 05:00:52 GMT

You can’t blame his constituents in Clacton for their pessimism – because they have been let down for years

Under battered England flags, cynicism, pessimism and exhaustion stalk the streets of Clacton.

As the byelection called by Nigel Farage approaches, one young couple do not know which candidates are standing. Neither has ever voted. Living in Britain is “depressing”, says the woman in a black floral dress. “The cost of living these days is stupid,” says her partner, wearing a black and grey mechanic’s shirt and a black and red cap. They both work 40 or 50 hours a week, he says, yet “we’re still struggling to pay rent, food, electric, everything else”. They rarely get a day off, and time spent together is rarer still.

No wonder they are not agonising over the £5m personal gift Farage received from a Thailand-based crypto billionaire, or the donations in kind from a convicted fraudster. Life is already taking up all their time.

Communities across Britain have endured stagnation and decline since the financial crash of 2008, but Clacton has more problems than most. Families still descend on the flashing arcades and fairground rides of Clacton pier, but nothing has replaced the economic world swept away by the decline of the English seaside holiday. Clacton is among the top 10% of deprived English constituencies. One neighbourhood is ranked the most deprived in England.

Yet the scandal over Farage’s income provokes precious little anger here. “I know how corrupt everything is,” says a former soldier, who served 22 years. “It’s just part and parcel of politics.” The belief that all politicians are on the take – and that Farage is therefore no different – is everywhere. Tell people that other politicians are not receiving £5m lump sums from foreign billionaires and many simply shrug. Contempt for politicians has become Farage’s protection.

Some come up with their own comforting explanations. A flat cap-wearing man in a wheelchair, who arrived here from Cyprus six decades ago, assumes Farage might invest the £5m in the local community.

There is concern, but it is crowded out by other grievances. “That’s the bit that bothers me,” says one elderly man, before adding something more revealing. “Do you want him as a prime minister? Probably not, but what choice do we have?”

Farage continues to profit from the belief that both Labour and the Conservatives have failed in office. A middle-aged man in a navy polo shirt says he will vote Reform because “the others have just given me a load of rubbish”. The deceit of the toppled prime minister has left its mark. “That Keir Starmer was a complete liar,” he says.

Farage also benefits from what voters project on to him. When I approach one elderly couple, the man is promptly abandoned by his wife, who correctly anticipates that he will answer at length. He regrets voting for Boris Johnson’s Conservatives – and, before that, Margaret Thatcher. “She sold us off,” he says. “Water, telecoms.”

Why, then, I ask, support someone who regards Thatcher as a political hero? “You’ve got to give them a chance,” he replies, apparently without noticing that he has repeatedly regretted doing exactly that.

Only around one in 20 residents here was born abroad, and 96% are white, yet migration and race loom over the constituency. Economic grievance inevitably plays a part. When I suggest to one affable young man covered in tattoos that migrants are blamed for the country’s problems, he agrees. “It’s an easy route out, isn’t it?”

He still intends to vote for Farage, because “I believe he does what he says he’s going to do”. Unfortunately, he cannot say what that is.

But economics cannot explain everything. Disinformation about migrants and refugees – promoted by sections of the media and spread online – has cut through. One middle-aged couple told me they would have voted for the far-right Restore party, had it fielded a candidate. They grow increasingly agitated as we speak.

“Eighty-five per cent of Muslim women can’t even speak English, and that’s a fact,” says the man. Where did he get this statistic? Annoyed at being asked for evidence, he eventually says it came “from news” and tells me to “go and look it up”.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

After they leave, I do. According to recent census data, two-thirds of Muslim women have English as their main language, with 87.7% speaking the language proficiently. Among British-born women, nearly all have English as their main language.

This is what happens when real anger at a country in crisis collides with lies about who has caused it. “This country’s in a right mess,” says a bald, weather-beaten, middle-aged man, his sleeveless shirt open at the chest. When I ask what is wrong, he answers pithily: “Everything about it, everything.”

Unless there is a secret army of shy Count Binface voters, the comedy writer turned “independent space warrior” – popular on social media – will not triumph here. I find only a couple of people intending to plump for him.

That’s not to say there isn’t dissent. Outside a cafe, an elderly man with a wispy grey ponytail and sunglasses pushed back on his head nurses a drink from a white mug, an England flag hanging in the window behind him. He tells me he has Asperger’s and has “always known from a young age that we’re all the same”.

Farage, he argues, is riding in “on a white charger to rescue them from the refugees”, even though “I don’t believe Nigel Farage is for the working man”. Politicians roll up their sleeves and affect the common touch, but “they’re a different class. They’re the ruling class, and it’s the same fucking ruling class all the time”.

He has lost his soulmate and says he rarely leaves home. In a town where so many are resigned to cynicism, he has a simple prescription: “We’ve got one world,” he says. “Let’s look after it and let’s look after each other.” Clacton is not uniquely prejudiced, nor is it afflicted by mass stupidity. You can’t blame the people here for their prevailing pessimism. Neither the Tories nor Labour have rescued coastal towns like this from their pronounced decline – nor Britain as a whole from a generation of stagnation. The anger is real: work that doesn’t pay, public services that have been stripped back, communities not invested in. The people of Clacton have concluded that if the main parties have no answers, why not bet on something else? But a crypto billionaire-funded multimillionaire with multiple jobs who blames migrants for their ills is hardly the solution. Indeed, Farage wants to double down on the very economic policies that have caused so much pain. One young man intending to vote for Farage complains about Labour attacking disability benefits. “Yeah, but they’re all trying to do that,” he says bleakly. “Everyone’s trying to do it.” The only way out is surely a politics which ends people’s resignation to decline – and offers some optimism.

Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist

Burnham the crowd-pleaser knows how to make friends, but he’ll be defined by how he makes enemies

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 04:00:53 GMT

The prime minister’s instinct to not upset people is set against a lifelong desire to effect transformative change. The two may not sit together easily

Andy Burnham has always liked to be liked. Studying at secondary school near Liverpool in the 1980s, he writes in his autobiography and manifesto, Head North, “involved me walking something of a tightrope. Because of my mum and dad’s insistence that I should aim for university, I would largely try to keep up to date with my work. But … I realised I could often make the class laugh and that won me credit with the in-crowd. It was hard to be both a good student and one of the lads.”

As the new leader of a divided country, he is still trying to appeal to opposing interests while establishing his own, upbeat brand. “Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose and positivity,” he said in his first speech outside 10 Downing Street. After a post-Brexit decade dominated by angry rightwing politics, Labour infighting, never-ending culture wars and online acrimony, Burnham’s affable, seemingly inclusive politics has a strong initial appeal. This week, for the first time in 18 months, Labour is ahead of Reform UK in the polls. It’s possible that some voters have finally had enough of divisive politics and would like to try something different.

As an insecure party, temperamentally and electorally, Labour is periodically drawn towards a politics of national unity. “New Labour is the political arm of none other than the British people as a whole,” claimed its general election manifesto in 1997, managing to sound both wildly over-confident and anxiously self-justifying. Lacking the Tories’ right to rule aura and association with deep Englishness – even though those politically priceless qualities depend on a deliberately partial reading of history – Labour tries to make its governments seem more legitimate by using patriotic, non-partisan language. Yet only its most articulate and assured leaders, such as Tony Blair, Harold Wilson and perhaps now Burnham, successfully pull this off.

Yet unlike Blair in 1997 and Wilson in 1964, Burnham is not launching a fresh Labour project in relatively benign economic and political times, and aiming to keep the status quo broadly intact. Instead, he is trying to rescue a two-year-old administration by promising “a new political model and a new economic model”, and “the biggest changes [in Britain] in the last 40 years”. None of these can be done, it seems reasonable to assume, without challenging many of the old order’s beneficiaries. So how is his politics of unity likely to fare once he starts making lots of enemies?

Those may include shareholders of privatised utilities, wealthy owners of under-taxed homes, people who like London’s national dominance, leaders of other parties who don’t want Burnham’s “more collaborative” politics, and journalists who prefer reporting on Westminster plots and rivalries rather than the progress of reforms in the rest of the country. The instantly hostile, sometimes hysterical reaction from much of the press and most other parties to his initial, relatively modest and non-partisan policy proposals gives a hint of the fury coming his way. As Gordon Brown, Ed Miliband, Jeremy Corbyn and Keir Starmer all painfully learned, any Labour leadership even fractionally to the left of Blair’s in any policy area will be widely presented as a return to the supposedly bleak 1970s or the beginning of a socialist dictatorship – even though such comparisons are dependent on crude caricatures and huge exaggerations. Many voters, across multiple parties, from Labour to the Greens to Reform UK, have been saying for years that they want Britain to be governed in a new way; but heaven help any government that dares to try.

Yet Burnham’s positivity may be less naive than it seems. As mayor of Greater Manchester and a candidate in Makerfield, his can-do air attracted support far beyond Labour’s shrunken strongholds. Many voters don’t pay close attention to government policies, to all their practical implications and precisely how they will be funded. If they did, Starmer would have got more credit for the painstaking and important improvements his government made to employment rights, for instance.

But voters do notice politicians with zest. “I think this might be the best day of my life,” said Burnham at the opening of No 10 North in Manchester. The apparent unguardedness, and the risk that it will come back to haunt him, both break the cautious rules of British politics as they have accumulated since the 1990s. The opening paragraphs of future articles about the rise and fall of the Burnham administration already write themselves. Yet successful governments put an appealing emotional and rhetorical frame around their unavoidably diffuse and incomplete activities, which makes these activities resonate and seem part of a bigger story. These governments, in short, are greater than the sum of their parts.

Burnham saw some of the pervasive impact of Margaret Thatcher’s premiership as a politically conscious teenager. His school bus passed the entrance to a local colliery, where striking miners were slowly but surely being defeated. As a junior minister, he served in the equally pivotal Blair government. As mayor, Burnham spent nine years away from Westminster, watching from a distance as several of Blair and Thatcher’s successors quickly failed. So it’s not surprising that Burnham gives the impression of having thought quite a lot about how to be an effective prime minister. “I am under no illusions about how hard this is all going to be,” he wrote last week, “but I have a clear plan and I know how to get things done.”

We’ll see. So far, his plan includes several elements – a 10-year time span, tight immigration restrictions, increased defence spending and a focus on working class and non-metropolitan Britain – familiar from Starmer’s premiership and other failed governments since Brexit. Burnham also appears to believe that less-than-revolutionary figures such as his new chancellor, John Healey, can help achieve his ambitious goal of “ending neoliberalism” in Britain.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Such appointments could be a cunning ploy: seeking radical ends by deceptively moderate, reassuring means. Or they could show that Burnham’s bolder ideas, developed relatively recently, are still outweighed by his instinct not to upset people. But as his year-long, often dismissed, but precisely executed leadership coup has just demonstrated, his capacity to surprise should not be underestimated.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

‘It makes you feel you’ve got a really dirty house’: what’s behind the UK’s plagues of flies?

The Guardian Thu, 30 Jul 2026 04:00:52 GMT

From Leicestershire to Carmarthenshire, neighbourhoods are struggling with wave after wave of houseflies. Why are they suffering while others are spared? And is there no alternative to nets and zappers?

Francesca Davies’s living room is absolutely teeming with flies. You can’t enter the contact centre worker’s home without a cluster of insects rising from the sofa or the floor to buzz around your face. Davies and her family live in West Heath, a suburb of the Cheshire town Congleton. Davies’s husband, Alex Andrew, a 29-year-old maintenance engineer, grew up in the market town and he used to think of West Heath as a desirable area, with its well-maintained houses and access to green space. When he and Davies were able to buy a new-build here in 2019 via a shared ownership scheme, they felt incredibly lucky. That is, until they moved in, and realised that every summer swarms of flies descend on their neighbourhood, an issue that is “getting worse”, Davies says.

At the moment, the 27-year-old swats flies out of her young daughters’ bedroom every night before she puts them to bed, and keeps doors and windows closed or covered with fly nets as much as possible. She and Andrew have even bought an industrial fly killer (like the ones often found in fish and chip shops) for their kitchen, as it is impossible to start cooking without attracting even more insects. The pair have become used to the sound of flies “getting zapped throughout the night”, Davies says.

The family have considered moving out of the area because of the flies, and say some of their former neighbours already have. But Davies is reluctant to give up on the house that is her “pride and joy”, she says. “It is a wonderful place to live. West Heath is so pretty, and everyone’s so lovely.”

Not to mention, “You would have to sell it in the winter,” Andrew points out, as prospective buyers would surely be put off by flies swarming around during a viewing. Instead, Davies is attempting to put pressure on the council and the Environment Agency to investigate by setting up a petition, which now has more than 1,000 signatures, asking local authorities “to take this matter seriously and to prioritise our community’s wellbeing”.

The petition has attracted a number of comments from other local people, including one who lives a 20-minute walk away from Andrew and Davies. “I’m shooing 40-plus flies out of my kitchen regularly throughout the day,” the commenter says. “It’s a constant battle.” Andrew says he has spoken to many neighbours who are struggling with the problem: one orders takeaways every day in the summer to avoid having to cook, while another has draped their newborn baby’s cot in a mosquito net. “They’ve all had enough,” Andrew and Davies’s neighbour Bryan Stahl says, when we walk over the road to his house, which the street’s residents generally consider to be the worst affected by the infestation.

Though it’s hard to believe as we swat flies away while we chat, today is a relatively mild day for flies, Stahl tell me, because it is breezier than it has been in recent weeks. At the height of the recent heatwave, the 54-year-old and his partner stayed inside, or in garden chairs under a gazebo walled with fly nets. Davies and Andrew have a similar structure for their garden, which they set up when their daughters want to use their paddling pool. Stahl, a higher level teaching assistant in a school, has spent about £500 on the gazebo and numerous fly screens, he thinks – and is considering forking out thousands more for permanent fly shutters. “It makes you feel like you’ve got a really dirty house,” he says.

Even though you would be hard-pressed to find anyone as anti-fly right now as the residents of West Heath, it’s not as if flies are popular with many people. Whether it’s Jeff Goldblum’s gruesome transformation into a fly in David Cronenberg’s 1986 horror film The Fly, or God sending swarms of flies as one of the 10 plagues inflicted on the Egyptians to persuade the Pharaoh to set the Israelites free in the Old Testament, the messaging is clear: flies are disgusting.

But could they be due a rebrand? After all, bees can be just as buzzy and annoying, and even sting us, but that doesn’t seem to have damaged their “cute” reputation, their likeness printed on T-shirts or tablecloths. Like bees, flies are pollinators and “essential to a healthy planet,” says Andrew Whitehouse, head of operations at the invertebrate conservation charity Buglife. In fact, he adds, there are some plants that are only pollinated by flies – including the cacao tree. “So if you didn’t have flies, you wouldn’t have chocolate.”

And though we might find it gross that flies are so attracted to faeces or rotting matter, it is actually a good thing that they are. “Fly larvae or maggots will eat lots of dead organic material,” Whitehouse says. “In doing that, they’re recycling nutrients back into the soil, they’re getting rid of those things like dead bodies and dung. That prevents the spread of disease as well. So it’s incredibly important.”

In addition, “loads and loads of other animals eat flies”, Whitehouse says. “Spiders spring to mind, but lots of vertebrates as well. So birds and bats and amphibians and reptiles and fish all feed on either adult flies or their larvae. And they’re a really important food source for lots of these animals.”

There are more than 7,000 species of fly found in the UK, including bluebottles, greenbottles, hoverflies, mosquitoes, fruit flies and crane flies (daddy longlegs). Houseflies (your classic chunky black fly; probably what comes to mind when most of us think of a fly) are generally considered the UK’s most common, although it is difficult to say for sure, because “weirdly, not enough people study flies”, says Erica McAlister, a fly expert and Natural History Museum curator.

Houseflies are important pollinators all over the world – in fact, McAlister says, a cousin of the common housefly is the dominant pollinator in the Arctic. “People are stuck on bees being the most important pollinators – and they are good, I’m not going to deny that,” she says. But while bee larvae don’t do anything except consume food until they have grown into their adult form, flies are “kicked out at birth”, and as larvae “they’re out there already helping clean up our environment”. And for anyone stuck on the idea that flies aren’t as cute as bees, she urges them to “go and look up a bee-fly”, which she says is “arguably one of the cutest species in the UK”.

Sure, a fly that has been “walking from faeces to food or decomposing food to another food” could be transporting pathogens, McAlister admits – but in “much the same way as if you handle money or if you go into a pub or if you shake hands with people”. As for flies “vomiting” on food, another complaint you often hear from fly-haters, it is not “vomiting” in the same way we think about humans throwing up, she says. “They’re not bringing up gut contents”, but releasing digestive enzymes on to food to break it down, “because they do not have biting mouth parts – they basically have a straw or a sponge with which they can suck up these ingredients.”

Instead of dwelling on flies’ negative associations, she says, “I try to get people to think of them as like, ‘It’s amazing, you’ve got these wild animals roaming around in front of your face.’” McAlister encourages people to learn about flies’ “fascinating” metamorphosis from larvae to adult fly, or the fact that they can land upside down, or that their eyes consist of thousands of facets that act like individual cameras. Every second, “they are processing thousands upon thousands of images”, she says.

It is all the more important to think positively about flies given that insects as a whole, including flies, are largely in decline. Although some migrant species are bucking the trend, the UK’s local species that rely on specific host plants or locations are “suffering badly” as the country becomes less accommodating to wildlife, McAlister says. “We need our politicians to really work at encompassing all of their decisions with an ecological framework,” she believes. And that’s in order to protect our own future, not just the future of flies: “If we die, insects won’t care,” McAlister says. “But if insects die, we are pretty much on a very downward spiral very quickly” – because of our reliance on their pollination services.

McAlister is not saying that we should all be living like Davies and Andrew. She is well aware that flies en masse can be a problem – but killing them, particularly in “a horrible and inhumane way” such as via fly tape, isn’t always the answer. Paradoxically, creating fly-friendly environments such as ponds in gardens, or even “a bucket on the veranda”, invites all kinds of wildlife, she says, including fly predators like birds and frogs, so flies actually get eaten and end up bothering humans less.

“There is an argument” for pest control when it comes to fly infestations, she says, but the most important thing to do is to “find out why that’s happened. Because the flies are an indicator that maybe something else is going on.” When fly infestations are reported, as they are every summer (currently, residents in Sileby, Leicestershire and Llanelli, Carmarthenshire are suffering along with those in West Heath), usually a link can be found “to some sort of waste event or some sort of environmental perturbation”, the curator says.

Davies and her neighbours think their fly problem is connected to a local recycling plant run by the company Tandom. In a statement sent to the Guardian, Tandom says it has “implemented a range of additional precautionary measures”, and is “working constructively with the Environment Agency, Cheshire East council and our independent pest control specialists”, but emphasised: “There is currently no evidence that flies are breeding on our site.” A spokesperson for the Environment Agency confirmed that it is in touch with Tandom, and says it has instructed the company “to take immediate steps to tackle the issue”, adding that it “will not hesitate to take appropriate enforcement action if required”.

Rather than automatically blaming flies when they bother us, we should look for potential human involvement, McAlister thinks. While we often think of house flies as dirty because they feed on faeces and are found in dirty areas, they actually “have to be the absolute opposite – they have to be exceptionally clean because they are sometimes in a bad environment”, she says. “But it’s our environment; we’re the ones who’ve made this environment. So, you know, we’re throwing stones at an indicator that something has maybe gone wrong.”

Perhaps it’s humans, then, not flies, who are the true pests.

What We Really Learned From the Fauci Hearing

The New York Times July 29, 2026

Guest Essay

By Rachael Bedard

Dr. Bedard, a contributing Opinion writer, is a geriatrician and a palliative care doctor.

Senate hearings are always theatrical. Even still, Wednesday morning’s Senate committee hearing to interrogate Dr. Anthony Fauci on, among other things, the origins of Covid-19 was a shocking performance: Dr. Fauci barely spoke, while everyone else spent some three hours projecting their emotions onto him.

Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky, the committee chair, has cast himself as a contemporary Joe McCarthy intent on ferreting out the truth about one man’s supposed crimes against his country. The Covid lockdown “could never have been inflicted without you aiding and abetting the crime,” he said to Dr. Fauci during his opening statement. And “you have for years avoided responsibility.”

Just before leaving office, President Joe Biden took the remarkable step of providing Dr. Fauci with a blanket pardon covering all of his activities from 2014 to early 2025. This pardon would not protect against new accusations of perjury if Dr. Fauci were found to have lied during sworn testimony after Mr. Biden left office in 2025. On the advice of his lawyers, the 85-year-old Dr. Fauci made the extraordinary choice during Wednesday’s hearing to plead the Fifth Amendment. As Republican senators peppered him with often hostile questions, he repeated over and over again that he respectfully declined to answer.

By doing so, Dr. Fauci became the speechless cipher to whom committee Republicans and Democrats argued their irreconcilable stories — about the pandemic, but also more broadly about science and public health in America. The effect was a useless drama that offered zero insights to a public desperate for them.

Mr. Paul personally and directly accuses Dr. Fauci of: funding dangerous gain-of-function research in Wuhan, China, that may have resulted in a lab leak, releasing SARS-CoV-2 into the world (which Dr. Fauci denies); promoting mitigation policies that infringed on civil liberties; profiting off his pandemic-era fame; and hiding the truth about what he knew about the virus’s origins and when.

Dr. Fauci has faced congressional grilling numerous times, before both the House and the Senate. In the days before this event, Mr. Paul released more than 1,100 pages of Dr. Fauci’s diary entries. (Dr. Fauci apparently wrote them on computers associated with his government account; they were retrieved by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his staff, who provided them to Senator Paul.)

Excerpts from Dr. Fauci’s private writings, including his reflections on his conversations with celebrities and his growing award collection, seem to affirm the right’s portrayal of him as a self-regarding operator who was flattered rather than humbled by the attention he received during a national crisis.

But many of the entries being cited as evidence that Dr. Fauci lied to the public or deliberately withheld information are really reminders of how uncertain the context was for pandemic decision-making. Some of the entries, in fact, give a useful glimpse into how decisions were hashed out among experts with different perspectives and concerns, with Dr. Fauci often playing the role of convener or informal chair. On Jan. 26, 2020, he wrote that the virus may have originated in animals and jumped to humans; later, he dutifully noted conversations he was having with other scientists who were discussing alternative possibilities.

In an interview with The New York Times’s David Wallace-Wells in 2023, Mr. Wallace-Wells pushed Dr. Fauci on the lab leak hypothesis and his role in funding research in Wuhan. When Mr. Wallace-Wells suggested more thorough responses that Dr. Fauci could’ve offered when questioned on the subject, he became irritated. “David, have you ever testified before a congressional committee?” he snapped.

Dr. Fauci seems to have concluded years ago that the more he says, the more his character and actions become subject to debate. And so, on Wednesday, he took abuse — and some praise — and stayed silent. Another Republican senator, Josh Hawley of Missouri, in a particularly aggressive performance, accused him of wanting “to be the sun god of science.” Senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, demanded to know, using an expletive, who Dr. Fauci thought he was for doing what he did.

Democratic senators, including Gary Peters from Michigan and Richard Blumenthal from Connecticut, commiserated with Dr. Fauci over his ordeal, and used much of their time to argue that the committee ought to be discussing all of the ways President Trump and Secretary Kennedy have ruined public health.

Only Senator Andy Kim, a Democrat from New Jersey, said anything insightful — and that was about what the hearing represented about the state of politics in America, and the implications for trust and a functioning democracy. “Right now, I feel the hyper-partisanship growing in this country in dangerous ways,” Mr. Kim said. “People calling our public servants criminals,” he lamented, is “undermining the very nature of the work of governance.”

He’s right, of course; show trials are bad for democracy and do nothing to get us closer to either truth or consensus. Hanging over every conversation about what happened during the pandemic of the recent past is anxiety about what might happen should we face a pandemic in the near future. In projecting all of a difficult era’s conflicts onto Dr. Fauci, Republicans evade the harder work of figuring out what we actually should learn from his, and our, mistakes.

Dr. Fauci is a complicated man who has been both elevated and reduced to a symbol. His legacy after a decades-long career at the intersection of science and politics is now defined by incompatible, contested accounts of his pandemic-era impact. There is little hope of resolving that contest any time soon.

Theater, at its most powerful, refracts truth through fiction so its force can be viscerally felt. This hearing was a performance that only entrenched the mistrust that increasingly defines Americans’ relationship to their institutions. Dr. Fauci, the ultimate institutionalist, has become that mistrust’s enduring target.

Rachael Bedard is a contributing Opinion writer, a geriatrician and a palliative care doctor.

Spain Mobilizes Military as Thousands of Migrants Cross Into Ceuta

The New York Times July 30, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The arrivals in Ceuta, a six-mile-long peninsula on Morocco’s northern coast that Spain has governed for centuries, have fueled political tensions.

By Jason Horowitz

Thousands of migrants climbed over a border fence or swam onto the shores of Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta on Thursday, prompting a mobilization of the Spanish military and fueling political tensions on the Spanish mainland.

In recent days, 1,500 migrants had entered Ceuta, a six-mile-long peninsula on Morocco’s northern coast that Spain has governed for centuries, according to the area’s president, Juan Jesús Vivas. At least 14 people have died attempting to enter the territory, a spokesman for the Spanish government said on Thursday.

The arrivals were so numerous — and the potential political and security ramifications so serious — that the Spanish government on Thursday evening said that it had mobilized its armed forces to reinforce the police in Ceuta. It said in a statement that it was dispatching military platoons to enforce border security, increasing air and naval support, and sending diving teams to patrol the waters. The European Union offered to send Spain support from Frontex, its border and Coast Guard agency, to reestablish order.

“We are in a situation of total humanitarian and social emergency,” Mr. Vivas told a Spanish radio station on Thursday.

On Thursday evening, the Ceuta government added in a statement that “this is an unprecedented situation that is testing our institutional response capacity and causing profound concern among the entire citizenry.” Fernando Rodríguez Contreras, an official in the government, said the working estimate for the number of people who had crossed was in the tens of thousands, though that figure could not be confirmed.

Migration at Ceuta, and at Melilla, another autonomous Spanish city in North Africa, has long been a point of tension between Morocco and Spain. The two areas constitute the European Union’s sole land border with Africa, and can draw large numbers of young men and other migrants seeking to enter the bloc. More than 10,000 people came over the border in two days in 2021, when the migration crisis reached its peak. In 2022, at least 23 migrants died in a stampede during an attempted mass crossing in Melilla. Many others have died at sea.

It was unclear on Thursday evening what had prompted the latest amassing of people in Ceuta. Analysts said it was too soon to draw conclusions but that Morocco, which controls migration flows across the border, may have been upset about Spain’s recent effort to deepen ties with Algeria. Right-wing critics blamed the Spanish government’s new plan to give undocumented migrants already in the country a path to legal status for attracting illegal arrivals.

What is clear is that the border, on the African mainland, has also been a major source of domestic political tension for Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez — both with anti-immigrant and conservative political opponents who accuse him of being lax on border control as well as pro-immigrant advocates who criticize the government for harsh immigration enforcement tactics.

Unlike the United States and some European neighbors defined by tough immigration stances, Spain’s left-wing government has projected an image of itself as the West’s new melting pot. It has embraced immigrants, especially Latin Americans who speak Spain’s language, share its religion and understand its culture. Some activists have argued that the warm welcome doesn’t extend to many Africans, and that Spain has a complicated historical relationship with Morocco, which accounts for the largest number of legal immigrants to Spain.

But the government made clear on Thursday that the high volume of illegal crossings was not part of its vision.

“The Spanish government is fully committed to providing an immediate response to the situation in Ceuta,” Mr. Sánchez wrote on social media on Thursday, as Spanish television stations broadcast footage of overwhelmed Spanish authorities watching as thousands of excited migrants streamed by.

The right-wing opposition seized the moment.

“This is an invasion,” said Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right party Vox, who accused Mr. Sánchez’s government of purposefully inviting in the migrants, who he suggested, without evidence, were criminals and rapists and potential left-wing voters.

The leading opposition party took a more measured tone but called on Mr. Sánchez to declare a national emergency.

“The situation in Ceuta is desperate,” said Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who leads the conservative Popular Party. “The government cannot shirk its responsibilities.”

Spain, eager to keep good relations with Morocco, in part to maintain its cooperation in deterring migrant arrivals, has downplayed criticism of the Moroccan government, saying that Morocco is helping prevent more people from entering Spanish territory. The Spanish government also said in a statement that it was directing more resources to the border, where the overwhelmed Spanish police and emergency services had been forced to focus only on treating those injured during the crossing.

Mr. Vivas, the Ceuta president, said the area’s reception centers and facilities for unaccompanied minors were overflowing.

Spain’s interior ministry said human-smuggling networks were seizing on a recent Supreme Court decision to encourage migrants to try to enter Europe through Spain. That decision barred the summary return of migrants intercepted at sea ​while attempting to reach the Spanish territories.

Spanish news media reports from Ceuta described some of those who had successfully completed the sea crossing as exhausted from the journey and near death, but others as jubilant, cheering “Long live Spain!” as they tossed flip-flops in the air or knelt to kiss Spanish soil.

But the footage of thousands of people, the vast majority of them young men, walking unencumbered onto Spanish territory touched a nerve for some in Spain and throughout Europe.

“The protection of the Union’s external borders is a crucial part of our efforts to fight illegal migration,” Magnus Brunner, the European Union’s commissioner for Internal Affairs and Migration, wrote on social media. “We are in contact with the relevant authorities on the evolving situation in Ceuta.”

Carlos Barragán contributed reporting from Madrid

Jason Horowitz is the Madrid bureau chief for The Times, covering Spain, Portugal and the way people live throughout Europe.

Father of Teenage Shooter in Georgia Sentenced to 15 Years in Prison

The New York Times July 30, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Prosecutors argued that Colin Gray bore responsibility for the 2024 shooting because he had given his son a gun and failed to act as the teen’s mental health deteriorated.

By Rick Rojas and Johnny Kauffman

Rick Rojas reported from Atlanta, and Johnny Kauffman from Winder, Ga.

The father of a teenager who fatally shot four people at his Georgia high school was sentenced on Thursday to 15 years in prison after a jury found he bore criminal responsibility for his son’s deadly attack in 2024.

The father, Colin Gray, had been convicted in March of murder and involuntary manslaughter, among other charges. Prosecutors argued that he shouldered significant blame for the shooting in Winder, Ga., because he had given his son, Colt, then 14, the rifle that was used and failed to heed signs of his son’s deteriorating mental health and growing obsession with violence.

Prosecuting the parents of juveniles who carry out mass shootings has become one of the latest fronts in the search for accountability in a country frustrated by recurring gun violence. The case against Mr. Gray has stood out for the severity of the charges. His potential sentence ranged from 10 years of probation to 243 years in prison; prosecutors had asked for an 80-year sentence — effectively a life sentence for Mr. Gray, 55.

Judge Nicholas Primm of State Superior Court in Barrow County noted the novelty of the case, describing it as the first of its kind in Georgia and the second in the country. He acknowledged that Mr. Gray had not orchestrated the attack, or even been aware of his son’s specific plans. But his actions — or, more precisely, his failure to act — allowed the attack to happen.

“You were convicted because the warning lights were flashing brighter and brighter and you didn’t get him help and you didn’t remove his access to the guns,” the judge said as he handed down the sentence.

“It is clear you failed as a parent,” the judge said, describing family turmoil and a lack of oversight for Colt Gray, who was frequently absent from school and missed his eighth-grade year entirely. “You did not provide a stable household,” he added. “He fell deeper and deeper into this obsession when he should have been in school.”

Brad Smith, the district attorney for Barrow County, said the sentence sent a message that he hoped would resonate beyond the Atlanta suburb where the shooting happened.

“People need to understand that this is a phenomenon going through our society, and do not take these things lightly,” Mr. Smith told reporters on Thursday. “These kids are not in a position where they are able to make rational decisions when it comes to things like firearms, and we need, as a society, to step up and realize who should and who should not have access to them.”

The younger Mr. Gray, now 16, pleaded guilty to 55 charges related to the shooting, and he was sentenced by Judge Primm on Tuesday to life in prison without the possibility of parole. The judge, in that sentencing, said that the younger Mr. Gray “understood the horror of what you were going to do,” but he also acknowledged that Colt Gray had been failed by the adults in his life, his father chief among them.

During his trial, the elder Mr. Gray had tried to convince jurors that his son’s intentions seemed clear only now with the benefit of hindsight.

Testifying in his own defense, he portrayed himself as ill-equipped to handle his son’s cascading behavioral problems. Giving him an AR-15-style rifle as a Christmas gift was, in his telling, a misguided attempt to connect with his son and pull him away from the internet and video games.

“No parent is trained to look at his own child and see a mass shooter,” Brian Hobbs, Mr. Gray’s lawyer, said in the sentencing hearing on Thursday.

But prosecutors said the shooting, at Apalachee High School on Sept. 4, 2024, had followed a litany of warnings in a childhood punctuated by upheaval, including repeatedly moving homes and changing schools, his mother’s addiction struggles and conflict between his parents.

In his bedroom, Colt Gray had created a “shrine” to the teenager convicted of killing 17 people in Parkland, Fla., in 2018, with photographs and news clippings. Sheriff’s deputies visited the Gray family home to investigate an online threat of a school shooting traced to their address. And the boy’s behavior worsened, with violent outbursts and anxiety-driven meltdowns, and statements to relatives about voices in his head.

His parents discussed and researched possible treatment options, but never followed through, prosecutors said. Instead, they gave him antidepressants prescribed to his mother.

Breanna Schermerhorn, the mother of Mason Schermerhorn, a 14-year-old killed in the shooting, acknowledged the challenges of parenting, the inevitable situations one feels unprepared for.

But this was not the situation with the elder Mr. Gray.

“He wasn’t left guessing,” Ms. Schermerhorn said in court on Thursday, as she gave a victim impact statement. “He knew his son was in crisis,” she added, pausing as her voice broke. “Instead of acting, he chose to look away. Instead of intervening, he chose inaction. Instead of protecting his son from himself and protecting the community from the danger he posed, he armed him.”

The case arose as gun violence prevention advocates and others have contended that blame for such shootings does not always end with the perpetrator.

Yet the pursuit of broader accountability has often ended in frustration.

Vast federal protections shield gun companies from most litigation. Efforts to prosecute law enforcement officers for flawed responses, like after school shootings in Parkland and Uvalde, Texas, were unsuccessful. The activism of victims’ families and survivors has yielded little in the way of restrictions on gun access.

In recent years, the parents of juvenile perpetrators of these shootings have emerged as another avenue for accountability, by way of criminal charges and through litigation.

James and Jennifer Crumbley, the parents of a 15-year-old boy who fatally shot four people at his Michigan high school, were convicted of involuntary manslaughter and sentenced to at least 10 years in prison.

After a 21-year-old opened fire on a crowd gathered for a Fourth of July parade outside Chicago in 2022, the gunman’s father pleaded guilty to misdemeanor charges and was sentenced to 60 days in jail for helping his son obtain a gun license despite being aware of his son’s mental health issues.

Last year, prosecutors in Wisconsin charged the father of a 15-year-old girl who shot and killed a student and teacher at her private Christian school before killing herself.

After the shooting at Apalachee, investigators quickly zeroed in on the elder Mr. Gray, and he was charged with second-degree murder a day after the attack.

In his trial, prosecutors pointed to the father’s actions as soon as word began to spread of a shooting at Apalachee. During the trial, they showed a portion of a text message exchange between Mr. Gray and his daughter, in which he asked if she had been in touch with her brother. “I think we’re thinking the same thing,” she replied. They also noted that he had asked his boss to leave work, saying his son had broken his arm.

And when the police arrived at the family home after the shooting, before officers could explain why they were there, Mr. Gray told them, “I knew it.”

Rick Rojas is the Atlanta bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of the South.

Trump Threatens to Withdraw Blanche as Attorney General, Dealing Blow to Nomination

The New York Times July 30, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump’s threat followed a day of fruitless negotiations with two Republican holdouts, Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis.

By Glenn ThrushMichael Gold and Carl Hulse

Reporting from Washington

Todd Blanche’s nomination to become attorney general suffered a serious blow on Thursday when President Trump threatened to withdraw Mr. Blanche’s name rather than scale back a tax immunity deal that would benefit himself and his family, as demanded by two Republican senators.

Mr. Trump’s threat, posted on social media, followed 24 hours of frenetic and fruitless negotiations among Mr. Blanche, the White House and the two senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who are not returning to Congress next year.

“I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office,” Mr. Trump wrote, in a fight that has exposed the limits of his power over Congress.

That set off a late-day scramble to rescue Mr. Blanche’s nomination, and the semblance of intraparty, inter-branch comity. Mr. Tillis and Mr. Cornyn met privately with Mr. Blanche Thursday afternoon in the offices of the National Republican Senatorial Committee near the Capitol. It was not immediately clear if they broke the impasse.

Mr. Cornyn and Mr. Tillis object to a deal negotiated by Mr. Blanche and Mr. Trump’s personal lawyers to resolve a lawsuit the president had filed against the I. R. S. The deal gave Mr. Trump, his family and his businesses broad immunity against I. R. S. audits, potentially saving them at least $100 million in penalties. Democrats and even some Republican lawmakers criticized the deal as a giveaway to the Trump family.

The two senators want to narrow the deal in order to advance Mr. Blanche’s nomination, demanding that he put in writing what he acknowledged at his confirmation hearing: that the provision applies to only Mr. Trump, two of his sons and the Trump Organization, and that it would be limited to audits of past tax returns. But the administration so far has refused.

Mr. Blanche cannot afford a single Republican defection on the Senate Judiciary Committee if he hopes to advance his confirmation to the Senate floor. The opposition of Mr. Cornyn and Mr. Tillis leaves him two short, forcing the committee to scrap its scheduled vote on Thursday.

Mr. Blanche, the president’s former top defense lawyer, can remain as acting attorney general indefinitely.

But the fact that some Republicans, emboldened by Mr. Trump’s declining popularity and alarmed by his lack of concern for their own political fortunes, even temporarily derailed a flagship nominee raised questions about Mr. Trump’s capacity to sustain the dominance over congressional Republicans that has allowed him to exert unmediated control over the department.

Mr. Trump’s threat is unusual, in at least two respects. First, there is no guarantee that Republicans will maintain their commanding majority in the upper chamber, or be more willing to accede to his demands after the midterms. Second, pulling Mr. Blanche’s nomination, even temporarily, would demonstrate Mr. Trump’s willingness to advance his personal interests over the institutional stability embodied by a Senate-confirmed attorney general.

The tax deal, tacked onto a Blanche-backed plan to create a $1.8 billion fund to compensate people who said they were victims of unfair prosecution by the government, pushed Senate Republicans to the brink. The fund raised the possibility of the government making gigantic payments to the people who stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6, and forced Mr. Blanche to declare it was dead, even as he declined to put that commitment in writing. But he gave no ground on the tax immunity deal.

At a closed-door meeting in May, several Republican senators browbeat Mr. Blanche for signing off on a wide-ranging agreement they saw as a vast conflict of interest that would be perceived by voters as an effort to line the pockets of Mr. Trump, his family and his political allies.

Mr. Trump nonetheless cast the objections as a personal vendetta against him. He accused Mr. Cornyn and Mr. Tillis of a sour-grapes revolt aimed at punishing him for withholding his kingmaker endorsement in their contested Republican primaries. Mr. Tillis decided not to seek another term after repeated public attacks from the president, while Mr. Cornyn lost his re-election bid to a challenger backed by Mr. Trump.

“John Cornyn, of Texas, and Thom Tillis, of North Carolina, both of whom I refused to Endorse, and whose political careers have been ended by my action, are refusing to vote for this Great Nominee, who will remain, in any event, as Acting,” the president wrote on Truth Social.

Mr. Cornyn quickly pushed back, suggesting that he and Mr. Tillis represented a much larger group of Senate Republicans who had reservations about the implications of the tax deal, but could not incur the political risk to publicly oppose the White House that their status afforded them.

“There are more than just two people who have reservations about the weaponization fund and about the scope of the settlement decree,” Mr. Cornyn said. “And you know, after the midterms, who knows who’s going to be the next United States senator from North Carolina or Texas?”

“This is not popular,” Mr. Tillis said at the Capitol. “The president’s not winning on this issue. It is killing some of our candidates because they can’t explain it. And now, it looks like they weren’t being honest when they said it was inoperative.”

Before Mr. Trump’s social media post, Mr. Cornyn told reporters that he believed “higher-ups at the White House” were blocking efforts to reach a deal to modify the settlement in Mr. Trump’s lawsuit against the I. R. S.

Mr. Cornyn said he had sent a proposal to the Justice Department that included limits on the provision in the settlement protecting Mr. Trump from I. R. S. audits, a guarantee he said he needed before voting to advance Mr. Blanche’s confirmation.

“I thought we were pretty close to landing the plane last night,” Mr. Cornyn said. “But this morning there’s been some more complications.”

Doubling down on his critique of the White House, Mr. Cornyn said pulling Mr. Blanche’s nomination would not resolve the president’s problems over the Senate confirmation. “I think the D. O. J. needs a Senate-confirmed attorney general,” he said. “And Todd Blanche is probably about as good as we’re going to get.”

Senator John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican who serves on the Judiciary Committee, said on Thursday that he was not surprised that the president said he may temporarily pull Mr. Blanche’s nomination.

“Obviously, the White House did not want to comply with what Cornyn and Tillis wanted,” he said.

The tax provision, signed by Mr. Blanche and dated May 19, appeared to be twofold. It ordered the I. R. S. to drop any criminal investigations or audits of Mr. Trump, his family and their businesses, as well as any “affiliated individuals.” It also told the agency to not start any new investigations into tax returns they had already filed.

Mr. Cornyn wants Mr. Blanche, in writing, to limit who receives protection. Only Mr. Trump, two of his sons and the Trump Organization should be subject to the order, Mr. Cornyn has said. That would mean that other members of Mr. Trump’s family beyond Don Jr. and Eric Trump, as well as other companies they work with, would no longer be potentially covered by Mr. Blanche’s order.

Mr. Cornyn also wants Mr. Blanche to clarify that the I. R. S. must abandon only audits of past tax returns — meaning that Mr. Trump could still be audited in the future — and state that the I. R. S. is the only agency bound by the order.

During his confirmation hearing this month, Mr. Blanche, under questioning by Mr. Cornyn, verbally conceded all three points. But, so far, he has been unwilling to reflect that in writing.

Even with Mr. Cornyn’s requested changes, the audit protection for Mr. Trump would still be an unprecedented gift to a sitting president, effectively exempting him from the legal requirement for all Americans to comply with the nation’s tax laws — or face I. R. S. scrutiny.

Mr. Trump and his family members have aggressively avoided taxes for years, repeatedly facing I. R. S. audits as a result. Just one known dispute with the agency, which was still going on before Mr. Blanche’s order, could have cost Mr. Trump more than $100 million if the I. R. S. prevailed.

Andrew Duehren, Maggie Haberman and Olivia Diaz contributed reporting.

An earlier version of this article misstated the circumstances of two Republican senators’ upcoming departure from Congress. Senator Thom Tillis decided not to seek another term, while Senator John Cornyn was defeated in a primary. They did not both lose their seat.

Glenn Thrush covers the Department of Justice for The Times and has also written about gun violence, civil rights and conditions in the country’s jails and prisons.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

As fears spread over a possible artificial intelligence bubble, some tech investors say: Bring it on.

Credit... Linn Fritz

Supported by

By Erin Griffith

Reporting from San Francisco

Michael Burry, the investor made famous in “The Big Short,” has warned about an artificial intelligence bubble. So has Dean Baker, an economist who identified the U. S. housing bubble ahead of the 2008 financial crisis. Even Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JPMorgan Chase, has expressed caution.

But in Silicon Valley, some people are less worried. In fact, they say, a bubble might be a good thing.

In particular, venture capital investors, the optimistic risk-takers who provide money for start-ups, view the frothiness as a necessary part of the innovation machine. The excitement created by a bubble can drive new breakthroughs, their thinking goes.

“Bubbles are a part of technology and innovation,” said Tomasz Tunguz, an investor at the venture capital firm Theory Ventures. These frenzies are important for allowing crucial infrastructure to get built, even if they lead to some “capital destruction” along the way, he added.

It is a common refrain in the nation’s tech capital. How else can risky, cutting-edge companies attract the money, talent and excitement they need to build the future?

“If you were to rely on a purely organic, rational way of financing big technology platform shifts, they would probably never happen,” said Samir Kumar, an investor at Touring Capital, a venture capital firm. Once you get past the excessive exuberance, he added, “there are long-term benefits.”

This counterintuitive thinking stands in contrast to rising concerns over a potential A. I. mania, with dealmaking that never seems to stop. This week alone, OpenAI and Nvidia were close to landing an elaborate $500 billion data center deal in Ohio. Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft said they had spent a combined $170 billion on capital expenditures in the second quarter, up 72 percent over last year.

Venture funding in the first half of the year also hit $413 billion, more than all of 2025, according to PitchBook, which tracks private investment. Young companies that have not released a product or earned a dollar of revenue are landing valuations that sound absurd, in one case reaching $32 billion. And there is so much money sloshing around Silicon Valley that nearby San Francisco has a mansion shortage.

The bubble-is-good philosophy reveals how much the tech industry is still pressing the pedal to the metal, four years into the A. I. boom. Many investors said the funding behavior was justified because companies were using the technology to hit unfathomable levels of growth.

OpenAI, valued at $730 billion, is generating $2 billion in revenue a month. Anthropic, valued at $900 billion, is producing nearly $4 billion a month. Google and Meta have boasted of nearly a billion people using their A. I. models. The demand for A. I., investors said, is seemingly unlimited.

“V. C. s only really make money when there are big technology shifts to invest behind,” said Pratyush Buddiga, an investor at Susa Ventures.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

William Quinn, an associate professor at Queen’s University Belfast and a co-author of “Boom and Bust: A Global History of Financial Bubbles,” said past bubbles, and the easy money that came with them, had obvious positive elements: They drove innovation and long-term economic growth.

“In Silicon Valley, there are things that everyone seems to believe that seem crazy to the rest of the world, and on a lot of those things, it seems like Silicon Valley was right and the rest of the world was wrong,” he said.

Bubbles also tend to go on for a lot longer than people think they will, Mr. Quinn said. Pessimists who see irrational behavior and sit on the sidelines can miss years of gains before any correction or crash. By the time the comedown happens, no one is listening to their bubble warnings anymore.

“There’s always the joke that they’ve predicted 10 of the last three crashes,” he said.

Tech industry veterans still carry scars of the 2000 dot-com crash and its painful aftermath. For several years after, it was nearly impossible for start-ups to raise money.

The handful of companies that powered through to the other side — Amazon, PayPal, eBay — went on to become behemoths. And over time, the fiber-optic network that exuberant investors overbuilt in that boom helped more people get online, fueling the growth of new tech companies like Facebook.

Investors who witnessed the dot-com crash remained wary of history’s repeating itself. In the early 2010s, they warned of a bubble among mobile apps with no revenue. Then came fears over “unicorn” start-ups that were valued at $1 billion or more, followed by nonsensical crypto projects and, eventually, the overlapping investment manias of 2021.

But none of those moments led to a major crash.

Charles Hudson, an investor at Precursor Ventures, said the 2021 frenzy taught him that investors got little credit from sitting things out in bubbly times. Some investors made lots of bad, silly bets in 2021, but their backers did not punish them for the excesses. The lesson, he said, was to keep investing, even when things felt overheated.

The A. I. boom has been trickier to navigate, with obscene dollar amounts and the market moving at hyperspeed. Even so, Mr. Hudson said he knew he could not sit it out. He has focused on backing even younger companies and homed in on the “application layer,” or software start-ups that use A. I.

“It would be incredibly dangerous, and maybe irresponsible, to just say, ‘I’m not investing in A. I. at all because I think pockets of the business are a bubble,’” he said.

Sudheendra Chilappagari, an investor at Battery Ventures, was in school when the dot-com bubble happened. (At 33, he is older than some of the top A. I. start-up founders, who were not yet born.) He joked that he felt jealous of his older colleagues because they started investing before there was so much noise and chaos.

He said he was taking a lesson from their experience in the 1990s search engine wars. At the time, Battery Ventures invested in Infoseek, one of the earliest search engines — only to get crushed by Yahoo and others that then got crushed by Google.

“It’s not always the first mover that captures the enterprise value,” Mr. Chilappagari said. In a so-called supercycle like the A. I. boom, he expects continuous waves of possible investments.

The investors acknowledge that many factors could set off a crash: geopolitical clashes, competitive threats from cheaper open-source A. I. models, societal backlashes against data centers or more safety problems like OpenAI’s rogue hacking of a partner company. Even disappointment over how long it takes investments to pay off could deflate the market.

“You don’t want to get delusional,” Mr. Kumar of Touring Capital said.

Darian Shirazi, an investor at the venture capital firm Gradient Ventures, said his profession had become more nerve-racking because the typical strategy of hitting one home-run deal to drive profits was so much more extreme. Venture capital firms might previously have hoped for a few of their investments to sell for $1 billion or $2 billion. In the A. I. boom, that potential outcome has increased to $50 billion.

“Your winner can be wildly outsized,” he said. “If it works, it works much better than anything we’ve ever seen in the history of venture capital.”

Erin Griffith covers tech companies, start-ups and the culture of Silicon Valley from San Francisco.
