The once-high-flying firm Situational Awareness, whose founder is 24, has been bailed out by Kenneth Griffin’s Citadel, according to three people briefed on the transaction.

By Rob Copeland

One of the hottest hedge funds in artificial intelligence received a bailout to stay afloat on Thursday amid a sudden drop in value for its investments.

The fast-moving crisis unfolded over just 36 hours at Situational Awareness, a once-envied investment firm in San Francisco led by 20-somethings, including a former employee of OpenAI. The firm put out an emergency call for help to rivals, seeking to sell more than $10 billion of its stock to shore up its plummeting portfolio, according to three people briefed on the call.

After a brief bidding war overnight, the hedge fund Citadel — founded by the billionaire Kenneth Griffin — agreed to step in with the needed cash, so long as it received a substantial discount on the investments, the three people said.

The move forestalled the immediate danger for Situational Awareness, but it has put many on Wall Street on edge. Several recent crises have begun with struggling hedge funds forced to unwind — most recently in 2021, when the collapse of the hedge fund Archegos ended up taking down the bank Credit Suisse along with it.

Situational Awareness was named after a 2024 essay by its founder, Leopold Aschenbrenner, a onetime employee of the philanthropic arm of FTX, the fallen crypto brokerage. His essay predicted that research labs would develop a superintelligent form of A. I. by 2027.

That thesis became a foundation of the firm’s investment strategy, and it began pouring money into A. I. companies. This worked wonderfully, for a while: Some of its investors, which include Patrick and John Collison, the founders of Stripe, had made a 200 percent return this year alone, according to two people briefed on the figures but not permitted to discuss them publicly.

The fund grew to tens of billions of dollars under management, and became a poster child for the boom. It hired a public relations firm, attracting attention from media old and new. One famous podcaster, Tim Ferriss, called Mr. Aschenbrenner the “Nostradamus of A. I.”

His fortune changed quickly. In recent weeks, markets have begun to question whether the A. I. renaissance will turn out to be as profitable or impactful as promised. Stocks for chipmakers and other firms closely tied to the industry cratered.

That hit Situational Awareness on two fronts at the same time, according to two of the people briefed. Its holdings in companies such as SK Hynix, a South Korean semiconductor maker, rapidly lost value, while so-called shorts, or bets, against older software companies suddenly turned in the other direction.

Plenty of A. I. companies and investors large and small are in a crunch. But Situational Awareness was in a particularly dangerous position. It had borrowed billions of dollars from Wall Street banks to amplify its bets, and those banks had in recent days begun asking for some of that money back, according to the three people briefed on the requests.

Faced with the potential of a forced fire sale, Mr. Aschenbrenner canvassed his onetime rivals for a bailout. His offer: to sell more than $10 billion of its stocks to shore up the firm.

Wall Street banks and other investment firms worked overnight to scour the firm’s portfolio to come up with bids. An auction was held overnight Wednesday and the winner was Mr. Griffin’s hedge fund, Citadel. The deal was closed early Thursday, one of the people briefed said.

It’s a familiar strategy for Citadel, one of the largest hedge funds in the world. In decades past, it has swooped in to buy cut-rate positions from firms in desperate situations, including Enron. It beat out other bidders including Millennium Management, another huge hedge fund, which did not want to pay as high a price for what it viewed as risky investments, one of the people briefed said.

The spotlight on Situational Awareness is sure to continue. It still holds a big chunk of harder-to-sell positions in privately held companies such as Anthropic. It remains to be seen if those companies will live up to their lofty valuations if and when they hit the public markets.

Mr. Aschenbrenner and a spokesman for Situational Awareness did not respond to requests for comment.

Eli Tan contributed reporting.

Rob Copeland is a finance reporter for The Times, writing about Wall Street and the banking industry.

With a democratic socialist, Francesca Hong, leading in polls, former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes said he was ending his campaign in the closely divided state.

By Mitch Smith

Mandela Barnes, the former lieutenant governor of Wisconsin, abandoned his campaign for the Democratic nomination for governor on Thursday.

His exit came as State Representative Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, has built a broad base of support and polled well ahead of Mr. Barnes and other more moderate candidates. In a message posted online announcing his exit, Mr. Barnes said “it has become very clear who our nominee is going to be.”

Ms. Hong’s campaign has energized voters across the state in recent weeks, drawing a younger crowd to campaign events and pressing a platform that includes allowing local governments to raise income taxes on high earners and putting a freeze on the construction of new data centers.

Some Democrats, however, have expressed concern that Ms. Hong’s policies might be unpalatable to moderate voters in the general election. Wisconsin is about evenly divided by Republicans and Democrats. Gov. Tony Evers, the Democratic incumbent, decided not to seek a third term.

Representative Tom Tiffany is expected to be the Republican nominee.

The primary election is set for Aug. 11. Ms. Hong still faces several opponents in the primary, including David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, who is running with Mr. Evers’s endorsement.

Mr. Barnes served for four years as lieutenant governor under Mr. Evers. But rather than seek a second term as lieutenant governor in 2022, Mr. Barnes ran for the U. S. Senate and lost to Senator Ron Johnson, a Republican, even as Mr. Evers won a second term. That loss raised doubts among many Democrats about Mr. Barnes’s electability.

Though Mr. Barnes entered the race for governor with strong name recognition, he struggled to build momentum in a large and fractious primary field. As Ms. Hong consolidated support from the party’s left wing this summer, establishment-oriented Democrats looked for a relatively moderate candidate but struggled to coalesce.

Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez seemed to be emerging as the establishment’s preferred candidate this month, but her bid unraveled when problems with her campaign finance reports emerged. After she withdrew from the race, Mr. Crowley, who had previously suspended his campaign amid woeful poll numbers, announced that he was getting back in. Mr. Evers bypassed Mr. Barnes, his former governing partner, and endorsed Mr. Crowley.

But Ms. Hong has remained in command of the race. A Marquette Law School poll released this week showed Ms. Hong with 46 percent of the vote, 25 points ahead of Mr. Barnes, her nearest rival. Mr. Crowley, who polled in a distant third place, moved quickly on Thursday to try to pick up some of Mr. Barnes’s supporters.

“To everyone who backed Mandela: there’s a place for you in what we’re building,” Mr. Crowley wrote on social media.

Ms. Hong made a similar pitch.

“To everyone who supported Mandela because you believe working people deserve a government that fights for them, I welcome you to our movement,” she said in a statement.

Reporting was contributed by Kellen Browning, Reid J. Epstein and Ruth Igielnik.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Big Tech’s A. I. Spending Keeps Rising. So Do the Jitters.

The New York Times July 30, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Amazon joined a procession of tech giants that ramped up their spending on artificial intelligence, as its capital expenditures soared 69 percent. Concerns over the industry’s spending are mounting.

By Karen Weise

Karen Weise, who covers Amazon and Microsoft, has visited data centers around the country to report on the building boom.

Tech giants are setting records every few months for how much they are spending on artificial intelligence — but this time, some jitters are also growing.

On Thursday, Amazon said its capital expenditures totaled $53 billion in the second quarter, up 69 percent from a year earlier, as it built A. I. data centers and other infrastructure. It joined a parade of other big tech companies, with Meta on Wednesday reporting that its costs had risen 55 percent from last year, while Microsoft said its capital expenditures had soared 69 percent. Last week, Google also disclosed that its costs had jumped and said it would boost its spending further.

These numbers are only set to skyrocket. Across this year and next, Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft are expected to spend a staggering $1.5 trillion building data centers and stuffing them with advanced chips, according to Wall Street estimates compiled by FactSet.

“The scale of it is nuts,” said Melissa Otto, who leads research at S&P Global’s Visible Alpha division.

Alarms are rising as Wall Street and others question whether this spending can be justified. On Thursday, shares of Microsoft, which did not change its spending forecast, jumped more than 15 percent, but Meta’s stock sank more than 7 percent after it revealed its A. I. outlays and that costs were growing faster than its revenue.

And last week, for the first time since going public in 2004, Google said it had “negative free cash flow,” which meant it was spending more on day-to-day operations and building new infrastructure than it was taking in from its businesses. Google’s stock fell more than 6 percent the next day.

Even so, the companies insist they are doing the right thing. “As long as we see these attractive opportunities to invest, we will continue to invest,” Anat Ashkenazi, Alphabet’s finance chief, told Wall Street analysts last week.

More than a dozen years ago, tech companies became the largest enterprises on the planet, fueled by their software and digital businesses. But A. I. has flipped tech’s “asset-light” model on its head. Multibillion-dollar data centers, which the industry likes to call “A. I. factories,” have become critical investments for developing advanced systems and making them available to customers.

From April through June, capital expenditures by the four companies totaled $170 billion, up 72 percent from a year earlier. The figures are ballooning — and projections keep rising every three months — as the companies race to open more data centers, and as the prices for necessary components like memory chips jump because of the demand. In April, Microsoft said soaring component prices would add $25 billion to its tab this year.

Despite all the building and spending, the tech giants say they still do not have enough computing power to meet demand. In effect, they say, they have been leaving money on the table.

“More capacity = more sales,” a Bank of America analyst, Justin Post, wrote last week in a research note after Alphabet, Google’s parent company, increased its spending forecast for this year by $15 billion to as much as $205 billion.

The pent-up demand has contributed to a backlog in signed contracts for Amazon, Google and Microsoft.

Much of the growing backlog comes from partnerships with OpenAI and Anthropic, the leading A. I. start-ups. That means the fate of the giants rests in large part on the start-ups’ needing all the computing power they have requested, and their ability to pay for it. That poses a concentration risk, creating “a more circular system that could mask true demand,” according to Moody’s Ratings.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The companies have denied the claims.)

The tech companies have borrowed more than ever to fund the A. I. building boom. Yet they are also able to rely on their lucrative established businesses, like digital advertising, which rain down cash.

“This party could go on for a while,” Ms. Otto said.

Amazon said on Thursday that it had $200.6 billion in sales in the second quarter, up 20 percent from a year earlier. Profit more than tripled to $62.6 billion, in large part because of the company’s investment in Anthropic.

Amazon’s core retail business in North America grew 16 percent, and its cloud computing business grew 37 percent to $42.2 billion in sales. The amount of cash from operating its business over the past year was $161.4 billion, up 33 percent. But after investments in data centers and other facilities, Amazon’s free cash flow plunged to negative $7.6 billion.

Investors pummeled Meta on Thursday after the company forecast disappointing sales a day earlier, while it raised the lower end of its capital expenditure forecast for the year to $130 billion, from the $125 billion it projected in April.

“I mean, look, the high-level observation is that there’s just nowhere near enough compute for all the demand,” Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, told investors as he made a case for why the investments will pan out.

Susan Li, Meta’s finance chief, said the company was focused on securing as much capacity as possible for 2026 and 2027, but keeping flexibility in mind for 2028 and beyond. That means locking up land and power for data centers now, even if the company has not figured out precisely how it will use the computing down the line.

Microsoft’s share price, which has been down this year, got some reprieve on Thursday as the company’s financial results a day earlier surpassed Wall Street expectations and it did not increase how much it planned to spend this year.

Sales of Azure, the cloud computing platform at the heart of Microsoft’s A. I. services, exceeded $100 billion for the first time for the fiscal year that ended in June, and quarterly sales grew at the fastest pace since 2022, when Azure was a much smaller business. Microsoft expects to spend more than $50 billion in the current quarter.

Satya Nadella, Microsoft’s chief executive, said the company had opened 31 data centers across five continents last quarter. The company, he said, is “on track to roughly double our overall capacity in just two years.”

Karen Weise writes about technology for The Times and is based in Seattle. Her coverage focuses on Amazon and Microsoft, two of the most powerful companies in America.

U. S. Revives Obscure Court in Bid to Deport Afghan Woman

The New York Times July 30, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

The case is a test of the Alien Terrorist Removal Court, where much of the evidence is presented in secret and defendants cannot challenge how it was collected.

By Alan Feuer and Adam Sella

An obscure court set up 30 years ago to expel immigrants accused of terrorism from the country heard its first case on Thursday, as the Justice Department asked a federal judge to deport an Afghan woman who prosecutors say supports the Islamic State.

The request took place at a nearly hourlong hearing in Washington before what is known as the Alien Terrorist Removal Court. During the hearing, prosecutors presented their initial claims that the woman, Nazira Haji Zada, should be removed from the United States even though she is a lawful permanent resident. The court was created by Congress in 1996 to handle deportation proceedings that largely rest on classified information.

The government contends that Ms. Zada, 47, is connected to a foiled terrorist plot inspired by ISIS to commit a mass shooting on Election Day in 2024. Last year, both her son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and her son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhedi, pleaded guilty to charges connected to the plot and admitted they had tried to buy two AK-47-style rifles and 500 rounds of ammunition to carry it out.

“The allegations in this case show the matriarch of an ISIS-sympathizing family aiding in a plot to launch a mass casualty attack on American voters on Election Day,” the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche, said in a statement before the hearing began. Ms. Zada, who appeared before a packed courtroom in a creamy white head scarf and flowing blue pants, was arrested on Tuesday at her home in Fort Worth, Texas, the court’s chief judge, Joan N. Ericksen, said.

The case against Ms. Zada is a test of a court where much of the evidence is presented in secret and defendants cannot challenge how it was collected. The Trump administration has used an expansive array of legal methods to carry out the president’s aggressive deportation agenda — many of them challenged in court. Now, it is seeking to use the sweeping powers of the terrorist removal court.

Ms. Zada has not been publicly charged with any crimes of terrorism and has no criminal history, according to court papers. Still, in an unclassified summary of her case submitted to the court, prosecutors said she “supported” the Election Day conspiracy and “pledged loyalty to ISIS.”

The summary also said she “worked to indoctrinate her children with ISIS ideology” and concealed a plan to relocate her family to ISIS-controlled territory from “her unsuspecting husband,” Abdul Haji Zada, who worked at the Bagram Air Base in Afghanistan from 2009 to 2016, court papers say.

The Alien Terrorist Removal Court is set up in a fashion similar to the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, which reviews sensitive requests for surveillance warrants. It has five judges drawn from courts around the country, including Judge Ericksen, who also sits in Federal District Court in Minnesota.

“This is the court’s first case and the court is in the early stage of implementing procedures,” she said as the hearing opened, acknowledging that there “may be moments of ineloquence” because the court “laid dormant and untested for three decades.”

Matthew Farley, one of Ms. Zada’s lawyers, began his remarks to Judge Ericksen by asking that his client be released. He called the administration’s efforts to deport her a “run around to bringing a criminal case” — one that afforded the government a lower burden when it came proving a nexus to terrorism.

Mr. Farley also raised concerns that prosecutors did not plan to grant the defense access to the classified material in the case. But while Judge Ericksen rejected his request for Ms. Zada’s release, she said her “working presumption” would be that the defense team will be able to review the classified information underlying the case.

The government filed its opening request to the court seeking to deport Ms. Zada on July 15, supported by multiple classified exhibits. The court held a closed-door hearing that next day, raising “a number of questions, both legal and administrative,” Judge Ericksen wrote in an order unsealed on Wednesday.

The government submitted a supplementary briefing last week to bolster its case that Ms. Zada was what it described as “an alien terrorist” whose removal from the country through normal immigration procedures would “pose a risk to the United States’ national security,” Judge Ericksen wrote.

The judge ultimately found there was probable cause to proceed with the case and will soon set out a schedule for further filings and hearings.

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

Adam Sella covers breaking news for The Times in Washington.

Apple will have a new chief executive in September, after 15 years with Tim Cook at the helm. He is passing the baton while the company is at a financial high, after another quarter of strong sales.

Apple on Thursday reported that revenue rose 16 percent from a year earlier to $109.42 billion, the most for a quarter ending in June. Profit grew 27 percent to $29.8 billion.

The new designs Apple unveiled for the iPhone include a thin model called the iPhone Air and a model of the iPhone Pro with a raised bump across the back for cameras. The company also increased the prices of some phones by $100. The changes have continued to lift iPhone sales, which grew 22 percent to $54.25 billion.

Apple also continued to recover from years of sluggish sales in China, the largest smartphone market in the world. Its iPhones made up 18 percent of smartphone shipments to distributors in China in the quarter — more than many local rivals — after lagging a year earlier, according to Counterpoint Research, which tracks the smartphone market. Apple’s sales in China rose 22 percent to $18.82 billion.

The results topped expectations. Wall Street analysts had predicted quarterly revenue of $108.85 billion and profit of $27.73 billion, according to FactSet.

Apple’s services revenue grew 12 percent to $30.74 billion, a record for the division. This month, the company quietly raised the prices for some of its services such as its music streaming service Apple Music, which now costs $11.99 per month, up from $10.99.

Apple saw modest growth in other parts of its core business. The company introduced in March a line of colorful entry-level laptops, called the MacBook Neo, driving sales of Macs, which rose 29 percent to $10.35 billion. Sales of wearables, which include products like the Apple Watch and AirPods, grew 6 percent to $7.88 billion. Sales of iPads fell 6 percent to $6.19 billion.

How Diamonds, Paprika and Fertilizer Won Relief From Trump’s Tariffs

The New York Times July 30, 2026

U. S. Tariffs and Trade

Advertisement

Supported by

A new round of tariff carve-outs has raised familiar questions about who should receive the lucrative exceptions, and why.

By Ana Swanson and Jeanna Smialek

Ana Swanson reported from Washington, and Jeanna Smialek from Brussels.

On Friday, as President Trump announced new global tariffs, the European diamond industry breathed a sigh of relief.

Natural diamonds had once again been exempted from tariffs.

The newly issued exemption followed negotiations with European officials last year, and months of sustained advocacy by a diamond group in Antwerp, which dominates the global industry. It also followed the presentation of a remarkable gift designed personally for Mr. Trump.

A few weeks earlier, the group, the Antwerp World Diamond Center, which handles most of the world’s rough diamonds and about half of its polished stones, had unveiled an 18-karat gold ring the size of a watch. The ring was encrusted with 321 diamonds and dozens of sapphires, emeralds and rubies, and it was a gift to Mr. Trump to mark America’s 250th anniversary.

The ring features two large diamond “Ts” on either side, and “45” and “47” — references to Mr. Trump’s presidential terms — ringed in diamonds in a Superman-style logo. On its interior is engraved, “Crafted in Antwerp for Donald John Trump.”

“A very special thank you to my friends from Antwerp for the magnificent Freedom 250 ring,” Mr. Trump said in a prerecorded video message played at an America 250 party in Brussels’s Cinquantenaire Park. The festivities featured Budweiser, bourbon and Alexis Wilkins, a country singer and the girlfriend of the F. B. I. director, Kash Patel, performing the national anthem.

The industry had won a reprieve from tariffs last year, after Mr. Trump reached a trade deal with the European Union. But when the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February and Mr. Trump replaced them with new ones, diamond imports were penalized again.

The batch of tariffs announced on Friday target more than 80 countries that the Trump administration claims have not imposed or enforced laws banning imports made with forced labor. But the tariffs, which range from 10 percent to 12.5 percent, contain more exemptions than before.

The tariffs will not apply to a wide range of items from oil and gas to copper, chip-making machinery, chemicals and diamonds. Those exemptions will save billions of dollars in tariff costs for U. S. consumers and certain industries, including makers of steel and aluminum, farmers and tech companies.

There is no evidence that the gift of the ring directly affected the president’s thinking on the tariff exclusion for the diamond industry. But the new list of exemptions has renewed questions about which industries should be exempt from tariffs, and why.

Kush Desai, a White House spokesman, said that the Trump administration had agreed to provide preferential tariff treatment for diamonds as part of the trade deal with the European Union that was agreed to last summer.

The exemption of diamonds in the current tariffs “reflects how the administration continues upholding our end of the deal,” he said, adding, “The only special interest guiding the Trump administration’s decision-making is the best interest of the American people.”

An official at the Office of the United States Trade Representative, which negotiates tariffs, said the agency had no awareness of the gift, and it was not an element in determining the exemption.

During Mr. Trump’s first term, the administration set up a process for companies to apply for exclusions, but it was criticized by some as rigged or disorderly.

Early in his second term, Mr. Trump and his supporters often said there would be no immediate exceptions or exclusions to tariffs, arguing that past exemptions created a “Swiss cheese” approach that did little to reduce the flow of imports into the United States.

More than a year later, Trump officials have modified their approach, saying they are working to fine-tune the tariffs and exempt certain categories of goods where they will not have a positive effect. Those include raw materials that could disrupt supply chains, “products that could cause economywide disruptions” if subject to tariffs and goods that cannot be grown or produced in the United States.

U. S. officials said they also issued certain exemptions that other governments, like the E. U, Bangladesh, Switzerland and Taiwan, negotiated for in their trade agreements.

A senior administration official told reporters last week that Mr. Trump had made determinations about which exemptions would make the most sense for American supply chains.

Some of the new exemptions echo earlier carve-outs to the 2025 tariffs that were ultimately struck down by the Supreme Court, including exceptions for products covered by trade deals with Mexico, Canada and Central America. In November, the Trump administration lifted tariffs on beef, coffee, bananas, tomatoes and other products as it tried to prevent the prices of some goods from becoming even more expensive at a moment when Americans were struggling with inflation.

Other exemptions are clearly meant to ensure that strategic industries, like chip manufacturing and data centers, can continue to thrive in the United States.

Tech executives have made their case to Trump officials for months that tariffs on the foreign machinery and components they need will slow their ability to build new factories and A. I. data centers. Farmers, who have also lobbied the administration for help reducing costs, saw equipment and fertilizer exempted.

Dan Anthony, the president of Trade Partnership Worldwide, which researches the impact of trade, said that the administration had exempted about half of all U. S. imports from the forced labor tariffs based on his initial calculations. That is similar to the level of exemptions offered under the previous 10 percent global tariff that expired last week.

The biggest new exemptions were related to metal waste and scrap, which are used to manufacture steel and aluminum; certain chemicals, including those needed by farmers; and machinery for high-tech manufacturing, he said.

Among trade experts, one criticism of tariffs is that they have exempted many industries that have persistent issues with forced labor, like textiles, coffee, gold, Brazil nuts, cocoa and minerals. Those products are all highlighted in an annual report about forced and child labor compiled by the U. S. Labor Department.

The department has specifically called out palm oil from Indonesia and Malaysia, both of which received exemptions specifically for those products.

“The exemptions list practically reads like a list of products we know to be made with forced and child labor, including many raw materials and finished products made in Xinjiang and in the Democratic Republic of Congo,” said Laura Murphy, a professor of human rights at Sheffield Hallam University in Britain who worked on forced labor enforcement in the Biden administration.

Ms. Murphy pointed to paprika, which is exempted from the tariffs. Paprika is a popular alternative to red food dye among Mr. Trump’s followers in the Make America Healthy Again movement.

But recent testing found that much of the paprika marked as made in the United States is actually made in China, with much of it coming from the Xinjiang region. The United States bans imports from Xinjiang because of concerns about forced labor. The world’s largest manufacturer of paprika, a Chinese company called Chenguang Biotech, was added to a U. S. government list of companies using forced labor in 2023.

U. S. trade officials have responded that their authority is over trade, not labor laws. They say that the recent tariff action represents the most sweeping international labor rights action the United States has ever taken.

They argue that the Trump administration strictly enforces other forced labor laws, and that the new tariffs are directed at getting countries to adopt their own import bans on forced labor goods, not at policing forced labor itself. The tariffs are focused on the trading partners responsible for the largest volume of trade, not small countries that may have worse issues with forced labor.

But to some analysts, that distinction is confusing or even irrelevant.

“You can’t address forced labor concerns when giving a Get Out of Tariffs Free card to the most problematic areas and products,” said Mr. Anthony of Trade Partnership Worldwide.

Mr. Anthony pointed out that the Labor Department had repeatedly flagged forced labor concerns with gold, tin, cobalt, tantalum and tungsten from the Democratic Republic of Congo. But neither Congo nor those minerals are subject to tariffs.

Some domestic manufacturers have also criticized a new mechanism the administration introduced for textiles, which will allow Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia and Malaysia to export some clothing to the United States tariff free, so long as they use U. S. cotton to make it. The program is intended to boost U. S. exports and reduce those countries’ purchases of cotton from China, which the United States has restricted because of forced labor.

But Kim Glas, the president of the National Council of Textile Organizations, a group of U. S.-based textile manufacturers, argued that the measures will further encourage outsourcing of garment production to Asia. Some of the administration’s trade moves would be helpful in combating forced labor in global supply chains, she said, but eliminating textile duties is “a step backward.”

Diamonds, too, frequently appear on government lists of goods made with forced and child labor. Belgium’s diamond sector has among the strictest standards for supply chain monitoring, but human rights organizations claim that some problematic products still slip through.

Diamonds are not commercially mined in the United States or Europe, though Europe plays a major global role in trading, cutting and distributing rough and polished natural diamonds. The tariff exemption will apply to natural diamonds of European origin — meaning they are cut in Europe but could be sourced from anywhere around the globe. Antwerp exports more than $2 billion in polished diamonds to the United States annually.

The U. S. Embassy in Belgium welcomed the tariff exemption, saying in a joint news release with the Antwerp World Diamond Center that it was “the result of constructive dialogue and close cooperation between the United States and Belgium.”

The Antwerp diamond group said on social media that the exemption followed “months of sustained advocacy” aimed at “exactly this outcome.”

As for the diamond-encrusted ring designed for Mr. Trump, it remains in the U. S. ambassador’s residence in Belgium, said Bill White, the ambassador.

An administration official said that the White House had not yet received the item, and that when it did, it would be sent to the National Archives, with an option for Mr. Trump to buy it later.

Ana Swanson covers trade and international economics for The Times and is based in Washington. She has been a journalist for more than a decade.

Jeanna Smialek is the Brussels bureau chief for The Times.

Trump officials have promised to “make visual arts great,” with a museum exhibition that includes artwork by several people with personal connections to the planners.

The fashion designer Kate Wasserbach Moore produced a silk dress, “America250 Gown,” for the exhibition “Passport to Patriotism” at the Art Museum of the Americas. Erin Scavino, one of the organizers, met the designer while shopping for her own wedding dress. Credit... Caroline Gutman for The New York Times

Supported by

By Zachary Small

Reporting from Washington

After intensifying its critique of how the Smithsonian presents American history, the Trump administration has decided to stage a museum exhibition of its own.

In the last month, the White House has accused the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History of presenting an ideologically biased and negative view of U. S. history. President Trump even signed an executive order requiring that signs be placed outside the museum, to encourage visitors to go elsewhere for “accurate information regarding America’s history.”

Offering an alternative view of national identity, the State Department has organized “Passport to Patriotism: 250 Years of Diplomacy,” which opened on Thursday at the Art Museum of the Americas, steps from the White House. The show includes 68 versions of the American flag, including one made with 44,500 toy soldiers, as well as realistic images of the founding fathers generated by artificial intelligence and a wedding dress inspired by Betsy Ross. The artist Pablo Barba also contributed classical-style paintings of three women symbolizing the virtues of valor, purity and justice.

According to four people involved in the show, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of repercussions from the administration, no historians or professional curators collaborated on the exhibition, which also features artworks by friends of the planners and by two artists who serve on the board of a nonprofit, the American Arts Conservancy, that helped organize the show. Several museum experts said they worried that officials had ignored ethics rules meant to safeguard institutions from political influence and conflicts of interest.

“The government is calling the shots,” said Sally Yerkovich, a Columbia University professor who recently led revisions to the ethics code of the International Council of Museums. “The public trusts museums because they are independent sources of information.”

Tommy Pigott, a spokesman for the State Department, said that its “career and civil service officers, who have served under several presidents apolitically, work on this team and are art professionals with curatorial expertise. We don’t need professional revisionists to dictate our nation’s history to us; we all know what our flag stands for, who our founding fathers are, and the exhibition will speak for itself.”

One of its organizers, Erin Scavino, who leads the State Department’s Art in Embassies program, has described the exhibition as a signature part of the president’s celebration of the country’s 250th anniversary, adding that she has a mandate to “make visual arts great.”

“This exhibition isn’t one that’s going to make you think about horribly dark things or things that have been a blemish on the face of America,” Ms. Scavino told Axios.

She collaborated on the exhibition with Jenni Parido, a friend she previously tapped to serve as the commissioner of the U. S. Pavilion at this year’s Venice Biennale, which opened in May. That was the last time the Trump administration tried its hand at cultural diplomacy. Much of the art world gave the sculptures by Alma Allen the cold shoulder, saying the pavilion’s exhibition was “insubstantial” and “pretentious.”

The State Department also took heat for bypassing its own selection rules to choose the friend of a White House insider to organize the pavilion, despite Ms. Parido’s having more experience in pet food than art curation. (The State Department insisted that it had mounted a rigorous selection process.) When the officials toasted the exhibition at a private reception, Mr. Allen wasn’t there — he and the pavilion’s curator, Jeffrey Uslip, were no longer on speaking terms.

Whether those same officials can gain a hometown advantage in Washington remains to be seen. “Passport to Patriotism” runs through Oct. 18, in a museum managed by a nonprofit that receives substantial funding through the State Department. The Art Museum of the Americas gained notice last year after its leaders canceled programming featuring Black and queer artists. Curators said those exhibitions would have contradicted Mr. Trump’s executive order that banned diversity and inclusion programs from federally funded groups.

Many artists included in the new exhibition have personal connections to Ms. Scavino, who in 2005 was a contestant on “The Apprentice,” the NBC reality show that Mr. Trump hosted. She has remained in the president’s orbit, marrying Dan Scavino, a White House deputy chief of staff, this year.

Ms. Scavino has included in the exhibition a silk wedding gown by a fashion designer, Kate Wasserbach Moore, whom she discovered while searching for her own wedding dress. She asked Ms. Moore to “create a dress that looks like something one of the wives of our founding fathers would have worn,” as she put it to Fox News. The designer told The New York Times that she planned on donating it to the Art in Embassies permanent collection.

Another artist in the exhibition, Romero Britto, is a Brazilian entrepreneur who attended Ms. Scavino’s wedding and gave the couple a custom portrait. Mr. Britto said he also designed banners for the Department of Health and Human Services.

“Some people create art that is a little dark. That is not my mission,” he said in an interview, adding that he offered paintings to previous administrations. “I want to create positive art and a hopeful message.”

The artist Fer Da Silva, another friend of the organizers, projects a similar message of love with his heart-shaped paintings. On social media, he highlighted one of his works that was going to the exhibition and said his participation would increase its value.

In a statement, Ms. Parido, who founded the American Arts Conservancy, said that “from the outset, the curatorial framework emphasized work that is family-friendly, accessible to visitors of all ages, unifying in spirit and nonpartisan. Artists and artworks were selected based on their connection to those themes, their suitability for a broad public audience and their contribution to a cohesive visitor experience.”

Ms. Yerkovich, the ethics expert, said museums made great efforts to demonstrate their authority and independence. “The processing of curating a show is supposed to be done with certain artistic standards,” she explained. “It begins to look suspicious if a lot of the artwork happens to be from friends of the curator. You begin to wonder what kinds of judgments were made.”

Museums often face criticism when favoritism appears to be in play. The artist Rashid Johnson, a board member of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation, and the producer Swizz Beatz, a trustee at the Brooklyn Museum, both stepped down from their positions before their museums produced shows that featured their artworks, to avoid the appearance of a conflict of interest.

The two artists in “Passport to Patriotism” who also serve on the board of the American Arts Conservancy, an organizer of the show, are Brendan Murphy and Brandon Ralph. (The American Arts Conservancy also planned the Venice Biennale exhibition.)

Mr. Murphy, a former professional basketball player, is displaying a shiny astronaut sculpture called “Serve the Flag.” (The artwork was not yet installed during a reporter’s visit on Thursday.) Mr. Ralph, a photographer and an advertising executive, has created realistic images of the founding fathers using artificial intelligence.

“I thought it would be an interesting opportunity to be part of these groups and have conversations to bring people together to talk about different views on America,” Mr. Ralph said in an interview.

In April, the Art Museum of the Americas said that a former director of the International Center of Photography, Mark Lubell, would curate the exhibition. One of the people involved in the show, who is familiar with the conversation, said Mr. Lubell decided not to work on the exhibition after he was told that participating artists would be screened for their political views. (Mr. Lubell declined to comment.)

The State Department and the exhibition’s organizers did not respond to questions about whether artists’ political views had been considered. But one artwork in the exhibition was a glittering red jacket by the fashion designer Deborah Yanna, founder of “Make America Sparkle Again.” Exhibition materials describe the artist as having been selected by President Trump as a national delegate for the state of Iowa in 2024. During rallies or political events, Ms. Yanna would wear jackets like these, described as “sequined, bold and patriotic.”

Zachary Small is a Times reporter writing about the art world’s relationship to money, politics and technology.

Senate Committee Approves Measure to Block Trump’s Effort to Gut Education Dept.

The New York Times July 30, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The bipartisan bill is a long way from becoming law, but it represents the strongest opposition yet from Congress to the administration’s agenda.

By Michael C. Bender

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration’s bid to dismantle the Education Department was rebuked on Thursday by the Senate education committee, which approved a bipartisan bill that would block the executive branch from gutting the agency.

The legislation faces a long road to becoming law. Competing legislation in the House would instead codify many of the administration’s actions, and President Trump is unlikely to sign into law a measure that directly undermines his policy agenda.

Still, the vote was the sharpest opposition lawmakers had registered over the administration’s attempt to eliminate the Education Department. Closing the agency would require an act of Congress, but the administration has embarked on a piecemeal approach to gut the agency by effectively subcontracting its functions to other departments.

Relying on so-called interagency agreements, which have generally been used to purchase supplies or lease space between federal agencies, the Trump administration has transferred tens of billions in government programs out of the Education Department.

The bill would “maintain the core components” of the department, said Senator Tim Kaine, Democrat of Virginia, who sponsored the legislation. Specifically, the bill would block moves that the administration has made to transfer services for disabled students to the Health and Human Services Department; programs for elementary, secondary and postsecondary students to the Labor Department; and programs for Native American students to the Interior Department.

Senators Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, both Republicans, voted with Democrats on the panel to send the measure to the Senate floor.

Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, the Republican chairman of the committee, said he opposed the administration’s move of special education services to the health department, but he ultimately voted against the bill, saying he did not want to block the administration from making changes.

Opponents of the measure pointed to lagging test scores for the nation’s students, saying the poor numbers showed the Education Department had failed in its mission.

“This bill is misguided and it clearly lacks the vision to address this failing education system that we have in this country,” said Senator Tommy Tuberville, Republican of Alabama. “It ain’t working.”

Savannah Newhouse, a spokeswoman for the Education Department, said lawmakers were committing “malpractice” by supporting the legislation.

“It is entirely premature to sabotage this effort before it has the chance to eliminate bureaucratic barriers and fully deliver the results that our students, families and educators deserve,” she said.

After the vote, several cabinet members involved in the changes to the department, including Education Secretary Linda McMahon, sent a letter to Republican and Democratic leaders in Congress defending the moves.

The letter claimed that $3 trillion had been spent on the Education Department since 1980 but that had resulted in low test scores, high student loan debt and excessive bureaucracy. It promised that the changes would streamline the agency’s processes and that students, parents and educators would face no disruptions.

Advocacy groups have argued that by moving the offices for special education and civil rights, the Trump administration was effectively weakening oversight after drastically reducing staffing in those areas.

Many of these groups have also warned that Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s views on autism make him unfit to oversee education programs for students with disabilities.

Michael C. Bender is a Times correspondent in Washington.

The New York Times July 30, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The statement by the nominee, Sarah B. Rogers, signaled a stark reversal of the president’s earlier efforts to shutter Voice of America and other federally funded news groups.

By Minho Kim

Reporting from Washington

President Trump’s nominee to oversee the parent agency of Voice of America, a government-funded news group that operates in countries with limited press freedoms, said on Thursday that if the Senate confirmed her, she would bring back many of the journalists who had been placed on paid leave since the early weeks of Mr. Trump’s second term.

The statement by the nominee, Sarah B. Rogers, during her confirmation hearing signaled a stark reversal of Mr. Trump’s earlier efforts to shutter Voice of America and other federally funded news groups. The turnaround came after lawmakers voiced for months a rare bipartisan opposition to the dramatic cuts to the newsrooms, which they believe are critical to counter misinformation and propaganda campaigns by American adversaries like Russia, China and Iran with factual reporting.

“I’m definitely going to bring back more of them,” Ms. Rogers said of the journalists while refraining from making exact commitments. “We do need to reform and modernize, but we should see people coming back to work.”

Kari Lake, a Trump ally who had been appointed as the leader of the parent organization, the U. S. Agency for Global Media, repeatedly tried to fire hundreds of journalists at Voice of America and cut funding to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty and other federally supported news groups last year. Ms. Lake’s efforts led to setbacks in federal courts that enjoined her directives and eventually declared that her appointment and actions as an acting chief executive were illegal and void.

Hundreds of journalists and support staff at Voice of America have been on paid leave since early 2025, when Mr. Trump signed an executive order that led to the closure of the news groups.

As recently as March, the government sought to overturn a Federal District Court order requiring the administration to bring back the V. O. A. workers it had put on leave. The U. S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit sided with the government, which argued that the courts lacked powers to order specific personnel decisions.

On Thursday, Ms. Rogers indicated that she might try a different approach, reinstating services to parts of Africa and investigating a possible return of V. O. A.’s Latin America service. She told the lawmakers that the parent organization, U. S. Agency for Global Media, would oversee a “careful, tactical resuscitation of resources” to parts of Africa, especially in the Sahel region, where Russia and China have engaged in heavy propaganda campaigns.

“I don’t want to make operational commitments,” she said. “But I strongly expect you’ll see more from us.”

Until March 2025, V. O. A. aired news programs in 49 languages to 360 million people every week. Voice of America now broadcasts in fewer than a dozen languages, including Persian, Mandarin and the two main languages in Afghanistan, Dari and Pashto.

Ms. Rogers, a staunch free-speech advocate who is also a top public diplomacy official at the State Department, received pointed questions on Thursday from lawmakers who raised concerns about her inflammatory style of communication, which has included disparaging remarks about immigrants.

If confirmed as the chief executive of the global media agency, Ms. Rogers would continue to serve in the State Department.

On Thursday, Ms. Rogers promised to stay clear of meddling with the editorial decisions of V. O. A. and other federally funded news organizations. She repeated that she would “commit to respect the professionalism and independence of international broadcasting.” The parent agency is currently overseen by an interim chief executive; Ms. Lake has been accused of trying to interfere with the news groups’ editorial independence during her tenure by making funding conditional on the hiring of executives aligned with the administration’s views.

In response to a question by Senator Chris Murphy, Democrat of Connecticut, Ms. Rogers said the law did not allow her to unilaterally cut funding to government-funded news services critical of foreign leaders allied with Mr. Trump.

“If you’re asking, ‘Am I going to pull funding from a grantee if any reporters criticize anybody the president likes?’” she said, referring to news groups that receive federal dollars. “I don’t think that’s what the statute envisions, and I don’t think that’s what my priorities are going to be.”

Minho Kim reports on breaking news for The Times from Washington.

State Department Map Mislabels African Countries at AIDS Conference

The New York Times July 30, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

Nigeria, a coastal country in western Africa, was landlocked in the Sahara, among other errors. The department said it had been “hastily altered.”

By Remy Tumin

A senior health official with the State Department presenting at an international AIDS conference in Brazil this week used a map of Africa to illustrate U. S. government funding for H. I. V. programs on the continent.

There was only one problem. The map incorrectly identified several African countries:

Nigeria, a coastal country in western Africa, was landlocked in the Sahara;

Mozambique, a coastal state in southeastern Africa, was similarly landlocked and relocated to the Horn of Africa;

Ivory Coast, a coastal country in western Africa, was made into a southern African state;

Uganda and Malawi were roughly in the correct vicinity of the continent, but the borders were inaccurate;

The legend also referenced Cameroon, but the map did not include the country.

The map appeared to show where the State Department might direct health grants during a pre-conference event at AIDS 2026, which is being hosted by the International AIDS Society in Rio de Janeiro. The session focused on the status of U. S. government relations with governments in Africa.

An analysis by Reuters, which obtained images from the session, found that the map contained an artificial intelligence watermark associated with tools from OpenAI. Screenshots of the map were first published ​in a Substack post by Emily Bass, an AIDS expert and writer, and were widely shared on LinkedIn.

The State Department called the misprint “an unfortunate error” in a statement and said it resulted from a team member who “hastily altered” a slide before the presentation. The department said it took “full responsibility” for the misprint.

Kenneth Ngure, the president-elect of the International AIDS Society, called the use of the map at the conference “disheartening.”

“African countries must be taken seriously,” he said in a statement. “The African continent continues to bear the greatest burden of the H. I. V. pandemic, and our focus must now return to advancing the H. I. V. response.”

The Trump administration’s cuts to the largest global H. I. V. program last year have resulted in drastic drops in both prevention efforts and treatment. The program, known as the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR, supported treatment for about 77,000 fewer children in 2025 than it had the previous year, a 14 percent decline, according to a study, the results of which are expected to be presented at the conference this week.

A State Department spokesman said the department was shifting away from a “legacy assistance model” to “genuine country ownership.”

Remy Tumin is a reporter for The Times covering breaking news and other topics.

Ebola Outbreak Is Now the Second-Deadliest Ever, and in Record Time

The New York Times July 30, 2026

Ebola Outbreak

Advertisement

Supported by

The disease has killed more than 1,500 people in the Democratic Republic of Congo in just over two months, causing deaths faster than officials have ever recorded.

By Zane Irwin and Stephanie Nolen

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has already become the second-worst on record, and it is spreading much faster than previous outbreaks, the nation’s health ministry reported on Thursday.

The official death toll has jumped to 1,521 people in fewer than three months. Put another way, the species of Ebola behind the current outbreak, Bundibugyo, has killed more than five times as many people as previous outbreaks did in the same amount of time, officials from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said at a press briefing on Thursday.

The last outbreak, which began in 2018 and was declared over in 2020, took more than 10 months to reach the same death toll.

“I’m not in a position to tell you we are in total control of this outbreak today,” said Dr. Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa C. D. C.

The virus ripping through eastern Congo is on pace to surpass the number of infections and deaths of the 2014-2016 Ebola crisis in West Africa, the worst outbreak ever that killed more than 11,000 people.

On Tuesday, Uganda, which borders Congo, declared an end to its related Bundibugyo outbreak after four weeks with no new cases. There were 20 cases and three deaths in Uganda.

Swift action and rigorous contact tracing in Uganda are credited with quickly controlling its outbreak. But across the border in Congo, the situation is rapidly deteriorating.

Since the current outbreak was first declared in May, Congo has confirmed 3,442 cases. As of Wednesday, the nation’s health ministry had counted 797 people who were hospitalized or in isolation. More than 80 percent of beds in treatment centers are occupied, and officials warn they could soon be overwhelmed.

Early surveillance and testing failed to spot the disease’s emergence, delaying the response. Tracing the virus was also made harder by fighting in eastern Congo that has displaced millions of people.

Africa C. D. C. officials said on Thursday that contact tracing efforts remained far off target. More than 80 percent of new cases in the epicenter of the disease were “not linked to known contacts,” officials said.

Every confirmed case from an urban area is expected to have 40 contacts, which means the current roster of exposed people being followed should be 134,400 people. Instead, it’s only 17,558 people, just 13 percent of what it should be.

And of those on the list, about a fifth are not being followed, either because there is a lack of health personnel to do the job or because armed conflict makes it impossible to check on them regularly.

Sixty percent of those who have died of the virus succumbed in a community, not in a health center, Dr. Kaseya said, in another indicator that the virus is spreading unchecked.

Efforts to save lives and slow the virus are nevertheless progressing.

While there are no vaccines or treatments for Bundibugyo, clinical trials of possible treatments, and of a drug that could prevent infection in people exposed to the virus, have begun in Congo. More than 40 patients are testing a combination of therapeutics.

And in a separate trial, 19 people have been started on a 10-day course of an experimental anti-viral drug to prevent people exposed to the virus from getting sick. This trial aims to enroll 1,200 people. If data analysis after 600 patients show promising results, the goal will be to extend access to the drug to all contacts.

“This is the hope we have,” Dr. Kaseya said.

In addition, a clinical trial of a first-ever vaccine for Bundibugyo began at Oxford University this month, where the first of 50 adult volunteers was immunized and will be monitored for vaccine safety.

On Thursday, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations announced that it would fund a Singapore-based research firm, Hilleman Laboratories, to develop another potential vaccine and make doses for testing. The goal is to get it into swift clinical trials in Congo. This vaccine uses the technology behind one made by Merck, already approved by regulatory agencies to prevent another species of Ebola.

Zane Irwin is an international reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Stephanie Nolen is a global health reporter for The Times.

‘This Is Very Strange’: Ancient Smallpox May Have Been Less Deadly

The New York Times July 30, 2026

Scientists have found smallpox viruses in the remains of people in Chile from around 500 years ago, revealing how the virus may have evolved into a global killer.

Scientists have found smallpox viruses in the remains of people in Chile from around 500 years ago, revealing how the virus may have evolved into a global killer.

For the first time, scientists have found ancient smallpox genomes from the Americas, hiding in skeletons in Chile that date back about 500 years. Credit... CDC/Phanie/Sipa Press, via Alamy

Supported by

By Carl Zimmer

Perhaps no disease has inspired more terror than smallpox. Edward Jenner, who invented the smallpox vaccine in 1796, called it “the most dreadful scourge of the human species.” In the 20th century alone, smallpox is estimated to have killed 300 million people. The eradication of the virus in the 1970s stands as one of the great triumphs of medicine. And yet, five decades later, smallpox still haunts us, as the world worries about its resurrection as a biological weapon.

For all the anxiety that smallpox inspires, its history remains remarkably mysterious. Researchers don’t know how smallpox first evolved or how long it has plagued humanity. But over the past decade geneticists have offered a new line of evidence, as they find smallpox DNA still lurking in the bodies of people who died centuries ago.

On Thursday, researchers revealed the latest genetic trace in a paper published in Science. For the first time, they have found ancient smallpox genomes from the Americas, hiding in skeletons in Chile that date back about 500 years.

These DNA fragments have prompted scientists to think about smallpox in a new light. It may not have begun as the dreaded killer we think of it as today. It’s possible that it was a relatively mild infection for centuries, taking many generations to evolve into Jenner’s dreadful scourge.

Hendrik Poinar, an expert on ancient smallpox at McMaster University in Ontario, Canada, who was not involved in the new study, said he was not aware of any other disease that had taken such a course. “This is very strange,” he said.

Scientists generally agree that the smallpox virus jumped into humans from another species. Other animals carry a variety of related viruses, but scientists have yet to find a virus that could have been the forerunner.

“We’re not any closer to knowing the actual reservoir species from which smallpox came, which to me is kind of amazing,” Dr. Poinar said.

To understand when smallpox first started killing humans, researchers have looked at mummified remains, searching for the sores and scars the virus creates. The mummy of Pharaoh Ramses V, which dates back 3,000 years, has pockmarks on its cheeks; many experts have suggested it’s the oldest trace of smallpox in human history.

But Dr. Poinar no longer shares that view. “I don’t buy Ramses,” he said.

Dr. Poinar changed his opinion after he discovered how well other pathogens can mimic smallpox. He and his colleagues examined the body of a child who had died in Italy nearly 500 years ago, considered the oldest physical evidence of smallpox there.

But Dr. Poinar and his colleagues found no smallpox DNA. Instead, they found genes from hepatitis B, which can cause a facial rash that resembles smallpox sores.

In 2016, Dr. Poinar and his colleagues offered up far more compelling proof of ancient smallpox: its DNA. They found genetic fragments of the virus in the body of child who lived in Lithuania in the 1600s.

Four years later, another team of researchers discovered smallpox DNA, in the leg of an 18th century infant preserved in a London museum. Even more surprising was the discovery by other researchers of four smallpox genomes from the Viking Age, in the bones of northern Europeans who had lived between 1,000 and 1,400 years ago.

The newest discovery of ancient smallpox was made 4,000 miles to the east, on a cliff-edged stretch of coastline in northern Chile, at a site called Camarones 9. It was there, in the 1950s, that archaeologists discovered an Incan cemetery.

Recently, researchers at the University of Chile took a fresh look at the cemetery remains, using new techniques to search for DNA, including for genes of viruses and bacteria. The scientists sifted through vast amounts of DNA left behind by soil microbes that had fed on the bones.

Constanza de la Fuente Castro, a biological anthropologist at the University of Chile and an author of the new study, said she had hoped they might find DNA from tuberculosis, which was present in South America long before the arrival of Europeans.

“Smallpox was definitely not in our picture,” she said.

But when she and her colleagues had finished searching through their data, they came up with genetically identical smallpox viruses, infecting a man and a woman who lived some time between the late 1400s and early 1600s.

Dr. Castro and her colleagues then compared the genetic sequence of the Camarones 9 viruses to older and younger smallpox samples. Based on the similarities and differences in the viral DNA, the researchers drew a family tree.

All known smallpox viruses appear to share a common viral ancestor that existed about 1500 years ago. As the smallpox virus found new people to infect, its descendants split into distinct branches of the family tree.

The Viking viruses belong to branches that are not closely related to any modern smallpox strains. It appears that they became extinct centuries ago.

The Camarones 9 viruses from Chile occupy an intermediate spot on the smallpox family tree. They’re more closely related to modern smallpox than the Viking viruses. But they split off on a distinct branch of their own, which also appears to have disappeared. The viruses from Lithuania in the 1600s and England in the 1700s, in contrast, are very closely related to modern strains of the virus.

Over the centuries, Dr. Castro and her colleagues found, smallpox had undergone a striking transformation. Mutations arose that completely disabled some of its genes.

By the time the Viking smallpox viruses evolved, over two dozen genes had been shut down. Even more were lost in the Camarones 9 viruses. And by the 1600s and 1700s, the viruses from Lithuania and England had lost even more.

“By our rough calculation, it looks like one or two genes per century,” said Shigeki Nakagome, a geneticist at Trinity College Dublin and an author of the Camarones 9 study.

Losing genes may have actually made smallpox better at infecting humans. The virus may have abandoned ones that had helped it infect other species. Over centuries, it became more efficient at multiplying inside human cells. And as it churned out more new viruses, smallpox may have grown deadlier.

In other words, early smallpox viruses might have been relatively mild. Dr. Poinar noted that there are no written records of smallpox outbreaks in northern Europe during the period of the Viking viruses. It’s possible that most people regularly survived smallpox and gained immunity to it.

The Camarones 9 study suggests that when the Spanish came to the Americas, they brought with them smallpox viruses that had been circulating in Europe in the 1400s; ultimately the viruses reached Indigenous people living in remote communities.

Historians have long suspected that Europeans brought smallpox to the New World, and that it then helped drive down the populations of Indigenous people there. But many historical records of outbreaks are ambiguous.

Sébastien Calvignac-Spencer, an evolutionary biologist at the Helmholtz Institute for One Health in Germany, said the new study dispels any doubt that smallpox played a role in the devastation of the Americas.

“It confirms that the virus was already spreading in the Americas at this time,” said Dr. Calvignac-Spencer, who was not involved in the new study.

Several factors could have made it deadlier in the Americas. For starters, people there had no immunity to the new virus. And the famine, slavery, and poverty ushered in under colonial rule could have weakened their defenses even further.

“Because the Native Americans had zero exposure to the virus, it caused a lot of problems in their societies, even if it was milder to Europeans,” Dr. Nakagome said.

But smallpox was still not done evolving, the new study suggests. It’s possible that the disease reached its modern levels of lethality in the 1700s. Dr. Poinar speculated that the growing population in Europe might have allowed smallpox to become even deadlier. Even if it was more likely to kill off a host in an epidemic, it was also more likely to find a new host to infect.

This scenario may fit the evidence that scientists have found so far, but there are huge swaths of history they don’t yet understand. Most of the research on ancient DNA has traditionally focused on Europe, but historical records suggest that smallpox also circulated in parts of Africa and Asia for centuries.

“All of these are total black boxes,” said Dr. Calvignac-Spencer. “Until we fill in these gaps, it would be difficult to create a global history of such an important disease.”

Carl Zimmer covers news about science for The Times and writes the Origins column.

Musk Plans to Spend at Least $100 Million to Help Republicans in the Midterms

The New York Times July 30, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Elon Musk, a year after a huge blowup with President Trump and the Republican Party, is said to be planning to spend in at least eight states to help them in November.

By Theodore Schleifer

Reporting from Washington

Elon Musk, a year after voicing deep frustration with the Republican Party and threatening to start a third party, appears to be back in the fold and prepared to spend big in the midterms to help G. O. P. candidates.

Mr. Musk, the world’s richest person, has authorized his super PAC to spend $100 million to $120 million on a new field program in at least eight states to help elect Republicans in November, according to two people briefed on the plans, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss the private deliberations.

The planned injection of cash from Mr. Musk, the biggest donor in the 2024 presidential election, would only add to Republicans’ yawning advantage over Democrats in funding from super PACs and party groups. While Democratic candidates in key Senate races are raising more than their Republican rivals, many in the Democratic Party have begun to worry about being badly outspent overall in the midterms.

Officials from Mr. Musk’s super PAC, America PAC, have communicated their nine-figure budget to other Republicans in recent weeks as part of an aggressive spending plan that is set to begin next month, according to a person with knowledge of the matter.

The precise amounts could change, but Mr. Musk’s financial commitment is seen as secure enough that officials at his super PAC have relayed its budget to groups like MAGA Inc., President Trump’s super PAC — which also has yet to reveal its midterm spending plan.

Mr. Musk’s group plans to initially target Senate races in at least five states — Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan and Ohio — and is having conversations about the contests in North Carolina, Georgia and Texas, according to two people with knowledge of the super PAC’s plans.

The super PAC is also planning to spend in House races in states including California, Wisconsin and Washington, according to two people with knowledge of the plans.

America PAC said that it would be active in battleground Senate and House races. The group declined to comment on its budget and targeted states. Some of its high-level plans were earlier reported by Axios.

Mr. Musk’s super PAC is closely coordinating with an ecosystem of outside groups that are preparing field campaigns, including Americans for Prosperity, which is part of the billionaire Koch brothers’ political network, and the Sentinel Action Fund, another conservative organization. Republican outside groups are planning to pool their field operations more than ever after a Supreme Court ruling in late June made it cheaper for party committees to work directly with candidates.

To help its efforts, America PAC is lining up firms that focus on knocking on voters’ doors, according to two people with knowledge of the matter. Chris Young, who is Mr. Musk’s top political adviser and oversaw the group’s huge spending in the 2024 election, is in charge again.

Mr. Musk spent close to $300 million on the 2024 campaign, hosting town halls that drew on his celebrity to try to help Mr. Trump. But Mr. Musk is not currently expected to play as front-facing a role as he did during the 2024 presidential race or during a major court election in April 2025 in Wisconsin, where his candidate lost.

After the defeat in Wisconsin, Mr. Musk appeared aware that his public presence in the race had backfired, The New York Times reported last year.

“In terms of political spending, I’m going to do a lot less in the future,” he told Bloomberg News in May 2025. “I think I’ve done enough.”

A few months later, Mr. Musk had a spectacular falling out with Mr. Trump. He left his role overseeing the president’s government-gutting initiative, known as DOGE, and immediately began bashing Mr. Trump’s major domestic policy bill and the Republican Party in general.

That summer, Mr. Musk threatened to start a third party, which made some of his advisers who are aligned with the Republican Party skittish. But he made no moves to start what he said would be called the America Party. By last fall, he had largely made up with Mr. Trump, and advisers began sketching out plans to help Republicans again.

Then again, Mr. Musk’s interest in, and commentary about, politics can seem erratic. In an interview with The Economist published last week, he said of his involvement in Mr. Trump’s administration: “I think I got a little too involved in politics. I got carried away, frankly.”

Theodore Schleifer is a Times reporter covering billionaires and their impact on the world.

Why Democrats Won’t Stop Forcing Votes on the War

The New York Times July 30, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Congressional memo

Even after winning approval of a measure calling on President Trump to end the war, they continue to call votes to force Republicans to answer for it.

By Robert Jimison

Reporting from the Capitol

For the 13th time this year, members of the Senate filed into the marbled chamber on Thursday to cast their votes on a Democratic measure calling on President Trump to halt military operations against Iran or seek authorization to continue waging war in the Middle East.

The resolution faltered when Republicans banded together to block it, surprising no one who has watched the same ritual unfold week after week as a conflict that was supposed to last four weeks has dragged into its sixth month.

It looked like an exercise in futility, not only because similar efforts have failed repeatedly — the vote was 50 to 49 on Thursday, similar to last week’s — but because one such resolution actually succeeded last month, winning approval in both the House and Senate only to have Mr. Trump ignore it completely.

Yet Democrats refuse to let the matter rest, viewing the successive votes as part of a broader political strategy to highlight the growing disconnect between voters — who have increasingly soured on the war — and Republican senators who continue to defer to Mr. Trump in backing it.

All but three Republicans — Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky — opposed moving forward with the measure to rein in the president’s war powers, which was offered this week by Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, Democrat of New York. A single Democrat, Senator John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, voted against the measure. He has consistently crossed party lines on the issues since the war began.

Democrats’ efforts to end hostilities not sanctioned by Congress appeared to have succeeded last month, when the Senate approved a war powers resolution, delivering a congressional rebuke after four Republicans crossed party lines to back the effort. But the concurrent resolution — which was also adopted in the House — does not carry the force of law, and the president has asserted that he has all the authority he needs to continue the war without a word from Congress.

And after Mr. Trump raged at Senate Republicans behind closed doors about that vote, they quickly held another one to block consideration of a similar measure. Subsequent attempts to muster enough Republican support for a war powers resolution have failed, including last week when the Senate blocked one offered by Senator Chris Van Hollen, Democrat of Maryland.

Democrats say the repetitive votes are still worthwhile, as opportunities to force G. O. P. senators to defend a war that has become more difficult to sell to voters.

“Are Senate Republicans listening? The country is clamoring for you to end this war,” Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, said in a speech ahead of Thursday’s vote. “I urge and plead with my Republican colleagues: Listen to the American people. Vote to end this war. We’re going to keep forcing Republicans to vote until we do.”

A poll released this week by IPSOS/Reuters found that overall support for the war has fallen to its lowest point since the conflict began, with 62 percent of American adults surveyed saying they disapprove of the U. S. attacks against Iran.

Recent surveys also show that support is slipping even among Mr. Trump’s most loyal base of voters. Those who self-identified as MAGA were less supportive of the war continuing given the economic costs than they had been two months earlier, according to a recent POLITICO poll.

Though Republican lawmakers continue to defer to Mr. Trump on the war, they have also expressed angst about its impacts.

“The rising gas prices are a real concern to everybody,” Senator Mike Rounds, Republican of South Dakota, who voted against the resolution, said on Wednesday. “The question on it is, what’s the best long-term fix? Part of it has to be stability in the Middle East.”

Republicans note that war powers resolutions are a blunt instrument, directing “the removal” of U. S. troops in what many of them argue is an irresponsible move that would only make a dangerous situation worse.

“Right now, if you simply walk away, there is no stability in the Middle East,” Mr. Rounds said.

Thursday’s vote followed renewed fighting in the region, with the two countries exchanging airstrikes that broke a dayslong pause that many hoped would be the restart to diplomatic negotiations. Fighting also expanded to allies in the Middle East, with the United States and Saudi Arabia conducting joint strikes and Egypt being drawn into the conflict when a drone struck two ships at a port near the Suez Canal.

“We’re here, we have to admit that,” Senator John Curtis, Republican of Utah, said of the current state of the conflict. He criticized the resolutions as “not really serious.”

But his vote, he said, does not mean that he is comfortable with ceding all authority to Mr. Trump.

“I do believe the War Powers Act of 1973 is very clear. It does give the president authority in that 60- to 90-day period,” he said. The law bars the president from carrying out military operations without congressional approval, unless he is responding to an imminent threat, and grants 60 days to terminate any such action with a 30-day extension. “My perspective is, we’re outside that period.”

Republicans including Mr. Curtis argue that the correct course is not a resolution to halt the war but an authorization for the use of military force that would give lawmakers more involvement in the scope and direction of the conflict.

“My strategy is to speak as a Congress, as Democrats and Republicans, about parameters that we are willing to authorize,” Mr. Curtis said. “It is incumbent on us to speak.”

Democrats say they would welcome such a measure.

“If our Republican colleagues have the strength of their convictions, they should bring an authorization to use military force in Iran to this floor,” Mr. Van Hollen said in speech last week. “We have not seen that.”

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.
