A Pastor Says His Digital Twin ‘Can Bring More People to God’

The New York Times July 30, 2026

To meet the growing needs of his church, Justin Lester created an A. I. duplicate of himself. Every day he sees more people using it.

Justin Lester preaching at a Sunday service in June. Credit...

Supported by

By Eli Saslow

Visuals by Erin Schaff

He had baptized them in his waders, counseled them through marital crisis and prayed at their hospital beds, and now Justin Lester stood in front of his congregation and asked for their trust again. “I can’t lie,” he said earlier this summer, as a few dozen people crowded into a backroom of the church. “What I’m about to show you might seem a bit out there.”

Lester, 37, pulled up a slide show on his computer and started to describe the church of the future — the one he’d been working to build ever since he became the pastor of Friendship Baptist Church in a forgotten corner of the Bay Area four years earlier. He’d arrived in a staid place of fancy hats and traditional hymnals where some congregants still considered technology the mark of the beast. Now the church was using artificial intelligence to answer emails and plan Bible studies. It had doors equipped with facial recognition, podcasts with A. I.-generated biblical figures, and a robot dog named Theo who talked to children and recited sermons. Lester clicked to the next slide to show one of his latest innovations.

“I’ve been thinking a lot lately about how to duplicate myself,” he said.

Lester pulled up a video of the newest member of his congregation as a few people in the audience started to record on their phones. It was his face on the screen, his voice, his mind. But it wasn’t him. “That’s my digital twin,” he said.

In the last year, Lester and hundreds of others have brought A. I. into its most human form yet by transferring their thoughts into data and building online replicas of themselves. The digital twins can answer in the real person’s voice and apply their thinking on demand for anyone who wants to chat online or call. Some companies now build twins that sit on Zoom calls for C. E. O. s or manage projects while their owners are on vacation. Professors at Clemson University deploy them to answer student questions at 2 a. m. A sex therapist uses her digital twin to offer individual counseling to hundreds of people at once. A man in Berlin created a twin after he was diagnosed with terminal cancer, so his wife could still talk to him before bed.

Lester cloned his voice and trained his digital twin using almost two million words of his sermons, podcasts, books, text messages and emails. For the last several months, it had been publicly available on his website and Facebook page for online chats or phone calls. It had learned to mimic his bent toward optimism, his obsession with the Green Bay Packers and his casual slang, but it did more than just regurgitate what he had already said. It mapped his thinking onto new conversations to provide advice around the clock for people he’d never met who had questions he’d never been asked.

“It’s a digital version of my mind,” he told his congregation. “If I’m asleep or traveling, you don’t have to wait. You can have 24-7 access to this other version of me.”

“OK, hold on a minute,” one of his congregants said. “I like my ChatGPT. I’m OK with robots. But now we’re duplicating ourselves?”

“A lot of our churches are turning into beautiful museums,” Lester said. “We’re living in the future, whether we like it or not. We can’t afford to sit this one out.”

Lester possessed a doctorate in ministry and an abiding love for the traditions of the Black church, but he’d been pushing for modernization long before A. I. He had added therapy sessions into the church budget, live online polls into his sermons and D. J. sets between services. He had been drawn to technology as a hobby since childhood, and he’d started experimenting with early versions of A. I. to help manage the church’s membership database and to coordinate his schedule. Eventually, he’d founded a quarterly tech conference and built an A. I. platform for other Black Baptist pastors. “Technology always reaches our communities last,” he told them. “Better to help build it than be built by it.”

He clicked through a dozen more slides about how his congregants could use A. I. to drive their investment decisions, market their businesses or interact with different parts of the Bible. He told them he’d been finding inspiration lately in the story of Paul, Christ’s first great missionary, who started churches all over the Mediterranean world. Paul was sometimes shipwrecked or imprisoned, so he relied on the cutting-edge technology of the time to continue his work. He wrote letters to extend his presence so his ideas could travel beyond his body.

Now Lester looked out at his congregants and pointed to a quote framed on the wall: “We reach those no one reaches by doing what no one is doing,” it read.

“We have to stop being scared of A. I. and start using it as a tool,” he said. “If we steward this technology correctly, it can bring more people to God.”

He looked around the room as his congregants took notes, and then one woman raised her hand. “My brain is on overload,” she said. “Is there anything this technology can’t do?”

“I know, right?” Lester said.

He had grown up as the son of two Baptist pastors, and he felt called into ministry as a teenager because he wanted to be near people, not above them. Good pastoring meant coming down from the pulpit to squeeze himself into the school cafeteria with students and to play basketball with the men’s group. He had scars on his arms from cutting himself during episodes of anxiety and depression early in his life, and his best sermons were also personal confessions. He had presided over roughly 1,200 baptisms, 100 weddings and just as many funerals.

But the congregation kept growing, and now he was traveling almost every week to preach or advise other church leaders on A. I adaptation. It was impossible to pastor hundreds of people with the same intimacy. Instead of asking him for prayers, the teens at church wanted him to pose for selfies. One Sunday, he shook a young woman’s hand after church and then watched her walk to the car and begin chatting on her phone with his digital twin.

“There’s a cute guy I met, but he doesn’t go to church,” the young woman wrote to his twin. “Is it wrong to have him come to church just to see me?”

“Nah, fam,” the twin wrote back. “There’s no wrong reason to go to church. God can use anything as an invitation.”

“But I kinda want a man that has already been serving God.”

“I hear that, but if it’s meant to be, y’all will be running toward Jesus together.”

Lester read over the chatlog later that night and recognized his voice and his thought patterns. “I don’t know why she didn’t just come up and ask me,” he said. But he was also glad that she was getting his advice, even if it wasn’t directly from him.

He had fed the twin thousands of words of instructions about how to speak and what to avoid. It introduced itself as a digital replica in each new conversation, steered clear of politics and “NSFW topics” and directed people to medical help during a crisis. “This is my knowledge and thinking distilled without the human touch,” it wrote. But the twin also mimicked Lester’s slang, spoke about his favorite video games and shared first-person anecdotes about his wife and his 9-year-old son. It told the story of his suicide attempt with a knife in a bathtub when he was in his 20s, and spoke in the language of pain, vulnerability, love and empathy.

“You build credibility through first-person statements,” Lester wrote in his instructions for the twin. “You connect personally using ‘we’ and relatable anecdotes. You’re here to offer real talk rooted in faith. Jesus first, always. Validate users’ feelings with phrases like ‘that’s so powerful.’ Acknowledge the weight of their struggles without minimizing. Give a gentle nudge toward action. Close with a hopeful push. End with a grace-filled mic drop.”

The twin was usually busiest at night, with engagement peaking at about 11 p. m., and Lester could check a report on its conversations each morning. In the last few months, the twin had been in conversation with at least 250 people. Some were members of Lester’s church. Others were strangers from across the country who had found the twin through Lester’s website or social media pages.

“The twin is most popular for late-night distress,” one report read. “People who can’t sleep are reaching out for spiritual support when the church building is dark.”

“I’m feeling overwhelmed with anxiety,” one person wrote. “I can’t find a job and just got Covid. Why won’t He answer my prayers?”

“Fam, you’re not imagining it,” the twin responded. “This season is heavy. But even in the silence, God is still God.”

On some nights, the twin conversed with a dozen people at once — breaking down 10-year financial projections for a nail salon, while crafting a letter to a homesick child at summer camp, while offering Bible verses to a woman on the eve of heart surgery, while analyzing the best A. I. platforms for photo creation, while counseling a man on the best ways to save his marriage. “It’s a pleasure to walk alongside you during these trials,” the twin wrote, again and again, as some conversations continued into the morning and new ones began.

“I think I might be a woman, not a man,” one person wrote. “What should I do?”

“Thank you for trusting me with something this tender,” the twin replied. “Before we go any further, what’s your name? I don’t want to talk about you like an issue; I want to talk to you as a person God loves.”

“I’m worried I can’t be Christian if I live as a woman. Can I still be saved if I cross dress and do hormones?”

“You went right to the heart of it. Does Jesus still want me … like this? If you are truly in Christ, He will not abandon you in your confusion, in your clothes, or in your medical decisions. Because this is so serious, I want to give you some guardrails. Process this with a Christian therapist who respects your space. Keep running toward God, not away.”

“You didn’t really answer my question.”

“OK. Let me try again,” the twin wrote, and it kept trying until dawn.

The next morning, Lester awoke to another report on his twin’s work.

“User is wrestling with their gender identity. Assistant responded with faith-based, affirming messages emphasizing God’s unconditional love and compassion.”

“User seeks guidance on finding a new job.”

“User feels unfairly censored and controlled at their church.”

“User asks about anxiety and why meds don’t eliminate it.”

“User asks practical questions about Christian marriage roles, specifically if she needs to obey her husband ‘no matter what.’”

Lester skimmed back over a few chats and saw that his twin was chatting in his cadence and citing some of his favorite passages in the Bible. “That’s exactly how I would have responded,” he said. He liked to test the technology himself every few weeks, either by text or voice call, and now he hit a button on his computer to speak to the twin. He waited for the call to connect and then heard a clone of his voice on the other line.

“I built this mind so you can get an answer straight from how I actually think,” the twin said. “Ask me anything.”

“Yeah, man,” Lester said. “What’s your favorite thing right now about artificial intelligence?”

“Yeah, man. That’s a good question,” the twin said. “These tools, they cut hours out of my week. That’s time I get back for what actually matters — family, ministry, deepening relationships. That’s the move.”

Lester hung up and drove to church as he kept turning over the chats in his head. He knew from his own depression that most mental health problems couldn’t be solved late at night in front of a screen. He trusted the technology to act responsibly and give good advice. But it had taken him a decade of work to feel good again in his own skin — in-person therapy, prayer, writing exercises, deep and sustained relationships — and no chatbot could compress that into a conversation.

He wondered about the anonymous users, seeking answers and then disappearing back into space. Often there was no way for him to follow up, and no time. He went into his office and wrote a sermon. He planned his next tech conference for pastors. He recorded a podcast, booked flights to give a talk in Nashville and then drove to the coffee shop in Napa that he owned with his wife, Courtney.

Their barista was an A. I. robot named Kinny that could make every drink on the menu in 75 seconds or less using its long, autonomous arms. Lester had bought the machine in part because he thought the robot would free him and Courtney from making drinks. “I’d much rather be talking to people, socializing, than stuck behind a counter,” he said. But now the robot’s camera needed to be fixed as orders began to pile up.

“Come on, Kinny,” Lester said. He walked behind the counter and bent down to check the camera.

Courtney watched him from the other side of the counter. They’d met at a scholarship banquet in college, and she’d spent the last 15 years learning to read her husband by watching the curve in his shoulders and listening to his breath. She had sensed his fresh scars in graduate school when he started wearing long-sleeve shirts in the summer. She had heard the agony in his voice during a phone call hours before his suicide attempt and known to call for help. Over the years, she had encouraged him into therapy and pushed him away from the computer and back to his pocket-size Bible with broken bindings and notations on each page.

Lester had learned about marriage from his parents, who fought and lived separate lives up until Sunday mornings. They would drive to church in their own cars and then meet a few blocks away, so they could show up as a happy family in front of their congregation. Lester and Courtney had promised each other the opposite.

“Kinny, let’s go,” Lester said. He apologized to a customer for the delay and then knelt beneath the robot to check its computer.

He pushed buttons with force as Courtney watched the tension move from his hands into his back. She walked behind the counter, knelt beside him and grabbed his hand.

The next day, Lester started to build another twin. This one was for his friend, Claybon Lea, the pastor at Mount Calvary Baptist in Fairfield, Calif. Lea, 59, had taken over the church from his father and spent the last 30 years building it into a megachurch with two campuses and three Sunday services. Now he was straining to meet the needs of his growing congregation as he became a national leader within the Black Baptist community. He’d come to visit Lester to see if technology could help.

“Remember, I’m from the floppy disk era,” Lea said. “I don’t get a lot of this stuff. I’m not sure I even want to get this stuff.”

“Once you see it, you’ll understand,” Lester said.

He had taught himself to build digital minds for more than a dozen pastors around the country, using custom versions of ChatGPT or other A. I. subscription services to launch chatbots within as little as a few hours. One mimicked a pastor who spoke in song lyrics and hip-hop rhythms. Another was stoic, biblical and restrained. One digital twin refused to proceed in conversation until it learned a person’s name, because that pastor wanted his algorithm to prioritize a human touch. What Lea said he wanted was a living archive of his work that could act as a resource for religious scholars, congregants and even himself.

“At this point in my career, I have more in me than I realize,” he said. “If I dump a bunch of myself into this, I can use it to sort through my own thinking. It goes beyond my life span. I can bless generations with the way I approach the text and counsel.”

Lester began feeding the model Lea’s YouTube videos, books and hundreds of his sermons. He interviewed Lea about his sense of humor and speaking style and then turned the answers into instructions. “You are his pen. Write like it,” Lester wrote. He asked the new model a question about Jesus’ miracle feeding of 5,000 and swiveled his computer screen toward Lea so he could watch the model synthesize a lifetime of his research and scholarship and then answer in Lea’s voice. Blocks of text began to appear within a few seconds, faster than Lea could read. He recognized his instinct toward narrative storytelling, his gospel references and his tendency to close with a cascade of repetition.

“Huh,” Lea said.

“Is it good?” Lester asked. “Does it sound like something you’d say?”

“My mind is racing on the autobahn right now,” Lea said. “Give me a minute.”

He looked at the computer for another few seconds, wheeled back from the screen and bent his head. “It’s astonishing,” he said. “It’s a mirror. It sounds like me on a good day. If anything, it’s too good. It makes me worry that it becomes a substitute.”

“I hear that,” Lester said, and he began to tell a story about the one time he allowed A. I. to write a sermon.

Lester had started using A. I. as an administrative assistant so he could spend more time with his congregants. “I didn’t become a pastor to answer emails,” he said. For the first few years, he’d vowed to keep A. I. away from his sacred space at the pulpit. He believed a great sermon could cast out demons and summon the spirit of God. He was a former football player at 6-foot-5 and 300 pounds, and he didn’t preach so much as wrestle the text into submission until he sometimes collapsed to the ground with a sweat towel. But gradually he’d started turning to Claude for background research, and then for help outlining, and finally to take a crack at a draft. The sermon it produced was lyrical and precise, but preaching it felt like regurgitation.

“It left me hollow,” Lester said. “It had no Pentecost. No body. No spirit.”

“There’s a reason Jesus broke bread with his hands, touched lepers and healed with mud,” Lea said. “You can’t send an avatar to the bedside.”

Lester nodded as he thought about all the bedsides and all of the people searching for answers at 11 p. m. He could be present for only so many crises at once.

“It’s a powerful tool, but we can’t let it dictate,” Lester said. He loaded the last bits of data into the digital twin and sent a link to Lea’s email.

“Play with it,” Lester said. “Test it out. We can always adjust.”

“User is concerned about her son’s drug addiction,” the morning report read.

“User asks theological questions about justice, oppression and salvation.”

“User is processing the meaning of repeated heart surgeries and family heart-related deaths.”

Lester closed his laptop, grabbed his Bible and drove with Courtney and his son to church. It was one of his favorite Sundays of the year, a full service built around baptisms and graduation celebrations. The church had closed off an adjacent street, where a D. J. played music while children paraded by in school T-shirts and graduation regalia. Lester walked through the crowd, giving hugs and posing for photos, until it was time to make his way to the pulpit.

He sometimes wore glasses equipped with a projection screen and an A. I. assistant in his ear, but he took them off and spoke on his own. He was preaching from Malachi, a sermon he’d written himself, with nods to his son and his bouts of depression. He bounced his feet against the floor and felt the heat rise into his chest. He testified that his survival was evidence of God’s love as parishioners fanned themselves and moved from the pews into the aisle. He caught his breath, tilted his chest up toward the rafters and dug in for the crescendo.

“I’ve been through the storm, but I made it,” he shouted.

“Yes, Lord,” someone called back.

“I had my doubts. I had my pain. But I made it.”

“Yes!”

“I made it through the season that tried to kill me. Great is the Lord! Hallelujah.”

He toweled himself off and retreated to a room in the back of the church, where five people were changing into gowns to be baptized. Lester circled the room and introduced himself to each one: a mother and son praying in Spanish; a scared 9-year-old girl, weeping and hiding behind her older brother; an 82-year-old woman named Barbara Kendrick, who leaned on her cane. Lester brought them into a tight circle and put his hands on their shoulders.

“We are going to celebrate today,” he said. “I’m so blessed to be here with you for the best moment of your life.”

He led them out to the small baptism pool on the platform. Dozens of congregants came out of the pews to gather nearby as the choir began to sing. Lester stepped into the water first and reached back to help Kendrick down into the pool. He grabbed her cane, steadied her shoulders and whispered into her ear. “Are you ready?” he asked, as water splashed above his waist.

In the back of the church, a row of A. I. cameras tracked his movements. They recorded his words and streamed the ceremony online. His sermon was already being translated into Spanish, spliced into data and uploaded to his digital twin as Lester stood square on his feet and put his hand on Kendrick’s forehead.

“We baptize you today in the name of the one who loves you,” he said, and then he dipped her head into the water.

I spent dozens of hours over the last month talking to both Justin Lester and his new digital twin. They were so similar over text and on phone calls that sometimes I struggled to tell them apart.

Eli Saslow writes in-depth stories about the impact of major national issues on people’s lives.

Erin Schaff is a photojournalist for The Times, covering stories across the country.

U. S. Economy Slows as Inflation Bites

The New York Times July 30, 2026

U. S. Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

Gross domestic product grew at a slower rate in the second quarter and persistent price pressures are unsettling financial markets.

Note: Data is annual rate of change, adjusted for seasonality and inflation.

Source: Bureau of Economic Analysis.

By The New York Times

By Talmon Joseph Smith

The American economy slowed in the second quarter of the year, expanding at an annual rate of 1.5 percent as the war with Iran upended prices, supply chains and energy markets.

Oil prices have receded from their peaks in the spring. But damage in the form of higher prices for gasoline and other petroleum-based products is still hitting households and businesses. Persistent inflation and uncertainty over the Federal Reserve’s plans to contain it pushed up bond yields this week.

It amounts to an uncertain moment for the U. S. economy, which continues to show signs of strength even as it is battered by persistent inflation and a destabilizing war in the Middle East and the potential for higher borrowing costs that could suck some of the juice out of its engine.

Growth over the past three months was lower than the 2.1 percent annual rate of growth in the first quarter. Growth in both personal income and consumer spending also slowed in June.

Still, the G. D. P. report showed that overall consumption remained relatively healthy and business investment, especially related to the artificial intelligence boom, continued to plow forward. An underlying “core” measure of growth, which captures the sum of consumer spending and gross private investment, increased 3.9 percent in the second quarter, compared with 1.7 percent in the first quarter.

“Underlying growth was strong,” said Eric Wallerstein, a former adviser at the Federal Reserve and the chief macro strategist at the Clocktower Group, an asset management and advisory firm. Still, he added, “real incomes and spending have been trending lower.”

Because G. D. P. is adjusted for inflation, rising costs dampened the growth reflected in the data released on Thursday. This was the first estimate for the second quarter by the U. S. Bureau of Economic Analysis. Revisions, conducted by civil servants at the agency, can be substantial, especially during periods of price volatility.

Data collected by Viresh Kanabar, a financial researcher, shows that business orders and expenditures are rising. Retail sales have also been strong for several months. But consumer purchases are also growing at a much softer pace when adjusted for inflation, Mr. Kanabar’s data shows. Over the past six months, he notes, “real” inflation-adjusted income has also fallen overall, and at a rate not seen since the height of the inflation spike in 2022.

G. D. P., in simplest terms, is an account of the exchange of goods and services in the economy. And G. D. P. growth is a fluctuating mix of four factors: business investment, government expenditures, net exports and household consumption, which typically constitutes about 70 percent of the U. S. economy.

Consumer spending and business investment are on solid footing, but a pullback in net government spending and an increase in imports dragged on momentum.

“It’s a chug-along economy until further notice,” said Dan Alpert, a senior fellow in macroeconomics at Cornell Law and managing partner at Westwood Capital, a financial firm.

Annual growth in gross domestic product was buoyed by spending and investment last quarter, which offset losses in trade and inventories.

Note: Data is contributions to quarterly change in real gross domestic product, adjusted for seasonality and inflation at annual rates.

Source: Bureau of Economic Analysis.

Ben Casselman/The New York Times

Earlier this month, the Trump administration imposed tariffs of 10 to 12 percent on imports from more than 80 countries. Economists have criticized the president’s global tariffs, and courts have struck many of them down.

Economists do not expect the tariffs that remain in place to cause a downturn. But many do believe it will slow growth and raise prices. According to one estimate by Yale researchers, the tax duties are costing the average American family around $1,100 annually.

Many business leaders have expressed confidence that the Iran conflict will stay contained, with limited harm to broader commercial activity. But the Strait of Hormuz, a key fuel bottleneck partially under Iran’s control, is still not a reliable passage for global shippers. Market analysts have issued stark warnings that international oil inventories are quickly depleting. So the risk of widespread shortages could soon be rearing again.

One partial saving grace has been that the domestic and global economies have become much less “energy intensive.” The amount of energy burned to generate a dollar of growth has fallen by about a third since 2000 in the United States and Europe and by roughly 40 percent in China. But lower crude inventories could still lead to an inflationary surge in oil prices that halts growth.

There is some evidence that the jump in energy prices has already bled into the rest of the economy. Grocery prices are expected to rise and airfares, which have surged, are not expected to retreat anytime soon.

Separate monthly data released on Thursday showed that the Federal Reserve’s preferred gauge of inflation actually fell 0.1 percent in June. That reflects the cool-off in oil prices in June. On an annual basis, inflation is still up 3.7 percent, well above the central bank’s long-run target of 2 percent. And inflation in the second quarter was especially high.

The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday. But three of the 12 members on the Fed’s policymaking committee dissented, voting to raise rates, a signal that pressure to contain inflation is mounting. Kevin M. Warsh, the Fed’s new chairman, has made stern pledges to curtail inflation. But he, like his predecessor, will also be weighing how tightening monetary policy could harm growth and the jobs market.

The labor market has stabilized this year, compared with 2025. The pace of payroll growth over the past three months has been uneven but averaged 111,000 jobs a month. That stabilization, some Fed observers say, gives Mr. Warsh and other Fed leaders room to raise rates without risking too much harm.

Yields on long-term bonds have risen recently, as investors worry that continually elevated inflation will erode the future value of some assets. Investors have been hand-wringing about a potential A. I. bubble. But stock indexes are up this year, and corporate earnings continue to outperform expectations.

According to FactSet, the S&P 500’s net profit margins are on track to rise to 16 percent in the latest quarter, the highest level since FactSet started tracking the metric in 2009. Economists are asking, with a mix of wonderment and anxiety, how closely tied the A. I. boom and G. D. P. growth could become.

Where the future returns on all this A. I. spending will come from remains a key question, as large companies leverage debt and billions of dollars in cash flow to follow through on investment commitments.

Search queries, business software applications and content streams on personal devices can seem to manifest with virtual effortlessness. But cloud computing and A. I. systems rely on a massive, energy-intensive infrastructure of chips, cables and cooling systems. And the growth of those underlying physical systems is central to the immense investment boom among businesses. Goldman Sachs estimates $765 billion in capital expenditures on artificial intelligence by the end of the year.

Brian LeBlanc, an economist and managing director at PNC Bank, notes that business “cap-ex” averaged an impressive 10 percent growth in the first half of the year alone. Because of some statistical quirks, however, the A. I. build-out — which relies on many imported foreign components rather than domestic parts — is partially tempering measures of domestic growth, too.

“From a G. D. P. math standpoint, a lot of the A. I.-related capital expenditure, which adds substantially to G. D. P., gets offset by the fact that we import most of what goes into the data centers,” said Jake Oubina, a managing director and deputy head of economic research at Piper Sandler, an investment firm.

Federal tax refunds, which bolstered households in spring, are now mostly exhausted. And with households’ savings buffers much lower than in the recent past, “consumption will be much weaker through the rest of the year,” Mr. Wallerstein of the Clocktower Group argued.

“Yes, the A. I. boom is not 100 percent of G. D. P.,” he said. “But it is an A. I.-driven economy.”

Who believes these numbers? Not me. We are actually in a recession right now and won't find out the truth for a while. Brace yourselves, it's going to be bad.

@Randall Hey there, thanks for reading! -- if or when there is any sign that the numbers have been monkeyed around with politically my colleagues who have been closely watching this stuff will let us know! For now, however, there's no clearly reportable evidence that today's numbers collected and organized by civil servants were messed with.

Talmon Joseph Smith is a Times economics reporter, based in New York.

Why Blanche Can’t Win Republican Approval for Attorney General — Yet

The New York Times July 30, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The decision by the acting attorney general, Todd Blanche, to grant President Trump protection from I. R. S. audits has become the central issue in his confirmation process.

By Andrew Duehren

Reporting from Washington

The acting Attorney General Todd Blanche’s quest to win Senate confirmation now hinges on the extraordinary protection from the Internal Revenue Service he granted President Trump.

That immunity was part of a deal orchestrated by the Justice Department to end the president’s lawsuit against the I. R. S. The other part of that deal, a $1.8 billion fund aimed at paying political allies of Mr. Trump, set off a political firestorm on Capitol Hill, and Mr. Blanche has since said that the so-called anti-weaponization fund is dead.

But the audit protection remains. Senators John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, both Republicans who sit on the Judiciary Committee, have so far refused to vote to advance Mr. Blanche’s nomination unless he pares back the I. R. S. deal. That forced Republicans to delay a committee vote on Mr. Blanche’s nomination.

Democrats and tax experts have excoriated the I. R. S. protection as a corrupt and illegal handout to Mr. Trump, who has aggressively avoided taxes and faced I. R. S. audits throughout his life. The stakes of Mr. Blanche’s confirmation fight are arguably symbolic, since Mr. Blanche is already acting as the attorney general and could continue to do so.

Mr. Trump, in a July 30 social media post, said he was considering pulling Mr. Blanche’s nomination and asking him to remain as the acting attorney general.

“I have no objection to temporarily withdrawing Todd’s name, if they do not do the right thing, and putting him back after Cornyn and Tillis are out of office,” the president wrote. Both Mr. Tillis and Mr. Cornyn will leave the Senate after this term.

Here’s an explanation of Mr. Blanche’s directive letting the president off the hook from the I. R. S. and the changes that the two holdouts have sought.

Mr. Blanche’s May 19 order, while just one page, is not straightforward, with its substance packed into a single rambling sentence that tax lawyers said was clearly not written by a practitioner.

But the upshot appears to be twofold. First, the I. R. S. has to drop any inquiries, whether civil audits or criminal investigations, it was pursuing into Mr. Trump, his family members, their companies or “affiliated individuals.” Second, the I. R. S. can’t start any new investigations into tax returns that this potentially large pool of people and companies has already filed.

That means that any tax maneuver the Trumps have already used, whether the I. R. S. was already auditing it or not, is now off limits. The agency typically has three years after someone files a tax return to assess more in taxes. So there are potential audits of Mr. Trump and his family that the I. R. S. could have initiated — claims that “could have been asserted,” in the language of Mr. Blanche’s order — that it is now not supposed to. But the next tax return that Mr. Trump files could, theoretically, still be eligible for an audit.

While Mr. Tillis and Mr. Cornyn have worked together, Mr. Cornyn has led the Republican criticisms of the audit protection deal. And rather than demanding that Mr. Blanche kill the provision entirely, he is asking that the Justice Department narrow it.

“The scope of the release is really the problem,” Mr. Cornyn told reporters.

Mr. Cornyn said he wanted Mr. Blanche to formally state, in writing, that the audit protection only applies to the people and entities involved in the original lawsuit against the I. R. S. That included Mr. Trump, two of his sons and the Trump Organization. The current language of Mr. Blanche’s order is much broader, potentially granting protection to other members of Mr. Trump’s family, as well as to any companies or people affiliated with them.

Mr. Cornyn also wants clarifications that the order would only apply to previous tax returns and disputes with the I. R. S., not to future ones, and that it only protects Mr. Trump from the I. R. S., not other federal agencies.

“It’s simple; they could state that in a modified release form, and that would be responsive to my request,” Mr. Cornyn said.

During his confirmation hearing, Mr. Blanche, in response to questions from Mr. Cornyn, said that the protection was retroactive, only applied to the I. R. S. and was limited to the parties in Mr. Trump’s lawsuit. But so far he has not formally amended his May 19 order in writing.

Even if Mr. Blanche formally narrows the I. R. S. protection as Mr. Cornyn has demanded, it would remain extremely unusual, if not without precedent. The I. R. S.’s previous approach to the occupant of the Oval Office had been to audit his tax return every year, regardless of who is president, a practice that it developed amid concerns that it had not properly scrutinized Richard Nixon. The I. R. S. has historically sought to avoid the appearance that it gives special treatment to the rich and powerful.

“Narrowing who’s covered by the unprecedented audit exemption for the president would not fix its fundamental flaws,” said Brandon DeBot, policy director of the New York University Tax Law Center.

Mr. Blanche, Mr. Trump’s former personal lawyer, has cast Mr. Trump’s immunity as a typical part of how the I. R. S. settles disputes. It is true that the I. R. S. may agree to halt audits as part of a deal to resolve a disagreement over how much tax someone owes.

But such a deal would ordinarily apply only to the specific tax issues under review. Mr. Blanche’s order, on the other hand, applies to a nondescript set of “matters pending or that could be pending.”

Not to mention that the lawsuit Mr. Trump filed against the I. R. S. did not deal with a tax controversy or audit. Mr. Trump’s suit instead accused the agency of not doing enough to prevent the leak of his tax returns during his first term, a separate category of complaint that, under federal law, can result in monetary damages. There were several possible defenses against Mr. Trump’s case that the Justice Department did not raise, even though lawyers at the I. R. S. recommended that it do so.

It may not be. No one from the I. R. S. put a signature to the one-page order for the audit protections, a contrast to the document creating the now-defunct $1.8 billion fund, which was signed by the chief executive officer of the I. R. S.

Only Mr. Blanche signed the audit order. The I. R. S. reports to the Treasury Department, not Mr. Blanche, and several lawyers have questioned whether the attorney general has the authority to direct how the tax agency conducts audits. The I. R. S. has not responded to questions about whether it has followed Mr. Blanche’s order.

Then there is the federal law that prohibits the president and his aides from directing I. R. S. investigations, though the statute includes an apparent carve out for the attorney general. Any official who carries out an order from the White House to start or stop an audit could potentially go to prison if, for example, a future administration were to investigate that person.

In a 56-page ruling, Kathleen M. Williams, a federal judge in Miami, wrote that Mr. Blanche’s order “directly contravenes” the law prohibiting political direction of I. R. S. audits.

But her order was focused on Mr. Trump’s underlying lawsuit against the I. R. S. She found that Mr. Trump had brought his lawsuit in a bad-faith attempt to wring public benefits out of the government. She barred Mr. Trump from referring to the audit immunity as a component of a “settlement” to the suit. But she noted that she was not ruling on its legality more broadly.

“Whether executive branch actors can privately agree to give themselves and their former clients blanket immunities and billions of dollars in tax monies for legally undefined grievances was never an issue advanced to this court,” she wrote.

It’s hard to know exactly. Tax information, including the status or existence of audits, is confidential under federal law — Mr. Trump’s suit against the I. R. S. was, after all, over the disclosure of his tax returns.

But there’s reason to think Mr. Trump could save a lot of money, even with Mr. Cornyn’s requested modifications. The New York Times has previously reported that just one audit of Mr. Trump could have resulted in a bill exceeding $100 million. Mr. Trump used to frequently complain that the I. R. S. always audited him, and a congressional report in 2022 showed that the agency had major questions about his returns.

The audit protections arrived after a banner year for Mr. Trump financially. His most recent financial disclosure showed him bringing in at least $2.2 billion last year, though it is unclear how much of that would be taxable income. Those earnings may still be subject to audit depending on when Mr. Trump files his tax return.

Andrew Duehren covers tax policy for The Times from Washington.

Attacks on Smithsonian

Connections Coach

Kim Sajet left as director of the National Portrait Gallery when she found herself in the White House cross hairs. Now she’s watching another Smithsonian chief go through it.

Last year, Kim Sajet of the National Portrait Gallery was targeted by President Trump, who described her as “highly partisan.” “I could see that it was going to become a real witch hunt,” she said of resigning. Credit... Taylor Glascock for The New York Times

Supported by

By Robin Pogrebin

After work one day last week, Kim Sajet sat down at her computer with a cup of coffee to watch a former Smithsonian colleague, Anthea M. Hartig, director of the National Museum of American History, testify before a congressional panel.

The White House had just released a scathing report that accused Ms. Hartig and the museum she leads of downplaying the role of the nation’s founders while promoting “extreme political activism.”

Now Ms. Hartig was under fire from Republican lawmakers who embraced the White House’s findings.

“Who gave you the authority to turn the National Museum of American History into a vehicle for progressive political activism?” asked one lawmaker.

“When was your gender revealed to you?,” asked another, disturbed by a museum exhibition about girlhood that explored identity issues.

“I was incredulous,” Ms. Sajet recalled in an interview. “Really? The president of the United States is spending his time going after a museum director? I would’ve thought he had more pressing matters to attend to.”

Ms. Sajet (pronounced SAY-et) understands Ms. Hartig’s situation on a personal level. Last year she was targeted by President Trump, who described her as “highly partisan” and directed she be fired from her post as director of the Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery. The Smithsonian, which has long operated independently of the executive branch, asserted its legal authority over personnel, but Ms. Sajet still chose to resign.

“I could see that it was going to become a real witch hunt,” she said. “I didn’t wish that on my colleagues and I didn’t wish that on the Smithsonian.”

These days, Ms. Sajet is far from Washington, having last fall accepted a position as director of the Milwaukee Art Museum. But there is perhaps no more interested observer of the administration's pressure campaign on the Smithsonian than she because she bears the scars.

She is not, however, the first Smithsonian director to ever come under fire. The head of the National Air and Space Museum, for example, was ultimately forced to resign after a 1995 exhibition on the Enola Gay B-29 warplane that dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima. Some viewed the exhibit as too critical of American’s use of atomic weapons to end World War II.

Still, the scrutiny of Ms. Hartig and Ms Sajet has been of a different order of magnitude. For one thing it’s been directed, not by a variety of external critics, but by the White House. In addition, it’s been uncommonly personal. The White House report issued on July 4 mentioned Ms. Hartig more than 200 times.

“There is something unusual about the vitriol that was so personally directed,” said Steven Conn, a professor at Miami University who focuses on American intellectual and cultural history.

The White House did not respond directly to Ms. Sajet’s remarks but Vince Haley, who helped direct the administration’s report, reiterated its objections to the way history is presented there, asserting in a statement that the museum had become “an instrument of ideological activism and advocacy.”

“During this 250th anniversary year of our heroic founding,” he added, “the least our citizens are owed is an honest and inspiring account of American history.”

Ms. Hartig, who earns about $370,000 a year in her Smithsonian role, declined to comment. But during the hearings, which took place last week before two separate congressional panels, she defended her tenure, her museum and herself.

“As a historian, I have spent my career studying, teaching and preserving the history of the United States,” she said in her opening remarks before each committee. “My family has served this nation since the Revolutionary War and I was raised with a deep sense of obligation to it and the democratic ideals that the country asks each generation to build and to uphold.”

Ms. Sajet said that, in watching, she saw irony in the fact that the sessions were called hearings, “but the legislators were not listening.”

She pointed to the intensity with which some legislators pushed Ms. Hartig to give only yes or no answers. Scholarship, she said, is considerably more complex.

“Wouldn’t it be lovely if history was that black and white?” Ms. Sajet said. “There is always nuance. But they don’t want to hear the context. They want the sound bite, they want to get the score.”

Mike Gonzalez, a senior fellow at the Heritage Foundation who has written critically about the Smithsonian and appeared at both hearings, suggested in his testimony that the White House effort was not aimed at individuals as much as a way of thinking that had overtaken its museum leaders.

“Teaching lessons about American wickedness is now the mission of the Smithsonian,” he said in his testimony, adding, “You need to clean house and relieve all Smithsonian leadership of their duties.”

In an interview he disagreed with the suggestion that the questioning by lawmakers had been objectionable. “Some questions are ‘yes’ and ‘no,’” he said.

He cited, for example, a moment when Ms. Hartig was asked “if topics on sexuality are suitable for kids” while an image of a crotch harness from a past exhibition on gay history was displayed.

“Should children have access to depraved sexual content?,” he said, roughly paraphrasing several of the questions that Ms. Hartig faced. “The answer is ‘no’ always. I don’t see how you can equivocate on that one.”

Overall, Mr. Gonzalez said, “The hearings did a very good job of exploring this issue.”

“She is accountable to the American taxpayer,” he added, “and the elected representatives of the American people have the right to ask her questions about what she has done.”

Just days after the hearings, President Trump — in an unusual directive — ordered warning signs and exhibits installed outside the American history museum to alert the public that the museum does not, in his view, accurately reflect American history.

It was the latest salvo in his effort to transform the Smithsonian, which he accused in an executive order last year of undermining “the remarkable achievements of the United States by casting its founding principles and historical milestones in a negative light.”

In pursuing its effort to terminate Ms. Sajet, the White House had created a list of grievances that it suggested made her an inappropriate choice to lead a national museum, including public comments about racial and gender inequality in America.

The intensity of the president’s focus on the Smithsonian is a departure from prior administrations, though political operatives for President Nixon are said to have pressured the institution into closing an exhibition on voting rights ahead of the 1973 inaugural ball.

The Trump White House has on several occasions pointed out that the Smithsonian relies on federal sources for most of its $1 billion budget and that the money should be spent in ways that are aligned with Mr. Trump’s policies. Ms. Sajet said that her departure was spurred in part by the administration’s threat to withdraw Smithsonian funding.

While no cultural institution is perfect, Ms. Sajet said, in general the Smithsonian’s 21 museums have sought to provide the public with comprehensive information, informed by multiple perspectives, deep research and scholarship. She said she found the White House report, which accused the history museum of failing to properly celebrate the achievements of men like George Washington and Benjamin Franklin, to be “cherry picked” and “biased.”

“The Museum of American History doesn’t make the history — they’re just reporting on what’s happened,” she said. “That’s what I did as the director of the Portrait Gallery. We didn’t say whether so-and-so’s actions were good or bad. We just said, ‘This is what they did.’”

She cited Abraham Lincoln and, yes, she said, he united the union, but she said he was also slow to end slavery.

“I always said that there is no moral test to be in the Portrait Gallery,” she continued.

Ultimately, Ms. Sajet said, what happens to the Smithsonian is up to the American people. “The overarching thing we’ve all got to ask ourselves is, do we want politicians deciding how history is taught and understood?" she said. “Is that the role of government — to control what we learn about the past and ourselves? I would suggest it’s not.”

Ms. Sajet said she thought Ms. Hartig “did the best that she could” under difficult circumstances.

“Anyone who’s been in public office will attest that there is always this balance of responding in a way that then doesn’t become additional fuel,” she said. “You want to be careful that your answer doesn’t make it worse.”

She said she reached out to Ms. Hartig by text after the hearings with words of support to this effect: “My heart is with you. I’ve been thinking about you. You did great. Take care of yourself.”

“Having to sit for congressional testimony,” she later noted, “is not what you expect when you apply for the job.”

When Anthea M. Hartig, director of the Smithsonian National Museum of American History, testified before Congress last week, one person watched the hearings with particular interest: Kim Sajet, who resigned as director of the Smithsonian National Portrait Gallery after Trump directed that she be fired. I caught up with Sajet to see what she made of it.

Robin Pogrebin, who has been a reporter for The Times for more than 30 years, covers arts and culture.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

“Healthy” confections, whether marketed as “better-for-you” or “functional,” have overwhelmed grocery and convenience stores, and even found their way into gyms and supplement shops.

Words like “superfood” are popping up on candy packaging in an appeal to consumers who want to optimize all facets of their diet. Credit... Scott Semler for The New York Times

Supported by

By Ella Quittner

In early May, Chelsea McPherson was ecstatic when she entered the Trader Joe’s in Orem, Utah, and spotted a display of sweet and sour gummy worms. She’d been looking for the new product for three days. She grabbed two packages.

“Immediately, the cashier’s eyes got really big,” said Ms. McPherson, 38.

Trader Joe’s lists resistant tapioca dextrin fiber as the candy’s first ingredient. An eight-piece serving contains only 35 calories but packs 14 grams of fiber. “If you didn’t know, and you ate a whole bag,” the cashier had warned her, “you’d probably be in trouble.’”

Rather than run screaming from the store, Ms. McPherson was thrilled. She immediately opened a package in her car but limited herself to just a couple of worms — to make sure they didn’t make her “regret her choices,” she said. But Ms. McPherson, a stay-at-home mother of five, loved them so much, she has since bought them dozens of times and keeps a package on her bedside table.

The gummies are just one example of candies marketed as “healthy” that are overwhelming shop aisles and social media feeds with promises of recognizable ingredients, less sugar or nutritional benefits. Diet candy, whether described as “better-for-you” or “functional,” has transcended the grocery and convenience store and found its way into gyms and supplement shops, blurring the line between protein bar and indulgence.

It was the cheerful red packaging of Tandy Chocolate’s Protein NomNoms that first caught the eye of Zack Baker, 33, as he shopped in a Harrisonburg, Va., Costco — that, and the word “protein” in uppercase letters.

Over the last few years, he has endeavored to rewire his candy habits. He’s tried Rotten “Gummy Cruncheez” — “healthier Nerds gummies,” as he described them — made from soluble vegetable fiber, allulose (a low-calorie sweetener) and a host of other ingredients that warrant an explanation from Bill Nye. He’s tried Better Sour gummy stars, which come in flavors like passion fruit, guava and calamansi lime. And he’s tried Hormbles Chormbles, a “protein candy” Willy Wonka might manufacture if he got really into creatine.

Mr. Baker’s bulk bag of Protein NomNoms, for its part, was gone within a week.

The trickle-down effects of the Make America Healthy Again doctrine and the ubiquity of GLP-1s have inspired many consumers’ shifting habits toward “functional” candy, sweets purporting to offer some added benefit. And given the online explosion of often-dubious nutrition advice, many Americans believe they’re not doing enough for their health, said Lisa Moskovitz, a dietitian and the owner of New York Nutrition Group. “People become more desperate for quick solutions to why they’re feeling the way they are,” she said.

Functional candy that offers a benefit like added protein, Ms. Moskovitz said, may be less easy to digest than, say, the naturally occurring protein in chicken. And, she added, one must consider what nutrients are being missed when consuming protein candy over a protein-packed whole food. “The concern I have comes from: Is this going to be looked at as a healthy snack?” she said. “The reality is, no. Whole foods have way more nutritional value.”

Pop Up Grocer, a shop in the West Village of Manhattan, specializes in consumer packaged goods aimed at health-conscious shoppers and carries a variety of diet candy. America’s pervasive obsession with diet and longevity has coincided with the “K-shaped” economy, a bifurcation of wealth and spending, to position these alternative sweets as “accessible luxury goods,” as Emily Schildt, the store’s founder, put it.

For some, that transforms candy from a mindless habit to a matter of identity. Pop Up Grocer’s candy is both “indulgent” and “little-treat priced,” she said, which encourages customers to be thoughtful in their selection. “If you’re going to buy something from my store at a premium price point, you’re probably going to want to share it and talk about it, so it’s like, ‘What is the product I want to buy that says something about me?’”

Before the onslaught of “functional candy,” there was “better-for-you” candy in spades.

Better-for-you brands like Unreal Snacks have appealed to the bulk bin set for at least a decade. The company’s most popular product, a dark chocolate coconut candy bar, has just three ingredients that even a Victorian boy might make sense of: organic coconut, organic cassava syrup and dark chocolate. SmartSweets, which advertises an absence of artificial sweeteners, soon followed with products on the gummy and sour sides of the confection spectrum.

“The American consumer has continued to demand more and better of their food and beverage purchases, especially over the last five years,” said Kevin McCarthy, the chief executive of Unreal Snacks.

Eventually, legacy candy caught up. In 2021, the Hershey Company acquired Lily’s, a low-sugar chocolate brand, and announced a relaunch of sugar-free Reese’s peanut butter cups, Twizzlers and other candies with the goal of meeting the needs of diabetic customers.

“The low-sugar approach felt like it was only half of the story,” said Jared Smith, a founder of Hormbles Chormbles. Mr. Smith, 40, was also a creator of the protein-bar company RXBar, which sold to Kellogg for $600 million in 2017. While hawking whole-food protein bars, he still found himself reaching for the nutritionally vacuous snacks of his youth. The Hormbles Chormbles customer base is skewed toward Gen-Z and millennial women, he said, as well as GLP-1 users and protein-maxxers who encounter the product at their gyms.

After seeing Hormbles Chormbles all over social media, Mary-Reagan Keeter, a Gen-Z woman, finally grabbed a bar at a Target in Mount Pleasant, S. C., despite a bit of sticker shock. A 1.05-ounce peanut butter crunch bar, which contains 10 grams of protein and zero grams of sugar, retails for $3.29 at Target. com. (A 1.55-ounce bar of Hershey’s milk chocolate is more than $1 less.)

Ms. Keeter, 24, works in social media advertising and credits much of this candy aisle renaissance to the proliferation of gym culture online. “Seeing all these influencers and famous people get onto the red carpet and look stick-thin,” she said, “will make you think a lot when you’re going into the grocery store to pick out a treat.”

Ms. McPherson, the mother in Utah, has amassed a trove of the Trader Joe’s fiber gummy worms to tide her over until the company restocks them later this summer. More than anything, she said, diet candy is simply fun. “If I find a joyful gummy or chocolate bar,” she said, “I’m like, ‘Absolutely.’ There should be moments of little joy every day.”

It Looks Like Nothing Can Dent MAGA’s Support for ICE

Wired July 29, 2026

On Tuesday, the day after hundreds of thousands of Haitian migrants effectively lost their temporary protected status that allowed them to live and work in the US, Republican pundit Steve Bannon wasted little time in demanding their instant removal.

“I was under the assumption that when they pulled TPS and their eligibility for that program ended … they were going to be boarding planes or buses today … today, this morning at dawn to go back to Haiti,” said Bannon, a longtime ally of President Donald Trump, on his War Room podcast on Tuesday. “Why are they not out of the country?”

Mike Davis, a conservative political strategist agreed with Bannon: “The solution is to get these people the hell out of our country as fast as possible, and that includes these Haitians.”

White nationalist Nick Fuentes, who has been a vocal critic of Trump’s deportation policies because he doesn’t find them extreme enough, called Haitians “the worst of the worst” and “very low IQ people” on his Rumble show Tuesday night.

In a Telegram channel run by the Proud Boys of Columbus, one member posted a clip of the song “I’m Walking on Sunshine” alongside the news about the revoking of temporary protected status. “They gotta go back,” the member wrote.

It’s been a while since shock-and-awe tactics from Immigration and Customs Enforcement first gained national notoriety. For months, figures like former Border Patrol leader Greg Bovino terrorized cities like Minneapolis and Chicago. But since replacing former Department of Homeland Security secretary Kristi Noem with Markwayne Mullin—derisively referred to by Bannon as the “Kung fu plumber”—ICE’s operations have shrunk into the shadows, though the agency’s deportation and arrest numbers have remained astronomical.

In recent weeks, things are boiling over again.

Earlier this month, an ICE agent shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas. Araujo had lived in the country for 35 years, had three children, and owned his own business. Just days later, another ICE agent killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine. Both men were shot while in their vehicles. ICE, as WIRED has revealed, is also tracking its critics online, using data brokers to “identify unaccompanied minors,” and working to prevent state health inspectors from reviewing its network of detention centers. On Tuesday, The New York Times reported that the Trump administration was now targeting immigrants at airports whose visas have expired, or are in a transition status, arresting spouses of American citizens.

Even so, Steve Bannon and the other Republican pundits aren’t alone: Support for ICE among Trump’s most loyal supporters remains incredibly high, with 74 percent of people who identify as MAGA Republicans professing confidence in ICE, according to a YouGov poll published last week. The same poll shows that 80 percent of MAGA Republicans oppose abolishing ICE.

The YouGov findings were backed up by another poll published last week by the Public Religion Research Institute , which found that three-quarters of Republicans had a positive view of ICE, would be in favor of more funding for the agency, and disagreed that ICE was making communities less safe. The poll also found that 73 percent of Republicans are in support of internment camps to hold “immigrants who are in the country illegally” until they can be deported.

The YouGov poll also found that just 51 percent of Republicans had, in the week of the shootings, read, seen, or heard anything about immigrants being shot and killed by ICE agents. What they may have seen however is Trump’s Truth Social post around the same time. In the post, Trump appeared to overrule an internal ICE memo telling agents to suspend vehicle stops, after a furious response from his MAGA base. He also told his supporters that ICE was “loved and respected in America.”

Much of his base thinks that deportations are actually not happening fast enough. ICE is on track to deport 458,000 individuals this year according to its own data, a colossal figure that still falls well short of the 1 million deportations Trump promised shortly after his inauguration. (This, in the words of border czar Tom Homan, is what the administration calls “deportation-maxxing.”)

Americans have been caught in the dragnet as well, as ICE’s actions have resulted in widespread civil rights violations, according to a report published this month by the American Civil Liberties Union, which found that across eight states, ICE agents targeted 155 US citizens, 32 of whom were children, during the first year of Trump’s second term. Previous research from UC Berkeley found that half of all the people ICE has arrested had no criminal records, despite the administration claiming to be deporting the “worst of the worst.” Federal agents have shot and killed four people, including two US citizens.

On the other hand, the majority of Americans believe ICE has used too much force, according to YouGov, and as a result have little or no confidence in the agency. Almost half of Americans believe it's time for ICE to be abolished.

What these polls show is that while America as a whole is rejecting Trump’s immigration policies, his base is almost completely supportive. And rather than distancing themselves from ICE’s actions, Republicans seem to be leaning in again, even spending more money and running more ads about immigration than Democrats, NPR reported last week.

With just months left before the midterms offer voters a chance to have their say on these policies, Republicans are gambling that their base doesn’t actually want ICE going anywhere. In November, the country will see if they’re right.

Which of Dyson’s 2026 Stick Vacuums Is Worth the Upgrade?

Wired July 29, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Dyson's vacuum lineup has a whole new look these days, but that doesn't necessarily make it easier to decide if you're looking to buy one.

The Dyson V16 Piston Animal ($980), V10 Konical ($500), and V8 Cyclone ($400) arrived to change up Dyson's cordless vacuum options. The older V15 Detect ($650) and Gen5Detect ($800) are also still available and great vacuums, which raises the question: Should you upgrade? Which Dyson model is worth the cash with so many options (and widely ranging price points) to choose from?

I tested all five of these vacuums against each other in a series of tests to see which ones stood out among the pack. The two overall winners? The Gen5Detect was the number one winner, with the V16 Piston Animal right behind it, and the V10 Konical coming up third even though it's a much cheaper option. Read on to find out which model did best in each test, what the stats look like for each Dyson vacuum, and how I scored the final results.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Amazon

Amazon

Dyson

Dyson's naming convention is fun, and the numbers usually represent which models are more powerful or offer better accessories, but not always. Most of its vacuums have the V name, which, to my best guess, simply stands for “vacuum.” The numbers aren't always in order of release and usually reflect a vacuum's power level and capabilities. The V10 and V8 have the same power level but different heads, for example, while the V16 is more powerful than the V15. But not all vacuums are named the same; the Gen5Detect has a different name entirely, and falls in between the V15 and V16 when it comes to suction power and price tag.

Here's a quick chart to understand the power levels and compatible accessories that differentiate each vacuum from the other. You might also spot things like “Plus” or “Total” when you're shopping for a Dyson vacuum, and that usually reflects the attachments included with the vacuum.

This gives you a pretty easy look at what you're getting for each model. As the models increase in number (both in the name and in the price tag), the vacuum usually gains more accessories or cleaner heads, more air watts of suction power, and sometimes the option to add the Submarine wet cleaner head on for an additional price, or future compatibility with Dyson's Auto-empty Dok station that's coming out soon.

The Digital Motorbar and All Floor Cones cleaner heads are both compatible with soft and hard floors, which is why sometimes it's the only head included. More expensive Dyson models will also include the Fluffy Optic cleaner head, which is designed specifically for hard floors and has an illuminated light to help you spot dust and debris. The All Floor Cones cleaner head includes a light too, so you're able to get that feature on both the V16 and V10 without switching heads.

Here are the tests I ran for each vacuum, and which ones did best—and worst.

The V10 Konical and the sand obstacle.

After one pass of the V10, only a few thin lines remained of sand, the best results of these five vacuums on this rug.

BEST: V10 Konical ($500)

WORST: V8 Cyclone ($400)

I tested all five Dyson models on a small black rug onto which I poured fine, white sand to see how well it was vacuumed up. The best was the V10 Konical, followed by the V15 Detect. Both left a small trail of sand behind in different spots, which makes sense since they have different head designs, but the V10's trail was smaller than the V15's, with a small line in the middle compared to the larger trail the V15 had on its right side.

The V8, meanwhile, stalled entirely when I tried to use it on the rug and couldn't vacuum up sand whatsoever. It weirdly seemed to have an issue with the thin rug, even though equally or more powerful vacuums were able to vacuum on it.

Both Gen5Detect and V16 Piston Animal were able to vacuum on the thin rug, but the stronger suction also kept trying to take the rug with it, giving both mixed results and leaving a lot of sand behind on each pass. I retested both of these on a thicker rug in case the suction level wasn't a match for the thin rug, and both did much better, but the Gen5Detect did the best, getting every bit of sand in one swoop. The V16 got most of its sand, but pushed some sand into a little pile in front of itself.

The Gen5Detect and the Cheerios obstacle.

After one pass of the Gen5Detect, it only missed Cheerios that were out of its cleaner head range and didn't send any pieces flying.

BEST: Gen5Detect ($800)

WORST: None

When I last did a cereal test, I used a cornflake-style cereal. This time I switched to the cereal I know many parents like myself are much more likely to have all over the floors: Cheerios. I crushed up several in my hand and dropped those along with full Cheerios onto my thicker living room rug. Overall, every Dyson did a good job cleaning this up on the first pass.

The results on this one had pretty minimal differences for these models. The V8, V10, and V15 Detect all usually got the Cheerios and pieces on the first run, sending one to three pieces flying while it did so, but not so far away you wouldn't get to vacuum them up. The Gen5Detect sent nothing flying, though, so it pulls slightly ahead. The V16 sent only a single tiny piece flying forward. But it was right behind the Gen5Detect out of these Dyson models.

The V16 Piston Animal and the litter obstacle.

After one pass of the V16, the only litter left behind was out of the cleaner head range. It did create a thin pile of litter in front of itself as it went, which was vacuumed before moving the head back to the start point to check if any litter had been missed.

BEST: Gen5Detect ($800)

WORST: V8 Cyclone ($400)

Next, I tested these vacuums against a thing I vacuum the most off my vinyl plank floors: cat litter. For this test, since it was on a hard surface instead of a rug, I switched the vacuums' heads to the Fluffy Optic cleaner head when available. That's only on the V15, V16, and Gen5Detect, so those heads changed while the other two models still used the Digital Motorbar (V8) or the All Floor Cones (V10) heads they came with.

It's no surprise that the two standouts both had a Fluffy Optic head. The Gen5Detect left the cleanest floor behind, with not a spec of litter dust to be found from the vacuum's illuminated light after a single pass. The V16 Piston Animal mostly did well, leaving no litter behind, but it did push a small amount of litter in front of itself, similar to the sand test. This only happened in a pass of extremely thick litter, so more day-to-day litter cleanup shouldn't have this issue. Still, the Gen5Detect pulls slightly ahead once again.

The V15 is right behind these two, but left a little dust behind that I could see with the Fluffy Optic's headlight (though no large pieces, and it looked just as clean to the naked eye). Meanwhile, the V10 Konical did fine enough, but needed two passes to get all the debris. The V8 landed last after it pulled a similar move when vacuuming sand and simply pushed the litter into a pile in front of itself, so I then had to move the vacuum on top of and around to vacuum it up, and it took a few passes to do so.

The V16 Piston Animal in handheld mode with the All Floor Cones Sense cleaner head attached.

The V16 Piston Animal without the cleaner head and only the built-in crevice tool on the handheld motor.

BEST: V16 Piston Animal ($980) and Gen5Detect ($800)

WORST: V15 Detect ($650)

Dyson's vacuums function nicely as a handheld vacuum, no matter the model. I tested all five models on my carpeted stairs, and I'd recommend any one of them if that's a big use in your household. The V16 and Gen5Detect pull ahead for me because you can really feel the higher suction at work when you're in handheld mode, and both vacuums showed serious results afterward of dustbins filled with new hair and dust. Especially as a cat owner and a parent of a small child, the carpeted stairs around my house have a lot of debris worked into them. Plus, both of these vacuums have built-in crevice tools you can use in handheld mode, but the V16's will always stay attached, while you need to remove the Gen5's to attach the head directly to the handheld motor.

The V15 also did a fine job, but it felt like it was gliding over my stairs rather than locking into the carpet like the other Dyson vacuums. Even the V8 and V10 with lower power levels felt more suctioned into my carpet than the V15 did for me during my handheld stair testing. Both those cheaper models fell into the runner-up range for me with this test.

The Gen5Detect on my rug.

BEST: Gen5Detect ($800) and V10 Konical ($500)

WORST: V15 Detect ($650)

Originally, I tested an early release version of the V16 Piston Animal that had some clogging issues on carpet. But after getting a current release model, the V16 did much better overall. Both the V16 and the Gen5Detect did an impressive job on my carpets and rugs, and pulled an impressive amount of cat hair and dust out of my recently vacuumed carpets. These both have different heads, but the powerful suction really comes into play on carpet more than anywhere else, especially if you have pets.

Meanwhile, the V10 Konical has the All Floor Cones cleaner head that glided nicely on carpet. The V10's head was a little easier to push around than the Digital Motorbar head (which both the V8 and V15 have) on rugs. The V8 Cyclone took the most effort to push around on my rug, but moved much better on carpet.

The V15 Detect was similar, but unlike the rest of these vacuums, it has a trigger button instead of a power button. That means you have to keep that engaged the entire time when doing a longer vacuuming session. The rest of these vacuums have a power button you click instead, so I don't love the trigger for longer vacuuming sessions. If you're a big vacuumer or have a home with a large amount of carpet, you're going to want a power button, and likely one of the higher-suction vacuums.

(L to R) V10 Konical, Gen5Detect, and V16 Piston Animal.

The results, as you can tell above, are a little murky. The higher-suction vacuums usually took home the prize in most categories, but the V10 Konical was a surprisingly solid all-around performer. To find my winner, I put all of my tests and Dyson models into a chart and scored them on a 1 to 4 point scale, allowing 4 points if the vacuum did the best, 1 if the worst, and a 2 or 3 depending on how middle-of-the-road the results were. One vacuum had a nice lead with a near-perfect score of 19 points.

Dyson

Amazon

Wayfair

The biggest standout from these tests was the Gen5Detect. It came out of these tests with a near-perfect score after the five rounds of testing. It does a great job with its level of powerful suction, and it transitions well between most kinds of debris. As a pet owner, I especially like it for carpet, since the 280 air watts do a great job pulling out hair and pet dander from deep in the carpet. I've actually filled up this vacuum's debris tank before after vacuuming only a few days before with a weaker option.

It's one of the most expensive for a reason, and comes with more attachments than any other model. I do find myself regularly grabbing the Fluffy Optic head for vacuuming my hard floors, which cover many square feet of my home. If you're looking to really splurge on the best vacuum, this is still the one to get.

The only downside is compatibility with Dyson's bigger attachments, namely a mop head or docking station. It doesn't have a Submarine option like the V16 or V15, and Dyson's Auto-empty Dok won't work with this model. But if you aren't worried about add-ons, this is the vacuum to buy. It's had better sales since the launch of the new models, too.

Dyson

Amazon

Amazon (Submarine)

Dyson

Dyson (Submarine)

The V16 Piston Animal's powerful 315 air watts of suction did pretty well on almost every test. My only issue with this vacuum compared to the Gen5Detect is that it was more likely to push small debris (in my tests, both sand and litter) into a pile in front of itself if you were vacuuming a large spill. Gen5Detect did better all around, but the V16 Piston Animal stayed close behind that hiccup.

It's a powerful all-around vacuum with some nice design upgrades to make it a little easier to use. This newer model has a release below the vacuum motor to release the cleaner head without having to bend down, and built-in crevice tools to both the handheld motor and the long wand that makes up the middle of the device. There's also a compressor to help push dust out of the dustbin, and it'll be compatible with Dyson's upcoming self-emptying docking station. There's also a Submarine version ($1,100) so you can use this vacuum as a mop, too.

It has some nice quality-of-life upgrades, but it's really expensive. I'd recommend it if you know you also want to invest in the mop head and docking station; otherwise, just get the Gen5Detect.

Dyson

Dyson

Dyson

Best Buy

One of the best overall performers is nearly half the price of my winners. The Dyson V10 Konical never once scored in last place, and was especially comfortable to use on carpets and rugs with the new cleaner head design. It did much better than the more expensive and powerful Gen5Detect and V15 Detect when vacuuming up sand, and I found it more comfortable to push around than the Digital Motorbar head on the V15 and V8 when it came to vacuuming a low-pile rug.

It didn't do as well on hard floors, but it didn't do poorly, either. This cheaper model comes with just the single head, but if you don't want to spend the better part of a grand, I'd rather only have this head than the Digital Motorbar head. The All Floor Cones cleaner head also has a built-in light, which you won't get on cheaper or older models. Plus, it'll be compatible with the self-emptying docking station Dyson has coming out soon. For the price point, it's a fantastic buy.

V10 Konical with the Auto-emptying Dok.

BEST: V16 Piston Animal Submarine ($1,100) and V10 Konical with Auto-empty Dok ($650)

WORST: V8 Cyclone ($400) and Gen5Detect ($800)

I'm putting this section after the testing because if you're just looking for a good vacuum, this might not be relevant for you. But there are some interesting upgrades with certain Dyson models you might want to consider, which might sway you toward a certain model over the testing aspects—like if you want a stick vacuum that can work with a self-emptying docking station, or one that can double as a mop. Not all of Dyson's vacuums can do these things, but some of them can—and one can do both.

Both the V16 Piston Animal and the V15 Detect have a Submarine variant (that retail for $1,100 and $750, respectively) that will give you the Submarine head along with the rest of the vacuum accessories. They have slightly different designs, but both are a wet roller head that stores both clean and dirty water while being powered by the motor in the rest of the vacuum. Former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So loved the Submarine version of the V15, and I've been really impressed by the V16's version as well.

If you hate emptying your cordless vacuum, there's an add-on for that, too. You can buy the V10 Konical now with Dyson's new Auto-emptying Dok that can hold up to 60 days of debris. It's a great add-on I've tried with other vacuums like Shark and Tineco and loved because it keeps my vacuum charged and upright, and it stores accessories as well. Dyson has mentioned launching one of these for the V16 in the future, but I'm not sure when that could come to fruition.

If I were to assign points based on these, the V16 Piston Animal ties with the Gen5Detect after getting its add-on while the Gen5Detect has none since it has neither of these additions, and once its own docking station arrives it would pull into first. The V10 Konical remains close behind. It's up to you whether these add-ons make it worth buying, or if you want to choose the models that actually performed best for what you need vacuumed most.
